115357.q: What did Lise Meitner study in Vienna, even though this was very rare for women at the time?
115357.e: Meitner studied physics in Vienna and got her doctorate there in 1906. She was one of the first women with a doctorate in physics.
115357.m: Lise Meitner was one of the first women physicists.

115358.q: Lise Meitner did research for decades with the chemist Otto Hahn. What did they work on?
115358.e: The two studied radioactive substances in Berlin. In the end, this led them to nuclear fission.

115359.q: Which process was Lise Meitner the first to explain in terms of physics, in 1939?
115359.e: Meitner realised that a uranium nucleus breaks into two medium-sized nuclei when hit by neutrons. A great deal of energy is released.

115360.q: Why did Lise Meitner have to flee from Germany in 1938?
a: She was persecuted because of her Jewish background
She wanted to travel round the world
115360.e: After Austria was annexed, she was regarded as Jewish in Germany and was in danger. With the help of colleagues she managed to escape.
115360.m: Lise Meitner fled from persecution by the Nazis.

115361.q: Lise Meitner found refuge in Stockholm in 1938. Which country is this city in?
115361.e: Stockholm is the capital of Sweden. Meitner continued working at a research institute there.
115361.m: Lise Meitner found refuge in Sweden.

115362.q: Which chemical element is named after Lise Meitner?
115362.e: Meitnerium has the atomic number 109 and is only made artificially. Only a few elements are named after women.
115362.m: The element meitnerium honours Lise Meitner.

115363.q: What did Lise Meitner become in 1926, the first woman in Germany to do so?
115363.e: She was given a professorship in physics at the University of Berlin. At the time this was a great exception for women.
115363.m: Lise Meitner was Germany's first woman professor of physics.

115364.q: What is released in the nuclear fission that Lise Meitner explained?
115364.e: When a uranium nucleus breaks apart, the pieces together are slightly lighter than the nucleus was before. This missing mass is released as a great deal of energy.
115364.m: Nuclear fission releases a lot of energy.

115365.q: What are the imaginary lines called today that Faraday used to show the force around a magnet?
115365.e: If you scatter iron filings around a magnet, they line up along these lines. Faraday called them lines of force and developed the idea of the field from them.
115365.m: Field lines show the magnetic field.

115366.q: In which country did Michael Faraday live and do his research?
115366.e: Michael Faraday was born near London in 1791 and did research in London all his life.
115366.m: Michael Faraday was an English scientist.

115367.q: What did Faraday discover when he moved a magnet back and forth in a coil of wire?
115367.e: A moving magnet produces a current in a coil. This discovery from 1831 is called induction and is used in every generator.
115367.m: A moving magnet produces a current in a coil.

115368.q: Why are you well protected in a car during a thunderstorm?
a: The metal shell carries the lightning around the outside
The rubber tyres keep the lightning out
115368.e: The metal body works like a Faraday cage. The current flows over the outside of the metal into the ground, and you stay protected inside.
115368.m: A metal shell protects you from lightning like a Faraday cage.

115369.q: Faraday hardly went to school. How did he still learn a lot about science?
a: He read many books and went to lectures
He learned everything from his father
115369.e: As a teenager, Faraday worked for a bookbinder and read the books he bound. He also went to lectures by famous scientists.

115370.q: What did Faraday's experiments on electricity and magnetism show?
a: They have nothing to do with each other
115370.e: A current produces a magnetic field, and a moving magnet produces a current. Faraday showed how closely electricity and magnetism are connected.

115371.q: For whom did Faraday give special Christmas lectures with experiments in London?
115371.e: Since 1825, exciting experiments have been shown to young people at the Christmas Lectures in London. The tradition still exists today.
115371.m: Faraday inspired young people with Christmas lectures.

115372.q: Which device did Faraday demonstrate in an early form in 1821, in which current produces a turning motion?
115372.e: In his experiment, a wire carrying a current turned around a magnet. Electrical energy was turned into motion.
115372.m: In an electric motor, current produces a turning motion.

115373.q: In which city with a famous leaning tower was Galileo born?
115373.e: Galileo was born in Pisa in 1564. Legend says he dropped balls from the Leaning Tower.

115374.q: What did Galileo discover at the planet Jupiter in 1610?
a: A red spot on the Moon
115374.e: The four largest moons of Jupiter are now called the Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. They showed that not everything circles the Earth.
115374.m: Galileo discovered the four large moons of Jupiter.

115375.q: Which view of the universe did Galileo defend?
a: The view with the Sun at the centre
The view with the Earth at the centre
The view with the Moon at the centre
The view of a flat Earth
115375.e: Galileo supported the heliocentric view of Copernicus. According to it, the Earth and the planets circle the Sun.

115376.e: Galileo had to take back his teaching and spent the rest of his life under house arrest. The Catholic Church officially cleared his name in 1992.
115376.m: Galileo was condemned by the Inquisition in 1633.

115377.q: Which instrument did Galileo improve in 1609 for observing the sky?
115377.e: Galileo heard about an invention from the Netherlands and built his own, stronger device. He was one of the first to point it at the sky.
115377.m: Galileo observed the sky with a telescope.

115378.q: What did Galileo realise about falling objects?
a: Without air resistance, all objects fall equally fast
Heavy objects always fall twice as fast
115378.e: A feather falls more slowly than a ball only because of the air. In a vacuum, both reach the bottom at the same time.
115378.m: In a vacuum, all objects fall equally fast.

115379.q: What did Galileo discover when he observed the Earth's Moon?
115379.e: At the time, people thought the Moon was a perfectly smooth ball. Galileo saw the light and shadows of mountains and craters.
115379.m: The Moon has mountains and craters.

115380.q: According to Galileo's observations, what does the time a pendulum takes to swing depend on?
115380.e: A longer pendulum swings back and forth more slowly. The mass of the weight makes practically no difference.
115380.m: Long pendulums swing more slowly than short ones.

115381.q: Which force, described by Newton, makes apples fall and keeps the Moon in its orbit?
115381.e: Newton realised that the same force of attraction acts on Earth and in space. It gets weaker with distance.
115381.m: Gravity acts on Earth and in space.

115382.q: At which university did Isaac Newton study and teach?
115382.e: Newton studied at Trinity College and became professor of mathematics there. He lived in this college for many years.
115382.m: Newton did his research in Cambridge.

115383.q: Roughly how big is the weight force of a 100-gram bar of chocolate on Earth?
115383.e: Weight force is mass times gravitational acceleration: 0.1 kg times about 9.81 N/kg gives about 1 newton.
115383.m: On Earth, 100 grams weigh about 1 newton.

115384.q: Which physical quantity is measured in newtons?
115384.e: In honour of Isaac Newton, the unit of force is called the newton. It is abbreviated to N.

115385.q: What did Isaac Newton study with a glass prism?
115385.e: Using a prism, Newton showed that white sunlight is made up of all the colours of the rainbow.
115385.m: Newton split light into colours with a prism.

115386.q: In which famous church in London is Newton buried?
115386.e: Newton was buried with great honours in 1727. Many kings and famous people of England rest in this church.

115387.q: What kind of telescope did Newton build in 1668?
115387.e: Instead of lenses, Newton used a curved mirror. This avoided coloured edges in the image.
115387.m: Newton built the first usable reflecting telescope.

115388.q: Which famous laws did Newton describe in his main work of 1687?
115388.e: In his main work, the ‘Principia’, Newton described the three laws of motion and gravity. It is considered one of the most important books in science.
115388.m: Newton described the laws of motion.

115389.q: An object with a mass of 2 kilograms has an acceleration of 3 m/s². How big is the force?
115389.e: According to Newton's second law, force equals mass times acceleration. 2 kg times 3 m/s² gives 6 N.

115390.q: What was Auguste Piccard the first to do in 1931?
a: Rise into the stratosphere in a balloon
Fly across the Atlantic in a plane
115390.e: Piccard rose in a gas balloon to a height no human had ever reached. He wanted to study cosmic radiation there.
115390.m: Piccard was the first to fly into the stratosphere.

115391.q: In which mountain range did Piccard's stratosphere balloon land in 1931?
115391.e: After the flight the balloon drifted into the Alps. Piccard and his companion landed on a glacier in Tyrol.
115391.m: Piccard's first stratosphere flight ended on a glacier in the Alps.

115392.q: What was new about Piccard's balloon so that he could survive at great height?
115392.e: In the stratosphere the air is too thin and too cold to survive. The sealed ball-shaped cabin kept up the air pressure inside.
115392.m: Piccard flew in a pressurised cabin.

115393.q: What did Auguste Piccard later develop a special submersible for?
a: To dive into the deep sea
115393.e: Piccard's submersible had a pressure-proof sphere for the crew. With it you could reach very great depths.
115393.m: Piccard built a submersible for the deep sea.

115394.q: Where did Auguste Piccard's son Jacques dive in the submersible ‘Trieste’ in 1960?
a: Into the Challenger Deep of the Mariana Trench
To the bottom of Lake Geneva
To the wreck of the Titanic
115394.e: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached a depth of almost 11 kilometres. It is the deepest known point in the world's oceans.
115394.m: Jacques Piccard dived to the deepest point of the ocean.

115395.q: What did Auguste Piccard's grandson Bertrand achieve in 2016?
a: A flight around the world in a solar plane
A crossing of the Sahara on foot
A dive to the Earth's core
115395.e: Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg took turns flying the solar plane ‘Solar Impulse 2’ around the Earth. It flew on solar energy alone.
115395.m: Bertrand Piccard flew around the Earth on solar power.

115396.q: What did Auguste Piccard want to study in the stratosphere?
115396.e: Piccard was a physicist. He wanted to measure radiation from space, which is stronger high up than on the ground.
115396.m: Piccard flew into the stratosphere to measure cosmic radiation.

115397.e: Auguste Piccard was a professor of physics. His balloon flights and dives were for research.

115398.q: Thanks to Tesla's inventions, which type of current won out for the power supply?
115398.e: Alternating current can easily be raised to high voltages with transformers. This means electricity can be sent over long distances with little loss.
115398.m: Our power grid runs on alternating current.

115399.q: For what is ‘tesla’ also the name of a unit?
a: For the strength of magnetic fields
115399.e: The tesla tells you how strong a magnetic field is. An MRI scanner in a hospital, for example, works with 1.5 to 3 tesla.
115399.m: The strength of magnetic fields is measured in tesla.

115400.q: Which device did Tesla demonstrate in New York in 1898 that seemed like magic at the time?
115400.e: Tesla steered a small boat in a water tank by radio. At first many spectators thought it was a trick.
115400.m: Tesla showed a radio remote control as early as 1898.

115401.q: Which device named after Tesla produces very high voltages and artificial lightning?
115401.e: The Tesla transformer is also called a Tesla coil. Museums use it to show impressive sparks.
115401.m: A Tesla coil produces high voltage.

115402.q: Which electric motor did Tesla develop that now runs in many machines?
115402.e: The induction motor, or asynchronous motor, runs on alternating current and needs no sliding contacts on the rotor. It is robust and very common.
115402.m: Tesla's induction motor drives many machines.

115403.q: Which famous inventor backed direct current instead of alternating current in his dispute with Tesla?
115403.e: Edison wanted to supply cities with direct current, Tesla with alternating current. In the end alternating current won, because it can be sent better over long distances.
115403.m: In the war of the currents, Tesla's AC beat Edison's DC.

115404.q: What did Tesla want to achieve with his tower at Wardenclyffe near New York?
a: Send energy and messages without wires
115404.e: Tesla dreamed of a worldwide wireless network. The project failed for lack of money and the tower was torn down in 1917.
115404.m: Tesla dreamed of wireless energy transmission.

115405.q: In which city did Nikola Tesla die in 1943?
115405.e: Tesla spent his last years alone in a hotel room. He died poor, even though his inventions changed the world.

115406.q: Which machine did James Watt improve decisively?
115406.e: Machines of this kind existed before, but they used a great deal of coal. Watt's improvements made them economical.
115406.m: James Watt improved the steam engine.

115407.q: Which fuel was usually burned in Watt's steam engines?
115407.e: Steam engines heated water with coal fires. Watt's improvements meant they needed much less coal.
115407.m: Steam engines were mostly fired with coal.

115408.q: Which unit of power did James Watt introduce to compare his engines with horses?
115408.e: This helped buyers understand how many horses an engine could replace. One metric horsepower is about 735 watts.

115409.q: A 60-watt lamp is on for 10 hours. How much electrical energy does it use?
115409.e: Energy is power times time: 60 W times 10 h gives 600 Wh. That is 0.6 kWh.

115410.q: Which era did the improved steam engine strongly drive forward?
115410.e: Steam engines drove factories, pumps and later locomotives. This completely changed work and life in Europe.
115410.m: The steam engine shaped the Industrial Revolution.

115411.q: Which physical quantity is measured in watts, the unit named after James Watt?
115411.e: Power tells you how much energy is converted per second. Its unit, the watt, honours James Watt, who improved the steam engine.

115412.q: A motor does 1200 joules of work in 60 seconds. What is its power?
115412.e: Power is work divided by time. 1200 J divided by 60 s gives 20 W.
115412.m: Power is work per unit of time.

115413.q: Which natural fibre consists of about 90 per cent cellulose?
115413.e: The seed hairs of cotton are about 90 per cent cellulose. Sheep's wool, silk and cashmere, on the other hand, are animal fibres made of proteins.

115414.q: Which bond links the glucose units in cellulose?
115414.e: The glucose units are linked by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds. As a result, every second unit is rotated by 180 degrees and the chain is stretched out.
115414.m: The β-1,4 bond makes cellulose a straight fibre.

115415.q: Why can humans not use cellulose as a source of energy?
115415.e: Human digestive enzymes such as amylase only split α-glycosidic bonds. We lack cellulase for the β-1,4 bonds of cellulose, which is why cellulose acts as dietary fibre.
115415.m: For humans, cellulose is indigestible dietary fibre.

115416.q: What are the bundles of parallel cellulose molecules in the cell wall called?
115416.e: Parallel cellulose chains are joined by hydrogen bonds into tear-resistant microfibrils. These form the framework of the plant cell wall.
115416.m: Cellulose microfibrils give the cell wall its tensile strength.

115417.q: Which industry processes cellulose from wood in particularly large quantities?
115417.e: To make paper, wood is broken down into pulp, which consists mainly of cellulose fibres. As it dries, the fibres mat together into a sheet.
115417.m: Paper consists mainly of cellulose fibres.

115418.q: Which polysaccharide differs from cellulose mainly by having α bonds instead of β bonds?
115418.e: Amylose, a component of starch, is also made of glucose, but it is linked by α-1,4-glycosidic bonds and therefore forms a helix instead of a straight fibre.
115418.m: Starch and cellulose are both made of glucose but linked differently.

115419.q: Which statement about cellulose is correct?
a: It is the most abundant biopolymer on Earth
It is the most abundant protein on Earth
115419.e: Since every plant cell wall contains cellulose, it is the most abundant organic compound, or biopolymer, on Earth by quantity.
115419.m: Cellulose is the most abundant biopolymer on Earth.

115420.q: How can cows make use of the cellulose in grass?
a: Microorganisms in the rumen break it down
Their saliva contains a lot of amylase
115420.e: Bacteria and single-celled organisms with cellulases live in the rumen of ruminants. They break down the cellulose and so supply the cow with energy.
115420.m: Ruminants use cellulose with the help of microorganisms in the rumen.

115421.q: Why is cellulose insoluble in water even though it is made of glucose?
a: The long chains are firmly joined by many hydrogen bonds
It has a strong electric charge
115421.e: The straight cellulose chains lie close together and are joined by a great many hydrogen bonds. Water molecules therefore cannot separate them.

115422.q: How do new plastids form in a plant cell?
a: By budding off from the Golgi apparatus
By forming anew from the ER
By bulging out of the nucleus
115422.e: Plastids cannot be made from scratch. They multiply by dividing and are shared out between the daughter cells when the cell divides.
115422.m: Plastids always come from other plastids.

115423.q: From which precursor do the different types of plastid develop in meristematic tissue?
115423.e: Meristematic cells contain small proplastids with little internal structure. Depending on the tissue and light, they develop into chloroplasts, leucoplasts or chromoplasts.
115423.m: Proplastids are the precursors of all plastid types.

115424.q: How many membranes surround the plastids of land plants?
115424.e: The plastids of land plants have an envelope made of an inner and an outer membrane. This double membrane is a clue to their origin.
115424.m: The plastids of land plants have a double membrane.

115425.q: Which feature of plastids suggests that they descend from bacteria?
115425.e: Plastids have their own circular DNA and their own ribosomes, like bacteria. This supports the endosymbiotic theory.
115425.m: Plastids have their own DNA, inherited from their bacterial ancestors.

115426.q: Which plastids give carrots and ripe tomatoes their colour?
115426.e: Chromoplasts contain carotenoids, which give fruits and roots a yellow, orange or red colour. When tomatoes ripen, they form from chloroplasts.
115426.m: Chromoplasts colour fruits and roots orange and red.

115427.q: Which plastids contain thylakoids with chlorophyll?
115427.e: Chloroplasts have a thylakoid system whose membranes contain chlorophyll and the light reactions of photosynthesis.
115427.m: Chloroplasts are the green plastids for photosynthesis.

115428.e: Plastids have their own ribosomes of the 70S type, like those of bacteria. The cytoplasm of the plant cell, by contrast, contains 80S ribosomes.
115428.m: Plastids have small 70S ribosomes like bacteria.

115429.q: Which plastids store starch in potato tubers?
115429.e: Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that store starch grains. They are found in storage organs such as potato tubers.

115430.q: Which pigments do chromoplasts mainly contain?
115430.e: Chromoplasts store yellow, orange and red carotenoids. Other plant pigments such as anthocyanins and betalains are not plastid pigments.
115430.m: Chromoplasts colour plant parts yellow to red with carotenoids.

115431.q: Which pigment in chromoplasts makes ripe tomatoes red?
115431.e: As tomatoes ripen, large amounts of lycopene build up in their chromoplasts. Lycopene is a red carotenoid.
115431.m: Lycopene is the red carotenoid of the tomato.

115432.q: From which plastids do chromoplasts often form when fruit ripens?
115432.e: As they ripen, many fruits break down their chlorophyll and the chloroplasts are converted into chromoplasts. That is how a green fruit turns yellow or red.
115432.m: During ripening, chloroplasts often turn into chromoplasts.

115433.q: Where in the cell are the blue anthocyanins of a cornflower found?
a: In the cell sap of the vacuole
115433.e: Anthocyanins are water-soluble and dissolved in the cell sap of the vacuole. Unlike carotenoids, they are not plastid pigments.
115433.m: Anthocyanins are in the vacuole, not in plastids.

115434.q: Which pigment in the chromoplasts makes carrots orange?
115434.e: The carrot root contains chromoplasts with a lot of β-carotene. The substance is even named after the carrot.
115434.m: Carrots are orange thanks to β-carotene.

115435.q: What ecological job do coloured chromoplasts in fruits have?
a: Attracting animals to spread the seeds
115435.e: Yellow, orange and red fruits catch the eye of birds and mammals. These eat the fruit and so spread the seeds.
115435.m: Coloured fruits attract animals that spread the seeds.

115436.q: Why should you eat carrots with a little oil or fat?
a: Because fat makes the colour stronger
115436.e: Carotenoids such as β-carotene dissolve in fat, not in water. With a little fat, the gut can absorb them much better.
115436.m: The body absorbs β-carotene better with fat.

115437.q: Which vitamin can the human body make from β-carotene?
115437.e: β-carotene is a provitamin A compound. In the gut it is split and converted into vitamin A (retinol).
115437.m: β-carotene is the precursor of vitamin A.

a: They contain a lot of chlorophyll
115438.e: Leucoplasts contain no pigments. The name comes from the Greek word for white.

115439.q: What are the leucoplasts that make and store starch grains called?
115439.e: Amyloplasts are leucoplasts that build up starch and store it as grains. The name comes from the Greek amylon for starch.
115439.m: Amyloplasts are the starch stores among the plastids.

115440.q: Which plastids give carrots and tomatoes their orange to red colour?
115440.e: Chromoplasts contain carotenoids such as carotene and lycopene. Leucoplasts, on the other hand, are colourless and serve mainly for storage.

115441.q: What is the umbrella term for cell organelles such as chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts?
115441.e: Plastids are organelles of the plant cell surrounded by a double membrane. They can change into one another, for example leucoplasts into chloroplasts.
115441.m: Chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts are plastids.

a: In the palisade tissue of the leaf
115442.e: Leucoplasts occur mainly in non-green tissues away from light, such as roots, tubers and seeds.
115442.m: Leucoplasts are found in tissues that get no light.

115443.q: What job do amyloplasts have in the root cap?
115443.e: Heavy amyloplasts in the cells of the root cap sink downwards and act as statoliths. This is how the root knows which way is down.
115443.m: Amyloplasts in the root cap show the root the direction of gravity.

115444.q: Why do potato tubers turn green in the light?
115444.e: When exposed to light, the leucoplasts of the tuber develop into chloroplasts with chlorophyll. At the same time, the tuber often produces more of the poisonous solanine.
115444.m: Potatoes exposed to light form chloroplasts and turn green.

115445.q: Which solution can be used to detect starch grains in amyloplasts?
115445.e: Iodine-potassium iodide solution, also called Lugol's solution, stains starch blue-violet to black. Fehling's solution detects reducing sugars, biuret detects proteins.

a: The membrane of the central vacuole
The outer envelope of the nucleus
The inner layer of the cell wall
115446.e: The tonoplast is the biological membrane that separates the large central vacuole of the plant cell from the cytoplasm.

115447.e: The tonoplast is a single biological membrane made of a lipid bilayer with embedded proteins, similar to the plasma membrane.
115447.m: The tonoplast is a single biological membrane.

115448.q: Which particles does the V-ATPase of the tonoplast pump into the vacuole?
115448.e: The V-ATPase uses the energy of ATP to pump protons (H+) into the vacuole. The resulting proton gradient drives other transport processes.
115448.m: The tonoplast pumps protons into the vacuole.

115449.q: How does the cell sap in the vacuole usually compare with the cytoplasm?
115449.e: Because protons are pumped into the vacuole, the cell sap is usually much more acidic than the almost neutral cytoplasm.
115449.m: The cell sap of the vacuole is usually acidic.

115450.q: Which channel proteins in the tonoplast make it easier for water to pass through?
115450.e: Aquaporins are water channels in biological membranes. In the tonoplast they allow water to be exchanged quickly between the cytoplasm and the vacuole.
115450.m: Aquaporins are water channels in membranes.

115451.q: What does the plant cell use the proton gradient across the tonoplast for?
a: To transport other substances into the vacuole
115451.e: When protons flow back out of the vacuole, they drive transport proteins. In return, these bring ions or sugars into the vacuole.
115451.m: The proton gradient drives transport into the vacuole.

115452.q: Why can the vacuole store substances such as tannins separately from the cytoplasm?
a: The vacuole has a cell wall
The vacuole has its own DNA
115452.e: The tonoplast only lets certain substances through and transports others in a targeted way. So defensive or waste substances can build up in the vacuole without harming the cytoplasm.
115452.m: The tonoplast separates the cell sap from the cytoplasm.

115453.q: What is the watery solution inside the tonoplast called?
115453.e: The liquid in the vacuole is called cell sap. It contains dissolved salts, sugars, acids and often pigments.
115453.m: The vacuole contains the cell sap.

115454.q: What does turgor mean in plant biology?
a: The internal pressure of the cell contents against the cell wall
The suction of the root hairs
The air pressure in the intercellular spaces
The pull of water in the xylem
115454.e: When the vacuole takes in water by osmosis, the protoplast presses against the cell wall. This internal pressure is called turgor.
115454.m: Turgor is the pressure of the cell's contents on the cell wall.

115455.q: Why do plants wilt when they are short of water?
a: The turgor in the cells falls
The roots take up too much salt
115455.e: Without enough water, the vacuoles lose volume, the turgor drops and the soft parts of the plant droop.
115455.m: Wilting means a loss of turgor.

115456.q: What is the counter-pressure that the cell wall exerts on the protoplast called?
115456.e: The elastic cell wall pushes back with equal force. This wall pressure stops the cell from taking in more water and bursting.
115456.m: Wall pressure and turgor balance each other.

115457.q: What makes the stomata of a leaf open?
a: The turgor of the guard cells rises
The wall pressure of neighbouring cells rises
115457.e: Guard cells take up potassium ions and therefore water. Their turgor rises and, because their walls are unevenly thickened, they bend apart.
115457.m: Guard cells open the pore through rising turgor.

115459.q: Why is turgor important for herbaceous plants?
a: It gives them firmness without wood
115459.e: Herbaceous plants have little supporting tissue. Their stability depends heavily on cells that are full to bursting, rather like a pumped-up balloon.
115459.m: Herbaceous plants stand upright thanks to turgor.

115460.q: What role does turgor play in the elongation growth of plant cells?
a: It stretches the loosened cell wall
It completely dissolves the cell wall
It doubles the number of chromosomes
It prevents any uptake of water
115460.e: During elongation growth, the cell wall is loosened, for example by auxin. Turgor then pushes it apart and the cell gets bigger.
115460.m: Turgor drives the elongation growth of cells.

115461.q: Why do plant cells not burst in pure water, while red blood cells do?
a: The cell wall withstands the pressure
Plant cells do not take up water
Pure water is hypertonic for plants
115461.e: Plant cells also take up water in pure water. But their rigid cell wall limits how far they can expand, while animal cells without a wall can burst.
115461.m: The cell wall protects plant cells from bursting.

a: The protoplast pulls away from the cell wall
The cell bursts by taking up water
115462.e: In a more concentrated outside solution, the vacuole loses water. The protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the cell wall.
115462.m: In plasmolysis, the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall.

115463.q: What is the reverse process called, when a plasmolysed protoplast expands again?
115463.e: If plasmolysed cells are put back into water, the vacuole takes up water again. The protoplast presses against the cell wall once more.

115464.q: Why is the skin of a red onion good for observing plasmolysis?
a: Its cell sap is coloured red
Its cells have no cell wall
It contains a particularly large number of chloroplasts
115464.e: The red pigment in the cell sap makes the vacuole easy to see under the microscope. That way you can follow how it shrinks.
115464.m: Coloured cell sap makes plasmolysis visible.

115465.q: During plasmolysis, what fills the space between the cell wall and the protoplast?
115465.e: The cell wall lets water and dissolved substances through. That is why the outside solution flows into the space left by the shrinking protoplast.
115465.m: The cell wall lets the outside solution through.

115466.q: What is the state called in which the protoplast is just starting to pull away from the cell wall?
115466.e: At incipient plasmolysis, the outside solution has about the same concentration as the cell sap. This can be used to determine the osmotic value of the cell.
115466.m: Incipient plasmolysis shows the osmotic value of the cell sap.

115468.q: Why do lettuce leaves quickly go limp in a very salty dressing?
a: The dressing contains too little sugar
The leaves take up too much water
115468.e: The salty dressing is more concentrated than the cell sap. The cells lose water, plasmolyse, and the leaves go limp.
115468.m: Salt draws water out of plant cells.

115469.q: In which kind of solution does plasmolysis occur?
115469.e: A hypertonic solution is more concentrated than the cell sap. Water therefore flows out of the cell.

115470.q: In which direction does water flow overall during osmosis?
a: Towards the higher concentration of dissolved particles
Towards the lower concentration of dissolved particles
115470.e: Overall, water flows to the side with more dissolved particles until the concentrations even out or a counter-pressure builds up.
115470.m: In osmosis, water follows the dissolved particles.

115471.q: What is needed for osmosis to take place?
115471.e: A semi-permeable membrane lets water molecules through but holds back dissolved particles. Only then does the osmotic flow of water occur.

115472.q: How does the osmotic pressure of a sugar solution change if you double its concentration?
115472.e: Osmotic pressure depends on the number of dissolved particles. Twice as many sugar molecules give roughly twice the pressure.

115473.q: When are two solutions described as isotonic?
a: When they have the same osmotic pressure
When they have the same temperature
When they contain the same dissolved substance
When they are the same colour
115473.e: Isotonic solutions have the same concentration of osmotically active particles. There is no net flow of water between them.
115473.m: Isotonic solutions exchange no net water.

115474.q: How does water move in relation to water potential?
a: From higher to lower water potential
From lower to higher water potential
115474.e: Water potential describes the free energy of water. Dissolved particles lower it, and water always flows towards the lower water potential.
115474.m: Water always flows towards lower water potential.

115475.q: Why do root hairs take up water from the soil by osmosis?
a: Their cell sap is more concentrated than the soil water
The soil water is more concentrated
115475.e: The cell sap of root hair cells contains more dissolved particles than the soil water. That is why water flows into the cells.
115475.m: Concentrated cell sap draws water into the root.

115476.q: What is needed for reverse osmosis to desalinate seawater?
a: A pressure greater than the osmotic pressure
A membrane that lets salt through easily
Heating the water until it boils
115476.e: If seawater is pressed against a membrane at a pressure above the osmotic pressure, water flows against its natural direction and the salt stays behind.
115476.m: Reverse osmosis pushes water through a membrane against its natural direction.

115477.q: At the same molar concentration, which solution has the higher osmotic pressure?
a: Both the same, if equally warm
115477.e: In water, sodium chloride splits into two ions, Na+ and Cl-. So the solution contains about twice as many osmotically active particles as a sugar solution of the same concentration.
115477.m: Osmotic pressure depends on the number of dissolved particles.

115478.q: What does the endosymbiotic theory state?
a: Plastids descend from bacteria that were taken in
115478.e: According to the theory, early cells took in bacteria without digesting them. These endosymbionts became mitochondria and plastids.
115478.m: Mitochondria and plastids were once free-living bacteria.

115479.q: How many membranes surround a chloroplast in a plant cell?
115479.e: Chloroplasts have a double membrane. The inner membrane comes from the bacterium that was taken in, which supports the endosymbiotic theory.

115480.q: Apart from chloroplasts, which cell organelles descend from bacteria according to the endosymbiotic theory?
115480.e: Like chloroplasts, mitochondria have their own circular DNA, their own ribosomes and a double membrane. They descend from bacteria that were taken in.

115481.q: Which American biologist helped the endosymbiotic theory achieve its breakthrough from 1967 onwards?
115481.e: In 1967 Lynn Margulis published a much-discussed paper on the origin of eukaryotic cells through symbiosis, bringing the theory to the attention of scientists.
115481.m: Lynn Margulis made the endosymbiotic theory well known.

115482.q: Why was the endosymbiotic theory only generally accepted in the second half of the 20th century?
a: Only then could the DNA of the organelles be studied
Only then were there light microscopes
Only then were plant cells known
115482.e: The idea already existed around 1905. But the evidence only came from electron microscopy and genetic analyses, which showed bacteria-like DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
115482.m: Genetic analyses made the endosymbiotic theory convincing.

115483.q: Which finding supports the endosymbiotic theory?
a: Plastids have circular DNA like bacteria
Plastids have a cell wall made of cellulose
115483.e: Plastids and mitochondria have their own DNA, usually circular and without typical histones. This matches the genetic material of bacteria.
115483.m: The bacteria-like DNA of plastids reveals their origin.

115484.q: What suggests that chloroplasts descend from a bacterium that was taken in?
a: They divide on their own, much like bacteria
They form anew from the nucleus
They have a cell wall made of cellulose
115484.e: Chloroplasts are not built anew by the cell but multiply by dividing. Together with their own DNA and their own ribosomes, this is reminiscent of bacteria.

115485.q: Why can chloroplasts no longer live freely today?
a: Many of their genes are now in the nucleus
They are too large for a free life
115485.e: In the course of evolution, most of the endosymbiont's genes were moved to the nucleus. Many plastid proteins are therefore made in the cytoplasm and imported.
115485.m: Plastids depend on genes in the nucleus.

115486.q: Which structure do mitochondria and chloroplasts have that is also reminiscent of bacteria?
a: A cell wall made of chitin
115486.e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts make some of their proteins themselves using their own ribosomes. These ribosomes resemble those of bacteria more than those in the cytoplasm.
115486.m: Their own ribosomes reveal the bacterial origin of the organelles.

115487.q: What does totipotency of a plant cell mean?
a: It can give rise to a whole plant
It can only form root cells
115487.e: A totipotent cell contains all the genetic information and can develop into a complete organism with all cell types.
115487.m: Totipotent cells can form a whole organism.

115488.q: Why can a whole plant grow from a leaf cutting of an African violet?
a: There are spores in the leaf
115488.e: Fully differentiated plant cells can become able to divide again and form new tissues and organs. Propagation by cuttings is based on this.
115488.m: Plant cells can revert to dividing cells.

115489.q: What is the disorganised cell tissue that forms in plant tissue cultures called?
115489.e: A callus is a mass of undifferentiated cells that can divide. It also forms at wounds and can produce new shoots and roots.
115489.m: A callus is a mass of undifferentiated plant cells.

115490.q: How can the totipotency of plant cells be shown in the laboratory?
a: A whole plant grows from a single cell
Seeds germinate on damp cotton wool
Plants keep growing in the dark
115490.e: In the 1950s, Frederick Steward grew complete carrot plants in a nutrient solution from single cells of the carrot root. This proved the totipotency of plant cells.
115490.m: Whole plants can grow from single plant cells.

115491.q: What do nurseries use the totipotency of plant cells for?
a: To propagate many identical plants in tissue culture
To make seeds keep for longer
115491.e: In micropropagation, many genetically identical plants, orchids for example, are grown in the laboratory from small pieces of tissue. Gottlieb Haberlandt is regarded as the founder of tissue culture.
115491.m: Tissue cultures produce many genetically identical plants.

a: Specialised cells become able to divide again
Cells die in a controlled way
115492.e: In dedifferentiation, specialised cells give up their function and become unspecialised cells that can divide again.

115493.q: In a callus culture, what does a high ratio of cytokinin to auxin promote?
115493.e: The ratio of plant hormones controls which organs form: a lot of cytokinin promotes shoots, a lot of auxin promotes roots.
115493.m: Cytokinin promotes shoots, auxin promotes roots.

115494.q: What do you call cells that can form many, but not all, cell types of an organism?
115494.e: Pluripotent cells can develop into many different cell types, but can no longer produce a complete organism.
115494.m: Pluripotent cells are versatile but not all-powerful.

a: A tissue that can divide and produce new cells
An outer covering tissue of leaves
115495.e: Meristems consist of small cells rich in cytoplasm that divide continuously. All other plant tissues develop from them.
115495.m: Meristems are the growth tissues of the plant.

115496.q: What are the apical meristems at the tips of shoots and roots responsible for?
115496.e: The apical meristems at the tips of the shoot and root continuously produce new cells and make the plant grow longer.
115496.m: Apical meristems are responsible for growth in length.

115497.q: Which meristem is responsible for the secondary thickening of trees?
115497.e: The cambium is a lateral meristem that produces wood towards the inside and bast towards the outside. This makes the trunk thicker every year.
115497.m: The cambium makes trees grow thicker.

115498.q: How do the annual rings in wood form?
a: Through varying cambium activity over the year
Through the bark shedding every year
115498.e: In spring the cambium produces wide, light early wood, in summer dense, dark late wood. The boundary between late wood and early wood makes an annual ring visible.
115498.m: Each annual ring stands for one year of cambium activity.

115499.q: Which structure protects the meristem at the root tip?
115499.e: The root cap (calyptra) sits like a cap in front of the root meristem. Its outer cells are rubbed off and turn slimy, which helps the root push into the soil.
115499.m: The root cap protects the growing root tip.

115500.q: Why does grass keep growing quickly after mowing?
a: It has meristems at the base of its leaves
It produces new seeds after every cut
It only grows with its roots
115500.e: Grasses have intercalary meristems at the base of the leaves and at the stem nodes. These are not removed by mowing or grazing.
115500.m: Grasses grow back from the base.

115501.q: What job does the cork layer in the bark of a tree have?
a: It protects the trunk from drying out and injury
It carries sugar to the roots
It stores water for the summer
115501.e: The cork cambium produces cork cells towards the outside, which die and fill with water-repellent substances. In this way they protect the trunk.

115502.q: Why are shoot tip meristems used to obtain virus-free potato plants?
a: Meristems only grow in the dark
115502.e: The shoot tip meristem has no developed vascular tissue yet, through which viruses spread quickly. If these cells are cultured, virus-free plants are often obtained.
115502.m: Virus-free plants can be grown from meristem cultures.

a: From cells that are already differentiated
From fungal threads in the soil
115503.e: Secondary meristems form when fully differentiated permanent cells become able to divide again.
115503.m: Secondary meristems develop from permanent tissue.

a: Cells with thick, usually lignified walls
115504.e: Sclerenchyma is a supporting tissue. Its cells have heavily thickened, usually lignified walls and are often dead when mature.
115504.m: Sclerenchyma strengthens plants with thick, woody cell walls.

115505.q: Which two cell types are distinguished in sclerenchyma?
115505.e: Sclerenchyma fibres are long and spindle-shaped, sclereids (stone cells) rather short and roundish. Both have thick walls.
115505.m: Sclerenchyma consists of fibres or stone cells.

115506.q: What causes the gritty texture of the flesh of some pears?
115506.e: The flesh of a pear contains groups of sclereids, known as stone cells. When you eat them they feel like fine grains.

115507.q: How does collenchyma differ from sclerenchyma?
a: Its cells are alive and not lignified
Its cells are dead and lignified
115507.e: Collenchyma is a living supporting tissue with unevenly thickened, unlignified walls. It stays stretchable and supports growing parts of the plant.
115507.m: Collenchyma is living, stretchable supporting tissue.

115508.q: Which substance makes the cell walls of sclerenchyma hard and resistant to pressure?
115508.e: During lignification, lignin is deposited in the cell wall. It makes it hard, resistant to pressure and not very permeable.
115508.m: Lignin makes cell walls woody and hard.

115509.q: Which textile is made from sclerenchyma fibres in the stem of flax?
115509.e: The long bast fibres of flax are sclerenchyma fibres. Linen is made from them.
115509.m: Linen is made of fibres from the flax stem.

115510.q: What is the hard shell of a walnut mainly made of?
115510.e: Hard nutshells and cherry stones consist of densely packed sclereids with heavily thickened walls.
115510.m: Nutshells and fruit stones are made of stone cells.

115511.q: Why does sclerenchyma form mainly in fully grown parts of a plant?
a: Its cell walls can no longer stretch
It needs a lot of light
It is only triggered by insects
115511.e: The rigid, lignified walls of sclerenchyma can no longer grow with the plant. In growing organs it would hinder elongation growth.
115511.m: Sclerenchyma strengthens plant parts that have finished growing.

115512.q: What absorbs the heat from inside a fridge?
115512.e: The refrigerant evaporates in the evaporator inside. To evaporate, it needs heat, which it takes from the food and the air.
115512.m: When it evaporates, the refrigerant absorbs heat.

115513.q: Why is the grille at the back of a fridge warm?
a: There the refrigerant gives off heat
There is a heater built in there
115513.e: In the condenser at the back, the refrigerant becomes liquid again. In doing so, it gives off the heat it absorbed inside.
115513.m: A fridge pumps heat from inside to outside.

115514.q: Which part of a fridge compresses the refrigerant gas?
115514.e: The compressor squeezes the refrigerant gas together. This makes it hot so it can then give off its heat to the kitchen air.
115514.m: The compressor is the heart of the fridge.

115515.q: Roughly which temperature is recommended for a household fridge?
115515.e: At about 5 degrees Celsius, most bacteria multiply only slowly. Colder is usually unnecessary and uses more electricity.
115515.m: A fridge should be at about 5 degrees.

115516.q: What happens if you leave the fridge door open on a hot day to cool the kitchen?
a: The temperature stays exactly the same
115516.e: The fridge only moves heat from the front to the back in the same room. On top of that, the motor gives off waste heat, so the kitchen gets warmer overall.
115516.m: An open fridge heats up the kitchen.

115517.q: Which refrigerants used in the past damage the ozone layer?
115517.e: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) release chlorine in the stratosphere, which destroys ozone. That is why they are banned today.

115518.q: Which natural refrigerant is in many household fridges in Europe today?
115518.e: Isobutane (R600a) is a hydrocarbon that does not damage the ozone layer and has only a very low global warming potential.
115518.m: Modern fridges often cool with isobutane.

115519.q: What does the international Montreal Protocol of 1987 protect?
115519.e: In the Montreal Protocol, countries committed themselves to banning substances such as CFCs that break down the ozone layer.
115519.m: The Montreal Protocol protects the ozone layer.

115520.q: Which particles in food are mainly set in motion by microwaves?
115520.e: Water molecules are electric dipoles. In the rapidly changing field of the microwaves, they turn back and forth, and this movement heats the food.
115520.m: Microwaves heat food through the water it contains.

115521.q: Which household device transmits at almost the same frequency as a microwave oven?
a: The X-ray machine at the dentist
115521.e: Many Wi-Fi routers transmit at 2.4 gigahertz, very close to the 2.45 gigahertz of the microwave oven. That is why a running microwave can sometimes disturb the Wi-Fi.
115521.m: Microwave ovens and Wi-Fi use similar radio waves.

115522.q: How was the microwave oven invented?
a: By chance while working on radar equipment
While looking for a better fridge
115522.e: In the 1940s, an engineer was working on radar equipment. A chocolate bar in his pocket melted. That is how he discovered that microwaves heat food.
115522.m: The microwave oven came from a chance discovery.

115523.q: Why shouldn't you put dishes with a metal rim in the microwave?
115523.e: Metal reflects microwaves. Strong electric fields can build up at edges and points, causing sparks and damaging the device.
115523.m: Metal does not belong in the microwave.

115524.q: What is the turntable in a microwave oven for?
a: So that the food heats more evenly
So that the device uses less electricity
So that the microwaves are produced
So that the food does not splash
115524.e: Inside the oven there are spots with strong and with weak radiation. By turning, the food moves through these zones and is heated more evenly.
115524.m: The turntable prevents cold spots in the food.

115525.q: What is the metal mesh in the door of a microwave oven for?
115525.e: The holes in the mesh are much smaller than the wavelength of the microwaves. So the microwaves cannot get through, but visible light can.
115525.m: The door mesh lets light out, but not microwaves.

115526.q: Why is defrosting in the microwave rather slow?
a: Ice absorbs the radiation less well than water
The microwave switches off in the cold
115526.e: In ice, the water molecules are firmly bound in the crystal lattice and can hardly turn. Only melted spots heat up quickly, which is why there is a special defrost setting.
115526.m: Liquid water heats up much better in the microwave than ice.

115527.q: Which part of a microwave oven produces the microwaves?
115527.e: The magnetron is a special electron tube. In it, electrons are steered in circles by a magnetic field and produce microwaves.

115529.q: Which ingredients in washing powder loosen grease and dirt from the fibres?
115529.e: Surfactants have a water-loving part and a fat-loving part. They surround droplets of grease so that these are rinsed away with the washing water.
115529.m: Surfactants are the real cleaning agents.

115530.q: What do enzymes in washing powder do?
a: They break stains down into small pieces
They give the washing a scent
115530.e: Enzymes break down, for example, protein from blood or egg and starch from sauces into small, water-soluble pieces. These are then rinsed away with the water.
115530.m: Enzymes break stains down into small pieces.

115531.q: Which stain consists mainly of starch?
115531.e: Potatoes, pasta and porridge contain a lot of starch. Special enzymes in washing powder break the starch down into small sugar units that dissolve in water.
115531.m: Starch stains come, for example, from potatoes or porridge.

115532.q: What are optical brighteners in washing powder for?
a: They make white washing look brighter
115532.e: Optical brighteners absorb invisible UV light and give off bluish light. This covers up a slight yellow tinge and the washing looks whiter.
115532.m: Optical brighteners make washing glow brighter.

115533.q: Why do you need more washing powder with hard water?
115533.e: Hard water contains a lot of calcium and magnesium. These ions bind some of the cleaning agents, so more washing powder or a softener is needed.
115533.m: The harder the water, the more washing powder is needed.

115534.q: Why were phosphates in laundry detergents banned in Switzerland?
115534.e: Phosphates got into the water with the waste water and made algae grow strongly. When the algae broke down, oxygen was removed from the lakes.
115534.m: Phosphate in waste water makes algae spread in lakes.

115535.q: Which ingredient in washing powder removes coloured stains such as tea or red wine?
115535.e: Bleaches such as sodium percarbonate release oxygen during washing. This destroys the dyes in the stains.
115535.m: Bleach destroys the dyes in stains.

115536.q: Why does washing at 30 instead of 60 degrees Celsius save energy?
115536.e: Most of a washing machine's energy is used to heat the water. Modern washing powders with enzymes work well even at low temperatures.

115537.q: What is making soap from fat and lye called?
115537.e: If you boil fats or oils with a lye, they split into glycerol and soap. This process is called saponification.
115537.m: Soap is made from fat and lye.

115538.q: Which part of a soap particle holds on to the grease?
115538.e: Soap particles have a long hydrocarbon tail that dissolves in fat and a charged head that points into the water.
115538.m: Soap particles are half fat-loving and half water-loving.

115539.q: How does soap remove grease from your hands?
a: Soap particles surround the grease and water rinses it away
Soap makes the grease rock hard
115539.e: Many soap particles gather around a droplet of grease and form a tiny ball, a micelle. This floats in the water and is rinsed away.
115539.m: Soap wraps up grease so water can rinse it away.

115540.q: Why is washing your hands with soap good against flu or coronaviruses?
115540.e: Many viruses such as flu and coronaviruses have an envelope made of fatty substances. Soap dissolves this envelope, and the viruses are rinsed off together with the dirt.
115540.m: Soap dissolves the fatty envelope of many viruses.

115541.q: What forms when soap dissolves in very hard water?
115541.e: Calcium and magnesium ions form insoluble lime soap with soap. It shows up as a grey ring in sinks and bathtubs.
115541.m: In hard water, soap forms lime soap.

115542.q: Why does a paper clip floating on water sink when you add soap to the water?
115542.e: Surface tension acts like a thin skin that carries the light paper clip. Soap weakens this skin, and the clip sinks.
115542.m: Soap weakens the surface tension of water.

115543.q: How does a solution of plain hard soap and water react?
115543.e: Soap is the salt of a weak fatty acid and a strong lye. Its solution therefore has a pH value well above 7.

115544.q: Which soap is soft and often used for cleaning floors?
115544.e: Soft soap is made with potassium hydroxide and stays soft. Solid soaps such as hard soap are made with sodium hydroxide.
115544.m: Soft soap is soft, hard soap is solid.

115545.q: Without protection, your skin goes red after 10 minutes. In theory, how long at most does a cream with sun protection factor 20 protect you?
115545.e: The sun protection factor is multiplied by your own protection time: 10 minutes times 20 gives 200 minutes. Experts advise using only about 60 per cent of that.
115545.m: Sun protection factor times your own protection time gives the theoretical protection time.

115546.q: Which UV radiation mainly causes sunburn?
115546.e: UV-B is high in energy and damages the top layer of skin, which leads to redness. The sun protection factor mainly refers to this range.

115547.q: What does UV-A radiation mainly do in the skin?
a: It goes deep and makes the skin age
It warms the skin without any effect
It makes the skin wet at once
115547.e: UV-A reaches deeper layers of skin and damages the elastic fibres there. This encourages wrinkles and can also contribute to skin cancer.
115547.m: UV-A makes the skin age early.

115548.q: Which substances do mineral sunscreens use as filters?
115548.e: Tiny particles of titanium dioxide and zinc oxide absorb most of the UV radiation. Only a small part is scattered or reflected.
115548.m: Mineral filters consist of tiny particles of metal oxides.

115549.q: What does putting cream on again after swimming do?
a: It keeps up the protection but does not extend it
It makes the skin brown at once
It is never needed with sun cream
115549.e: Water and drying off remove some of the cream. Putting more on restores the protection, but the maximum protection time does not start again.
115549.m: Putting on more cream does not extend the protection time.

115550.q: From which UV index is sun protection recommended?
115550.e: According to the World Health Organization, a UV index of 3 or more means a moderate level at which you should protect yourself.
115550.m: From UV index 3, you need sun protection.

115551.q: How does UV radiation change as you climb higher in the Swiss Alps?
115551.e: At altitude, the layer of air above you is thinner and filters out less UV radiation. That is why you need especially good sun protection in the mountains.
115551.m: UV radiation is stronger in the mountains.

115552.q: Why is sun protection especially important when skiing?
a: Snow produces its own UV radiation
The sun shines longer in winter
115552.e: Fresh snow reflects a large part of the UV radiation. The skin is then hit from above and below.

115553.q: What is the main aim of preserving food?
a: To slow down the growth of microorganisms
To make the taste ever sweeter
115553.e: Bacteria, yeasts and moulds make food go off. Preserving methods take away their water, warmth or oxygen, or kill them.

115554.q: Why does salted fish keep for a long time?
a: The salt draws water out of bacteria
The salt makes the fish cold
The salt forms a plastic layer
115554.e: Through osmosis, salt draws water out of the food and out of the bacterial cells. Without enough free water, germs can hardly multiply.

115555.q: Why do gherkins pickled in vinegar keep for a long time?
115555.e: Vinegar lowers the pH value a lot. In such an acidic environment, most bacteria that cause rotting cannot multiply.
115555.m: Acidic food goes off more slowly.

115556.q: Who is considered the inventor of preserving food by heating it in airtight containers?
115556.e: At the beginning of the 19th century, the French cook Nicolas Appert heated food in sealed glass bottles. He is seen as the founder of tinned and bottled food.

115557.q: Why does jam go off only slowly despite the fruit?
a: Lots of sugar binds the water
The jar is coated with salt inside
115557.e: The high sugar content binds the water, so microorganisms find hardly any free water. In addition, the jam is filled into jars while hot.

115558.q: Why does dried fruit hardly go off?
a: It contains only a little water
It contains a lot of salt
115558.e: When drying, most of the water is removed from the fruit. Without water, bacteria and moulds can hardly multiply.
115558.m: Dried food keeps for a long time.

115559.q: What does cooling in the fridge do to most bacteria?
115559.e: Cold slows down the bacteria's metabolism, but does not kill most of them. That is why even chilled food goes off after a while.
115559.m: Cooling slows bacteria down but usually does not kill them.

115560.q: Why does vacuum-packed meat keep longer?
a: Many germs need oxygen to grow
It is very hot in a vacuum
The vacuum makes the meat dry
115560.e: When vacuum packing, the air is sucked out of the packaging. Without oxygen, many spoilage germs grow more slowly, and the fat goes rancid less quickly.
115560.m: Without oxygen, food goes off more slowly.

115561.q: Which old preserving method uses the smoke of smouldering wood?
115561.e: When smoking, the surface of the food dries, and substances from the smoke slow down microorganisms. This makes ham or fish, for example, keep longer.
115561.m: Smoking makes meat and fish keep longer.

115562.q: What is the difference between sterilising and pasteurising?
115562.e: Sterilising heats well above 100 degrees Celsius. This kills all germs, including tough spores, which pasteurising does not.
115562.m: Sterilising kills all germs, pasteurising only most.

a: Brief heating below 100 degrees kills most germs
Exposure to light colours the milk
115563.e: A food is briefly heated to a temperature below boiling point. This kills most germs that cause illness.

115564.q: Roughly which temperature is milk heated to in short-time pasteurisation?
115564.e: In short-time heating, milk is heated to about 72 to 75 degrees Celsius for about 15 to 30 seconds and then cooled immediately.
115564.m: Pasteurised milk was only heated briefly.

115565.q: Why does unopened UHT milk keep for months without refrigeration?
a: It was briefly heated to a very high temperature
It contains a lot of salt
115565.e: UHT means ultra-high temperature: the milk is heated to over 135 degrees Celsius for a few seconds. This kills almost all germs, including most spores.
115565.m: UHT milk keeps for a long time.

115566.q: Among other things, pasteurising protects against which once-feared illness from cow's milk?
115566.e: In the past, germs of bovine tuberculosis could be passed on to humans through raw cow's milk. Pasteurising reliably kills these bacteria.
115566.m: Pasteurising protects against germs in milk.

115567.q: For which drink did Louis Pasteur originally develop the process?
115567.e: In the 1860s Pasteur investigated why wine goes off. He showed that brief warming kills the harmful microorganisms.
115567.m: Wine was the first thing to be pasteurised.

115568.q: From which milk is the Swiss cheese Le Gruyère AOP made?
115568.e: Unheated raw milk is used for Le Gruyère AOP. The long ripening and the way it is made ensure safety and the typical taste.
115568.m: Many Swiss hard cheeses are made from raw milk.

115569.q: What advantage does pasteurisation have over long boiling?
a: Taste and vitamins are better preserved
It is guaranteed to kill all spores
It makes food keep for years
It needs no energy at all
115569.e: Because the food is heated less strongly and for less time than when boiling, the taste, appearance and heat-sensitive vitamins change less.

a: Frozen water evaporates in a vacuum
The food is dried in the sun
115570.e: The food is frozen first. Then the air pressure in a chamber is lowered a lot, and the ice turns directly into water vapour.
115570.m: In freeze-drying, ice disappears directly as vapour.

115571.q: What is the direct change from solid to gas called?
115571.e: In sublimation, a solid becomes a gas without first becoming liquid. This happens to the ice in freeze-drying.
115571.m: Sublimation goes directly from solid to gas.

115572.q: Why is a vacuum needed for freeze-drying?
a: Ice only sublimates quickly at very low pressure
It gets very hot in a vacuum
The vacuum kills bacteria at once
115572.e: At normal air pressure, the ice would first melt when warmed. At very low pressure, however, it turns directly into vapour.
115572.m: Without low pressure, the ice would first turn liquid.

115573.q: Which well-known drink powder is often freeze-dried?
115573.e: For instant coffee, strong coffee is frozen and freeze-dried. With hot water, it quickly becomes a drink again.
115573.m: Instant coffee is often freeze-dried coffee.

115574.q: Why do mountaineers like taking freeze-dried meals with them?
115574.e: Because almost all the water has been removed, the meals weigh very little. On the way, you add hot water.
115574.m: Freeze-dried food is light to carry.

115575.q: What advantage does freeze-drying have over drying with heat?
a: Shape, flavour and nutrients are better preserved
115575.e: Because the food stays cold, heat-sensitive flavours and vitamins are protected. The shape also stays largely the same.

115576.q: Why does freeze-dried food keep for a long time?
a: Without water, germs can hardly multiply
It contains a lot of sugar
115576.e: Bacteria and moulds need water to grow. Because almost all the water has been removed, the food hardly goes off.
115576.m: Without water, food goes off much more slowly.

115577.q: Why do freeze-dried strawberries soak up water again very quickly?
a: They are full of tiny pores
They contain a lot of salt
115577.e: Where there were ice crystals before, fine holes are left after drying. Water quickly gets back in through this porous structure.
115577.m: Freeze-dried food is porous like a sponge.

115578.q: What does the non-stick coating of a frying pan do?
a: The pan stays cool on the outside
115578.e: Many non-stick pans are coated with the plastic PTFE. Water, fat and bits of food hardly stick to it.
115578.m: Food hardly sticks to a non-stick coating.

115579.q: How was the non-stick plastic PTFE discovered in 1938?
a: Through a find in a cave
115579.e: A chemist was investigating refrigerants and found a white, waxy powder in a gas cylinder. It was PTFE, which later turned out to be very slippery and heat-resistant.

115580.q: How can you tell that a non-stick pan should be replaced?
a: The coating is scratched or peeling off
The handle gets warm when cooking
115580.e: If the coating is damaged, food sticks and small particles can come loose. Then it is time for a new pan.
115580.m: A scratched non-stick pan should be replaced.

115581.q: Why does hardly anything stick to a PTFE coating?
a: Other substances are hardly attracted to it
115581.e: The fluorine atoms on the surface form almost no attractive forces with other substances. That is why water and fat roll off and food comes away easily.
115581.m: Non-stick surfaces hardly attract other substances.

115582.q: Why shouldn't you stir with a metal fork in a coated pan?
115582.e: Metal edges can scratch the thin coating. Food sticks to damaged spots, and the layer peels off over time.
115582.m: Use wooden or plastic utensils with coated pans.

115583.q: Why shouldn't you heat an empty coated pan on the highest setting?
a: The coating can break down and give off fumes
The hob switches off for ever
115583.e: An empty pan gets very hot very quickly. At too high temperatures, PTFE can break down and give off harmful fumes.
115583.m: Never overheat an empty non-stick pan.

115584.q: Which other kind of non-stick coating is made without PTFE?
115584.e: Ceramic coatings consist of a glass-like layer based on silicon. They are also non-stick, but often wear out faster.
115584.m: Ceramic is an alternative to PTFE.

115585.q: What else do plumbers use PTFE for?
115585.e: Thin PTFE tape is wrapped around threads. It seals the joint and makes screwing it together easier.

115586.q: What do the E numbers on food packaging refer to?
115586.e: Every food additive approved in the EU and Switzerland has an E number. This means it can be recognised whatever the language.

115587.q: Why is vitamin C added to apple juice, for example?
a: So that it does not turn brown
115587.e: Vitamin C, E 300 on packaging, protects against oxygen. This keeps the colour of the juice fresh for longer.
115587.m: Vitamin C stops food changing colour.

115588.q: What is citric acid often used for in drinks and sweets?
115588.e: Citric acid, E 330 on packaging, is an acidifier. It occurs naturally in lemons.

115589.q: What is an emulsifier such as lecithin in chocolate or margarine for?
115589.e: Fat and water normally do not mix. Emulsifiers have a fat-loving and a water-loving part and so keep both evenly spread.

115590.q: What is the gelling agent agar-agar obtained from?
115590.e: Agar-agar is obtained from the cell walls of certain red algae. It is a plant-based alternative to gelatine.
115590.m: Agar-agar is a gelling agent made from algae.

115591.q: Which gelling agent from apples or citrus peel is used for jam?
115591.e: Pectin is part of plant cell walls. Together with sugar and acid, it makes jam set.

115592.q: What are antioxidants used for in food?
a: So that fats do not go rancid
115592.e: Oxygen from the air can change fats and colourings. Antioxidants slow this reaction down, so food stays fresh longer.

115593.q: What do preservatives such as sorbic acid do?
a: They slow down moulds and yeasts
They make dough light and airy
115593.e: Sorbic acid (E 200) slows the growth of moulds and yeasts. It is used, for example, in baked goods or cheese.

115594.q: Which country runs the satellite navigation system GPS?
115594.e: GPS was built by the US Department of Defense and is now freely available to civilian users worldwide.
115594.m: GPS is the navigation system of the USA.

115596.q: Where are the satellites of a navigation system such as GPS?
a: At a height of 10 km like aeroplanes
115596.e: The GPS satellites orbit the Earth at a height of about 20,000 km. From there, they constantly send signals that a satnav receives.
115596.m: Navigation satellites orbit high above the Earth.

115598.q: How does a navigation receiver work out its distance from a satellite?
a: From the travel time of the radio signal
From the colour of the signal
With a laser beam to the satellite
From the loudness of a sound
115598.e: Each satellite sends the exact time. The distance comes from the time the signal takes to reach the receiver and the speed of light.
115598.m: Travel time times speed gives the distance.

115599.q: Why do navigation satellites carry atomic clocks?
a: Time must be measured extremely precisely
So that astronauts know the time
So that the satellites do not crash
115599.e: Even tiny time errors lead to big position errors. Atomic clocks are among the most accurate clocks there are.
115599.m: Satellite navigation needs very accurate clocks.

115600.q: A radio signal travels at 300,000 km/s. How far does it get in a millionth of a second?
115600.e: 300,000 km/s is 300,000,000 m/s. Times 0.000001 s gives 300 metres. That is why even a microsecond of clock error leads to a big mistake.
115600.m: Radio signals travel 300 metres in a microsecond.

115601.q: Apart from the satellite signal, what does a car satnav need to calculate a route?
115601.e: The satellite signal only provides the position. Only with a digital map can the device recognise roads and calculate the shortest or fastest route.
115601.m: A satnav combines position and a digital map.

115602.q: Besides temperature, what else does air conditioning often control?
115602.e: An air conditioner cools the air and removes moisture from it in the process. The first modern air conditioner, from 1902, was meant to do exactly that in a printing works.
115602.m: Air conditioning controls temperature and humidity.

115603.q: Where does the water that drips from an air conditioner come from?
a: From the moisture in the air
115603.e: The air cools down at the cold heat exchanger in the indoor unit. The water vapour in it condenses into drops, as on a cold glass.
115603.m: Air conditioners remove moisture from the air.

115604.q: Why does an air conditioner need a unit outside the room?
a: There it releases the heat outside
There it sucks in cold air
115604.e: The heat from the room has to go somewhere. The refrigerant carries it to the outdoor unit, where a fan releases it into the outside air.
115604.m: An air conditioner carries heat outside.

115605.q: How can a reversible air conditioner heat in winter?
a: It works as a heat pump
115605.e: If the cycle is reversed, the unit takes heat from the outside air and releases it in the room. It then works as a heat pump.
115605.m: A reversed air conditioner is a heat pump.

115606.q: Why does the air conditioning in a car help against misted-up windows?
115606.e: When the air cools, moisture condenses in the system. The drier air then takes up the mist from the windows.
115606.m: Dry air makes misted-up windows clear.

115607.q: How can you keep a flat cool in summer without air conditioning?
a: Close the blinds during the day and air the rooms at night
Open all the windows wide during the day
115607.e: Closed blinds keep the sun's rays out. At night the air is cooler and can cool the rooms.
115607.m: Blinds and airing at night keep rooms cool.

115608.q: Why does an air conditioner need electrical energy?
a: Heat does not flow from cool to warm by itself
Cold has to be stored in batteries
The room has to be lit
The refrigerant has to be melted
115608.e: By itself, heat always flows from a warm body to a cold one. To pump it from the cool room into the hot outside air, the compressor needs energy.
115608.m: Pumping heat the wrong way takes energy.

115609.q: In a split air conditioner, what connects the indoor unit to the outdoor unit?
a: An air shaft with fresh air
A water pipe with drinking water
A gas pipe with natural gas
115609.e: The indoor and outdoor units are connected by thin pipes in which the refrigerant circulates. So only a small hole needs to be drilled through the wall.
115609.m: In a split unit, refrigerant flows between inside and outside.

115610.q: Which cells form new bone matrix in bone?
115610.e: Osteoblasts are the bone-building cells. They sit on the bone surface and release the components of the bone matrix.
115610.m: Osteoblasts are the builders of bone.

115611.q: Which protein is the main organic component of the bone matrix that osteoblasts form?
115611.e: Around 90 per cent of the organic bone matrix is collagen. It makes bone resistant to pulling and slightly elastic.
115611.m: Collagen makes bone resistant to pulling.

115612.q: Which mineral is deposited in the matrix made by osteoblasts and makes bone hard?
115612.e: Osteoblasts first form a soft matrix. Only then are calcium phosphate crystals deposited in it, creating hard bone.

115613.q: From which cells do osteoblasts arise?
115613.e: Osteoblasts develop from connective tissue stem cells, which can also give rise to cartilage and fat cells.

115614.q: Which vitamin does the body need to absorb enough calcium from the gut for building bone?
115614.e: Vitamin D helps the gut absorb calcium. Without it, osteoblasts get too little building material and the bones become soft.
115614.m: Vitamin D helps absorb calcium for the bones.

115615.q: How do osteoblasts react when a bone is regularly put under load, for example through sport?
115615.e: Load is a signal for building bone. That is why people who do sport usually have higher bone density.

115616.q: Why do osteoblasts and osteoclasts work closely together in bone?
a: So that the bone is constantly remodelled and renewed
So that the bone can store blood
So that the bone never grows again
So that the bone turns into cartilage
115616.e: Osteoclasts break down old bone and osteoblasts build new bone. Osteoblasts even help control the formation of osteoclasts through signalling substances.
115616.m: Building and breaking down keep bone young.

115617.q: What happens if, over a long time, more bone is broken down than built up?
115617.e: If breakdown by osteoclasts outweighs building, bone density falls. This causes osteoporosis, in which bones break more easily.
115617.m: Too much breakdown makes bones brittle.

115618.q: Roughly how long does it take for an adult's skeleton to be completely renewed once by breakdown and rebuilding?
115618.e: About a tenth of the bone mass is replaced each year. Osteoblasts and osteoclasts are both involved.
115618.m: The skeleton renews itself about every ten years.

115619.q: Which cells break down bone substance?
115619.e: Osteoclasts are large eating cells of bone. They dissolve mineral and matrix and so make constant remodelling of the skeleton possible.
115619.m: Osteoclasts are the demolition crew of bone.

115620.q: Which cells of the immune system are osteoclasts related to?
115620.e: Osteoclasts come from precursors of the same cell line as the phagocytes (macrophages). Like them, they break down material.
115620.m: Osteoclasts are relatives of the phagocytes.

115621.q: How many cell nuclei do osteoclasts typically have?
115621.e: Osteoclasts form when several precursor cells fuse. That is why they usually have several, sometimes even dozens of nuclei.
115621.m: Osteoclasts are large giant cells with many nuclei.

115622.q: Where does the calcium go that osteoclasts release from bone?
115622.e: When bone is broken down, calcium is released and enters the blood. In this way the skeleton also serves as the body's calcium store.
115622.m: The skeleton is the body's calcium store.

115623.q: What role do osteoclasts play in healing a broken bone?
a: They remove excess bone and reshape it
They glue the broken ends together
115623.e: After a fracture, a thick callus of new bone forms first. Osteoclasts later break it down until the bone has its original shape again.
115623.m: Osteoclasts reshape the bone after a fracture.

115624.q: Which two components of the bone matrix must an osteoclast dissolve?
115624.e: The osteoclast dissolves the calcium phosphate with acid and breaks down the collagen with enzymes. Only then is the bone completely broken down.

115625.q: How do osteoclasts dissolve bone mineral?
a: They acidify the gap with protons
They release caustic soda into the gap
They split the mineral with lipases
They heat the bone strongly in one spot
115625.e: A proton pump in the ruffled border pumps H+ ions into the sealed-off gap. In the acidic environment the calcium phosphate dissolves.
115625.m: Acid dissolves the bone mineral beneath the osteoclast.

115626.q: Which thyroid hormone directly inhibits osteoclasts and so lowers the calcium level?
115626.e: Calcitonin is made in the C cells of the thyroid. It slows the osteoclasts, so that less calcium passes from the bone into the blood.

115627.q: What helps most in everyday life to prevent osteoporosis?
a: Exercise and enough calcium and vitamin D
Lots of sugar and little sleep
115627.e: Load stimulates bone building, and calcium and vitamin D provide the building material. Smoking and lack of exercise, by contrast, encourage bone loss.
115627.m: Exercise and calcium strengthen the bones.

115628.q: What are bone cells called that are completely enclosed in calcified matrix?
115628.e: Osteoblasts that have walled themselves in become osteocytes. They stay in the bone for many years and keep it alive.

115629.q: In which small cavities of the bone matrix do the cell bodies of osteocytes lie?
115629.e: Each osteocyte sits in its own small cavity of the matrix, a lacuna. From there fine channels run in all directions.
115629.m: Osteocytes live in small bone cavities.

115630.q: How are osteocytes connected to each other?
a: Not at all, they are isolated
115630.e: The cell extensions of osteocytes run in bone channels (canaliculi) and are linked by gap junctions. This creates a network through the whole bone.
115630.m: Osteocytes form a fine network through the bone.

115631.q: What main task is attributed to osteocytes today?
a: They sense load and control remodelling
They store fat for hard times
115631.e: Osteocytes register mechanical deformation and fluid flow in the bone. They then send signals to osteoblasts and osteoclasts.
115631.m: Osteocytes are the load sensors of bone.

115632.q: How do osteocytes react when a bone is hardly loaded, for example during long bed rest?
a: They send signals for more bone breakdown
They do not react at all
115632.e: Osteocytes sense that load is missing. They then slow down building, among other things with the protein sclerostin, and the bone gets thinner.
115632.m: Without load, osteocytes signal bone breakdown.

115633.q: Which cells are by far the most common in mature bone?
115633.e: Over 90 per cent of the bone cells in the adult skeleton are osteocytes. Osteoblasts and osteoclasts are much rarer.

115634.q: According to which law does bone adapt its shape and density to the load acting on it?
115634.e: The surgeon Julius Wolff described in 1892 that bone adapts to the forces acting on it. Osteocytes are considered the cells that sense this load.
115634.m: Bone becomes stronger where it is loaded.

115635.q: What happens to astronauts' bones during a long stay in weightlessness?
115635.e: Without load the signals for the osteocytes are missing, and breakdown outweighs building. Astronauts therefore lose bone mass and train against it every day.
115635.m: Without load the body breaks down bone.

115636.q: Where is hydroxyapatite found in the human body?
115636.e: Hydroxyapatite is a calcium phosphate mineral. It makes bones and teeth hard and stable.
115636.m: Hydroxyapatite makes bones and teeth hard.

115637.q: Roughly what percentage of bone weight is made up of mineral?
115637.e: By weight, bone is about 60 to 70 per cent mineral, mainly hydroxyapatite. The rest is organic matrix and water.
115637.m: More than half of bone weight is mineral.

115638.q: Which human tissue contains the highest proportion of hydroxyapatite?
115638.e: Tooth enamel is about 95 per cent hydroxyapatite and is the hardest tissue in the body. Bone and dentine contain much more organic material.
115638.m: Tooth enamel is almost pure mineral.

115639.q: Which ion can replace the hydroxide group of apatite in tooth enamel and make it more resistant to acid?
115639.e: Fluoride replaces OH- and fluorapatite forms, which dissolves less easily in acid. That is why many toothpastes contain fluoride.
115639.m: Fluoride hardens tooth enamel against acids.

115640.q: Which two minerals are the main components of hydroxyapatite?
