115640.e: Hydroxyapatite contains calcium ions and phosphate groups. That is why the skeleton is the body's largest store of calcium and phosphate.
115640.m: Bone mainly stores calcium and phosphate.

115641.q: Hydroxyapatite has the formula Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2. What is the ratio of calcium to phosphorus atoms?
115641.e: The formula contains 10 calcium and 6 phosphorus atoms. 10 divided by 6 is about 1.67.
115641.m: In hydroxyapatite there are 10 calcium atoms for every 6 phosphorus atoms.

115642.q: Which class of minerals does hydroxyapatite belong to?
115642.e: Hydroxyapatite is a mineral of the apatite group and belongs to the phosphates. It also occurs naturally in rocks.

115643.q: What is artificially made hydroxyapatite often used for in medicine?
a: As a coating for bone implants
As a contrast agent in ultrasound
115643.e: Because hydroxyapatite resembles bone mineral, bone grows onto it well. Hip replacements and dental implants are therefore often coated with it.
115643.m: Hydroxyapatite helps implants grow together with the bone.

115644.q: What is the cylinder-shaped basic unit of lamellar bone in compact bone called?
115644.e: An osteon (Haversian system) consists of several bone lamellae arranged around a central canal. Many osteons lie parallel along the long axis of the bone.
115644.m: The osteon is the building unit of compact bone.

115645.q: What runs through the central Haversian canal of an osteon?
115645.e: Small blood vessels and nerve fibres lie in the Haversian canal. They supply the osteocytes in the surrounding lamellae.
115645.m: The Haversian canal is the supply line of the osteon.

115646.q: How are the osteocytes deep inside hard bone supplied with nutrients?
a: Through blood vessels in fine canals
Through the air in the bones
Not at all, they need no nutrients
115646.e: Blood vessels run through the bone in lengthwise and crosswise canals. From there nutrients reach the cells through fine channels.
115646.m: Fine canals bring blood deep into the bone.

115647.q: How are the bone lamellae arranged in an osteon?
a: Stacked at right angles to the long axis
115647.e: The lamellae surround the Haversian canal like the growth rings of a tree. An osteon usually has about 4 to 20 such rings.
115647.m: The lamellae of an osteon lie in rings around the canal.

115648.q: Why are there often remains of old osteons between complete osteons?
a: Because the osteons are made of cartilage
115648.e: During bone remodelling, old osteons are partly broken down and new ones formed. The remains stay in between as interstitial lamellae.
115648.m: Remains of old osteons show the constant remodelling of bone.

115649.q: Roughly what order of magnitude is the diameter of an osteon?
a: A few tenths of a millimetre
115649.e: Osteons are usually about 0.1 to 0.4 millimetres thick and several millimetres long. They are easy to see under a light microscope.
115649.m: An osteon is only a fraction of a millimetre thick.

115650.q: In which part of the bone are osteons mainly found?
115650.e: The dense outer layer of bone, the compact bone, consists mostly of osteons. Spongy bone, by contrast, is built from fine struts.
115650.m: Osteons make compact bone firm and dense.

115651.q: Why do the collagen fibres of neighbouring lamellae run in different directions?
a: This increases the strength of the bone
This prevents any bending at all
115651.e: As in plywood, the fibres in each lamella run at a different angle. This lets the bone withstand forces from many directions.
115651.m: Changing fibre directions make bone especially stable.

115652.q: What is meant by intramembranous ossification?
a: Direct bone formation from connective tissue
Bone formation via a cartilage model
115652.e: In intramembranous ossification, osteoblasts arise directly in embryonic connective tissue (mesenchyme) and form bone. There is no cartilage stage.
115652.m: Intramembranous bones form without going through cartilage.

115653.q: Which bones typically form by intramembranous ossification?
a: Flat bones of the skull roof
115653.e: The frontal bone, the parietal bones and parts of the occipital bone ossify directly from connective tissue. They are therefore also called dermal bones.
115653.m: The skull roof forms directly from connective tissue.

115654.q: Why is a baby's skull not yet completely closed?
a: The skull bones have not fully ossified yet
The skull consists only of muscles
The brain lies outside the skull
The skull only forms at the age of ten
115654.e: In babies there are soft spots between the skull bones, the fontanelles. They let the brain grow and close during the first years of life.

115655.e: Calcium phosphate crystals are deposited in the bone matrix. They make bone hard, while collagen fibres make it elastic.

115656.q: What does the Greek word “desmos”, from which the German term “desmal” (intramembranous) comes, mean?
115656.e: In Greek, “desmos” means band or fetter. The name shows that the bone forms directly from connective tissue.

115657.q: Which thin membrane surrounds bone on the outside and is important for healing fractures?
115657.e: The periosteum has a good blood and nerve supply. Cells come from it that form new bone after a fracture.
115657.m: The periosteum helps broken bones heal.

115658.q: Why do children's bones often only crack instead of breaking right through?
115658.e: Children's bones contain more collagen, fewer minerals and a thick periosteum. That is why they tend to bend like a green twig rather than snap cleanly.
115658.m: Children's bones are more flexible than adults' bones.

115659.q: What are the places in connective tissue called where ossification begins?
115659.e: In ossification centres, mesenchyme cells gather, become osteoblasts and form bone struts. From there ossification spreads outwards.

115660.q: What is meant by endochondral ossification?
a: Bone formation via a cartilage model
Direct bone formation from connective tissue
Ossification of tendons in old age
115660.e: First a model of cartilage forms, which is then gradually broken down and replaced by bone. Most bones of the skeleton form this way.
115660.m: In endochondral ossification, cartilage is replaced by bone.

115661.q: Which bones form from a cartilage model?
a: Most bones, such as long bones and vertebrae
Only the bones of the skull roof
115661.e: Most bones of the skeleton are first laid down as cartilage and later replaced by bone. These include the long bones and the vertebrae.
115661.m: Most bones form from a cartilage model.

115662.e: Osteoblasts form bone substance. Osteoclasts, on the other hand, break bone down, so bone is constantly remodelled.
115662.m: Osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts break it down.

115663.q: Where does a long bone grow in length?
a: In the middle of the shaft
115663.e: The growth plate is a disc of cartilage between the shaft and the end of the bone. There, cartilage cells multiply and are then replaced by bone.
115663.m: Bones grow in length at the growth plates.

115664.q: What is the growth plate of a long bone made of in teenagers?
115664.e: The growth plate is a thin disc of cartilage between the shaft and the end of the bone. There, cartilage cells multiply and are later replaced by bone.
115664.m: Growth plates are made of cartilage.

115665.q: Which hormone from the pituitary gland stimulates bones to grow in length?
115665.e: Growth hormone (somatotropin) is made in the pituitary gland. It stimulates the cartilage cells in the growth plates to divide.
115665.m: Growth hormone drives growth in length.

115666.q: Where do adults still have smooth cartilage that allows gliding?
a: In the marrow cavity of bones
In the skin of the fingertips
115666.e: The joint surfaces are covered with smooth hyaline cartilage. It lets the bones glide in the joint with little friction.
115666.m: Joint cartilage lets the bones glide in the joint.

115667.q: Which hereditary disease with disturbed endochondral ossification is the most common cause of disproportionate short stature?
115667.e: In achondroplasia the gene FGFR3 is altered, so the cartilage cells in the growth plates are slowed down. As a result the arms and legs stay short while the trunk is almost normal in size.
115667.m: Achondroplasia slows growth at the growth plates.

115668.q: How can you tell on an X-ray that a bone has finished growing in length?
a: The shaft is made of cartilage
115668.e: As long as there is cartilage in the growth plate, it shows up as a light gap. Once it has been replaced by bone, the bone can no longer get longer.
115668.m: Closed growth plates mean the end of growth in length.

115669.q: In which organ is parathyroid hormone made?
115669.e: Parathyroid hormone comes from the chief cells of the parathyroid glands, of which there are usually four. They lie on the back of the thyroid gland.
115669.m: The parathyroid glands make parathyroid hormone.

115670.q: Which change in the blood triggers the release of parathyroid hormone?
115670.e: If free calcium in the blood falls, the glands release more parathyroid hormone. The hormone then makes sure that the calcium level rises again.
115670.m: Parathyroid hormone raises a calcium level that is too low.

115671.q: How does parathyroid hormone affect phosphate excretion in the kidney?
a: It has no effect on phosphate
115671.e: Parathyroid hormone inhibits the reabsorption of phosphate in the kidney tubules. As a result more phosphate is excreted and fewer calcium phosphate crystals form in the blood.
115671.m: Parathyroid hormone flushes phosphate out in the urine.

115672.q: How does parathyroid hormone affect calcium in the kidney?
a: It increases the reabsorption of calcium
It stores calcium in the kidney
115672.e: In the distal tubule, parathyroid hormone promotes the reabsorption of calcium into the blood. This means less calcium is lost in the urine.
115672.m: Parathyroid hormone keeps calcium in the body.

115673.q: Which vitamin does the kidney activate under the influence of parathyroid hormone so that the gut absorbs more calcium?
115673.e: Parathyroid hormone stimulates the kidney to make the active vitamin D hormone. This increases calcium uptake in the gut.
115673.m: Parathyroid hormone boosts the formation of active vitamin D in the kidney.

115674.q: What is an abnormal overactivity of the parathyroid glands called?
115674.e: In hyperparathyroidism too much parathyroid hormone is made, often because of a benign lump. Consequences can be a high calcium level, kidney stones and bone loss.
115674.m: Hyper means too much, hypo means too little.

115675.q: Which symptom is typical of a lack of parathyroid hormone?
115675.e: Without parathyroid hormone the calcium level falls. Nerves and muscles then become overexcitable, leading to tingling and cramps.
115675.m: Too little calcium in the blood leads to muscle cramps.

115676.q: Which group of hormones does parathyroid hormone belong to?
115676.e: Parathyroid hormone is built from amino acids, so it is a peptide hormone like insulin. Steroid hormones such as cortisol, by contrast, are made from cholesterol.
115676.m: Parathyroid hormone is a peptide hormone.

a: The active hormone form of vitamin D
115677.e: Calcitriol is 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, the most effective form of vitamin D. It acts like a hormone in the body.

115678.q: Which mineral in the blood does active vitamin D (calcitriol) mainly regulate?
115678.e: Calcitriol makes sure that enough calcium is absorbed from food. This keeps the calcium level in the blood stable, which is important for bones, muscles and nerves.
115678.m: Active vitamin D regulates the body's calcium balance.

115679.q: Where in the body is vitamin D3 made with the help of sunlight?
115679.e: UVB rays from the sun trigger the formation of a precursor of vitamin D3 in the skin. The liver and kidneys then convert it into the active form.
115679.m: Vitamin D forms in the skin with sunlight.

115680.q: Which kind of radiation does the body need to make vitamin D3 itself?
115680.e: In the skin, UVB rays convert 7-dehydrocholesterol into a precursor of vitamin D3. In winter, UVB radiation in central Europe is often too weak for this.
115680.m: The skin needs UVB light for vitamin D.

115681.q: What is the main effect of calcitriol in the gut?
115681.e: Calcitriol stimulates gut cells to make more calcium transport proteins. As a result more calcium from food is absorbed into the blood.
115681.m: Calcitriol helps the gut absorb calcium.

115682.q: Which disease develops in children from a severe lack of vitamin D?
115682.e: In rickets the growing bones are not properly mineralised and stay soft. Bow legs and deformities of the ribcage are typical.
115682.m: Lack of vitamin D makes children's bones soft.

115683.q: In which organ is vitamin D converted into active calcitriol in the final step?
115683.e: The liver first makes a storage form of vitamin D. In the kidney this becomes the active hormone calcitriol.

115684.q: How does calcitriol mainly act in its target cells?
a: Through a receptor in the cell nucleus
Through an ion channel in the membrane
Through a receptor on nerve cells
115684.e: Calcitriol is fat-soluble like a steroid hormone and enters the cell. There it binds to the vitamin D receptor, which acts as a transcription factor and switches genes on and off.
115684.m: Calcitriol acts directly on the cell's genes.

115685.q: After a cruciate ligament operation, how long does it usually take before competitive sport is possible again?
115685.e: The tendon graft first has to heal in and be remodelled. That is why athletes usually only return to competition after 6 to 12 months of rehabilitation training.
115685.m: After a cruciate ligament operation you need a lot of patience and training.

115686.q: Which movement does the anterior cruciate ligament mainly prevent?
115686.e: The anterior cruciate ligament runs at an angle from the shinbone backwards and upwards to the thigh bone. It stops the lower leg from sliding forwards relative to the thigh.
115686.m: The anterior cruciate ligament holds the lower leg back.

115687.q: In the Lachman test, how does a doctor check whether the anterior cruciate ligament is torn?
a: She measures the circumference of the thigh
115687.e: With the knee slightly bent, the shinbone is pulled forwards. If it slides far and without a firm stop, this suggests a tear.
115687.m: The Lachman test checks whether the shinbone slides too far forwards.

115688.q: Which type of accident typically leads to a torn anterior cruciate ligament?
a: Twisting the knee while the foot is fixed
115688.e: Often the body twists while the foot stays fixed on the ground or in a ski boot. This often happens when skiing or playing football or handball.
115688.m: Twisting movements with a fixed foot put the cruciate ligament at risk.

115689.q: Which imaging method shows a torn cruciate ligament best?
115689.e: Ligaments are soft tissues and hardly visible on an X-ray. MRI shows ligaments, menisci and cartilage in detail.
115689.m: MRI is the best imaging for ligaments.

115690.q: In an operation, what is a torn anterior cruciate ligament usually replaced with?
a: One of the patient's own tendons
115690.e: Usually a tendon from the back of the thigh or part of the patellar tendon is used. It is anchored in the bone and over months turns into ligament-like tissue.
115690.m: Cruciate ligament reconstruction usually uses one of the body's own tendons.

115691.q: Besides the anterior cruciate ligament, which structures belong to the classic “unhappy triad”?
115691.e: The “unhappy triad” is a combined knee injury of the anterior cruciate ligament, medial ligament and medial meniscus. It often happens through twisting with the knee bent inwards.
115691.m: The unhappy triad is a triple knee injury.

115692.q: Which finding suggests a tear of the posterior cruciate ligament?
a: The lower leg can be pushed backwards
The foot can no longer be stretched
The hip can no longer be turned
115692.e: The posterior cruciate ligament stops the shinbone from sliding backwards. If it is torn, a posterior drawer sign appears.
115692.m: The posterior cruciate ligament holds the lower leg forwards.

a: A sideways curve of the spine with twisting
An increased backward curve of the upper back
Wear of the spinal joints in old age
115693.e: In scoliosis the spine bends to the side and the vertebrae are also twisted. An increased backward curve, by contrast, is called kyphosis.
115693.m: Scoliosis is a spine bent and twisted to the side.

115694.q: Which form of scoliosis is the most common?
115694.e: In about 80 to 90 per cent of all cases of scoliosis no clear cause is known. This is then called idiopathic scoliosis.
115694.m: Most cases of scoliosis have no known cause.

115695.q: Which examination can measure the extent of scoliosis exactly?
115695.e: On the X-ray you can see the curve of the spine and measure its angle. This shows how severe the scoliosis is.
115695.m: Scoliosis is measured on an X-ray.

115696.q: At which stage of life is scoliosis in young people most likely to get worse?
a: During the growth spurt at puberty
In the first year of life
115696.e: As long as the spine is growing quickly, a curve can increase fast. That is why young people with scoliosis are checked regularly during this time.
115696.m: Scoliosis can get worse during the growth spurt.

115697.q: In the forward bending test, what typically shows on one side of the back?
115697.e: Because the vertebrae are twisted, the ribs on one side are pushed backwards. When bending forwards, this rib hump becomes clearly visible.
115697.m: When bending forwards, a rib hump gives scoliosis away.

115698.q: How is moderate scoliosis in growing young people often treated?
115698.e: A brace, for example a Chêneau brace, is meant to stop the curve getting worse during growth. Special physiotherapy is used as well.
115698.m: A brace slows scoliosis during growth.

115699.q: Why is very severe scoliosis operated on?
a: It can keep getting worse and squeeze the heart and lungs
Without an operation you stop growing
115699.e: Very severe curves often keep increasing even after growth has finished. They can deform the ribcage and so affect the heart and lungs.
115699.m: Only severe scoliosis is operated on.

115700.q: Which group is much more often affected by scoliosis in adolescence that needs treatment?
115700.e: Mild curves are about equally common in girls and boys. Stronger forms that need treatment, however, occur many times more often in girls.
115700.m: Girls more often have severe adolescent scoliosis.

115701.q: What comes out of the disc in a slipped disc?
115701.e: The spinal disc has a soft jelly-like core inside (nucleus pulposus) and a fibrous ring outside (annulus fibrosus). If the ring tears, core tissue can escape and press on nerves.
115701.m: In a slipped disc the jelly-like core pushes through the fibrous ring.

115702.q: In which section of the spine do slipped discs occur most often?
115702.e: The lumbar spine carries the most weight and is very mobile. Most slipped discs affect the segments L4/L5 and L5/S1.
115702.m: Slipped discs usually affect the lower back.

115703.q: Which symptom is typical of a slipped disc in the lumbar spine?
115703.e: If disc tissue presses on a nerve root, the pain radiates along the nerve into the leg. Numbness or tingling is often added.
115703.m: Pain radiating into the leg points to an irritated nerve root.

115704.q: Which sign counts as an emergency with a slipped disc?
115704.e: Problems with the bladder or bowel can point to cauda equina syndrome, in which many nerve roots are squeezed. A quick operation is then necessary.
115704.m: Bladder problems with back pain are an emergency.

115705.q: How is a slipped disc without paralysis usually treated first?
a: With weeks of strict bed rest
With a plaster cast around the trunk
115705.e: Most symptoms improve within weeks without an operation. Painkillers, physiotherapy and moving as normally as possible are recommended.
115705.m: Most slipped discs heal without an operation.

115706.q: Which lifting technique puts particular strain on the discs of the lumbar spine?
a: Lifting with a rounded back and straight legs
Lifting from the knees with a straight back
Holding the load close to the body
115706.e: Lifting with a rounded back and the load far from the body puts large lever forces on the discs. To protect your back, lift from the legs with a straight back.
115706.m: Lifting from the knees protects the discs.

115707.q: Where does pain from a slipped disc in the cervical spine typically radiate?
115707.e: The nerve roots of the cervical spine supply the shoulder, arm and hand. That is why slipped discs there cause pain and tingling in the arm.
115707.m: The neck and the arm are linked by nerves.

115708.q: What is a bulging of the disc called in which the fibrous ring has not yet broken through?
115708.e: In a protrusion the disc bulges out, but the fibrous ring stays intact. In a prolapse the ring has torn.
115708.m: In a protrusion the fibrous ring is still intact.

115710.q: A car starts from rest and accelerates steadily at 2.5 m/s² for 8 seconds. What speed does it reach?
115710.e: From rest, v equals a times t. So 2.5 m/s² times 8 s gives 20 m/s, which is 72 km/h.
115710.m: With no starting speed, the final speed is acceleration times time.

115711.q: A body starts from rest and accelerates steadily at 3 m/s² for 6 seconds. How far does it travel?
115711.e: s equals ½ times a times t². So 0.5 times 3 m/s² times 36 s² gives 54 m.
115711.m: From rest, the distance grows with the square of the time.

115712.q: Which quantity is constant in uniformly accelerated motion?
115712.e: Uniformly accelerated means that the speed changes by the same amount in equal intervals of time. The acceleration therefore stays constant.
115712.m: With uniform acceleration, the speed changes by the same amount every second.

115713.q: What shape does the velocity-time graph of uniformly accelerated motion have?
115713.e: The speed increases linearly with time. In a v-t graph this gives a straight line whose gradient is the acceleration.
115713.m: The gradient in a v-t graph is the acceleration.

115714.q: What shape does the position-time graph of uniformly accelerated motion from rest have?
115714.e: The position depends on the square of the time. The graph of a quadratic function is a parabola.
115714.m: Accelerated motion shows a curved line in an s-t graph.

115715.q: A skateboard is accelerated steadily from 4 m/s to 10 m/s. What is its average speed during this phase?
115715.e: With constant acceleration, the average speed is the mean of the starting and final speeds. 4 plus 10 gives 14, divided by 2 gives 7 m/s.
115715.m: With uniform acceleration, the average speed lies exactly in the middle.

115716.q: A car is travelling at 108 km/h and brakes steadily at 5 m/s² until it stops. How long is the braking distance?
115716.e: 108 km/h is 30 m/s. The braking distance is v² divided by 2a, so 900 divided by 10, which gives 90 m.
115716.m: At double the speed, the braking distance becomes four times as long.

115717.q: A train accelerates steadily from 0 to 30 m/s in 60 seconds. What is its acceleration?
115717.e: Acceleration is the change in speed divided by the time. 30 m/s divided by 60 s gives 0.5 m/s².
115717.m: Acceleration is change in speed per unit of time.

115718.q: What is the position-time law for uniformly accelerated motion with starting position s0 and starting speed v0?
115718.e: To the starting position you add the distance due to the starting speed and the distance due to the acceleration. The acceleration part is ½·a·t².
115718.m: In the position law, the acceleration term has the factor one half.

115719.q: Which equation of motion links speed and distance without time?
115719.e: If you substitute t from v equals v0 plus a·t into the position law, you get v² equals v0² plus 2·a·s. This form is useful for braking distances.
115719.m: Without a time, the equation with v squared helps.

115720.q: A body starts at 3 m/s and accelerates at 1.5 m/s² for 4 seconds. What speed does it have afterwards?
115720.e: v equals v0 plus a times t. 3 m/s plus 1.5 times 4 gives 3 plus 6, so 9 m/s.
115720.m: Acceleration times time is added to the starting speed.

115721.q: How far does a body fall from rest in the first 2 seconds (g = 9.81 m/s², no air resistance)?
115721.e: s equals ½·g·t². 0.5 times 9.81 times 4 gives about 19.6 m.
115721.m: The falling distance grows with the square of the fall time.

115722.q: A locomotive slows down steadily at 4 m/s² from 30 m/s to 10 m/s. How far does it travel while doing so?
115722.e: From v² equals v0² plus 2·a·s it follows that s equals (900 minus 100) divided by 8. That gives 800 divided by 8, so 100 m.
115722.m: Without a time, you calculate with the squares of the speeds.

115723.q: A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance). How high does it rise?
115723.e: At the highest point, v is zero. From v0² equals 2·g·h it follows that h equals 400 divided by 20, so 20 m.
115723.m: The height reached is v0 squared divided by 2g.

115724.q: A ball is thrown straight up at 15 m/s (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance). After what time does it reach the highest point?
115724.e: The speed decreases by 10 m/s every second. Until it reaches zero takes 15 divided by 10, so 1.5 s.
115724.m: The rise time is the starting speed divided by g.

115725.q: A car is travelling at 10 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 seconds. How far does it travel in that time?
115725.e: s equals v0·t plus ½·a·t². That gives 10 times 5 plus 0.5 times 2 times 25, so 50 m plus 25 m equals 75 m.
115725.m: With a starting speed, v0 times t is added to the acceleration distance.

115726.q: Into which two component motions is an angled throw without air resistance split?
a: Uniform horizontally and uniformly accelerated vertically
Uniformly accelerated horizontally and uniform vertically
115726.e: No force acts horizontally, so the speed stays constant. Vertically, gravity acts and accelerates the body downwards at g.
115726.m: In a throw, two independent motions are combined.

115727.q: A ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 60 degrees to the horizontal. What is the horizontal component of its velocity?
115727.e: The horizontal component is v0 times cos α. 20 m/s times cos 60° gives 20 times 0.5, so 10 m/s.
115727.m: The horizontal component is calculated with the cosine.

115728.q: A ball is thrown at 30 m/s at 30 degrees to the horizontal. What is the vertical starting speed?
115728.e: The vertical component is v0 times sin α. 30 m/s times sin 30° gives 30 times 0.5, so 15 m/s.
115728.m: The vertical component is calculated with the sine.

115729.q: One ball is thrown horizontally while a second one is dropped from the same height at the same moment. Without air resistance, which hits the ground first?
115729.e: The vertical motion is the same for both balls: they start with zero vertical speed and are accelerated at g. The horizontal speed does not change the fall time.
115729.m: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent of each other.

115730.q: At which point is the magnitude of the velocity smallest in an angled throw without air resistance?
115730.e: At the highest point the ball is no longer rising and not yet falling; only the horizontal motion is left. That is why it is slowest there.
115730.m: A thrown ball is slowest at the very top.

115731.q: A ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 30 degrees (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance). After what time does it reach the highest point?
115731.e: The vertical starting speed is 20 times sin 30°, so 10 m/s. Until it falls to zero takes 10 divided by 10, so 1 s.
115731.m: The rise time depends only on the vertical starting speed.

115732.q: A ball is thrown at 40 m/s at 30 degrees and lands at launch height (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance). How long does it fly?
115732.e: The vertical component is 40 times 0.5, so 20 m/s. The rise time is 2 s, and because the path is symmetrical, the whole flight takes 4 s.
115732.m: The flight time back to launch height is twice the rise time.

115733.q: What acceleration acts at the highest point of an angled throw without air resistance?
115733.e: Gravity acts unchanged throughout the whole flight, even at the highest point. That is why the acceleration is g vertically downwards everywhere.
115733.m: Gravitational acceleration acts downwards unchanged during the whole flight.

115734.q: A ball rolls horizontally at 2 m/s over the edge of a platform 1.8 m high (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance). How far from the edge does it land?
115734.e: The fall time is the square root of 2 times 1.8 divided by 10, so 0.6 s. In this time the ball travels 2 m/s times 0.6 s horizontally, so 1.2 m.
115734.m: In a horizontal throw, the height of the drop determines the flight time.

115735.q: In which type of throw is the highest point of the parabola exactly at the launch point?
115735.e: In a horizontal throw the vertical starting speed is zero, so the body starts at the highest point. The path is a descending half of a parabola.
115735.m: A horizontal throw begins at the top of its parabola.

115736.q: What is the path equation y(x) of an angled throw from the origin with launch angle α and speed v0?
115736.e: You solve x equals v0·cos α·t for t and substitute it into y equals v0·sin α·t minus ½·g·t². This gives the quadratic equation in x.
115736.m: The path curve is obtained by eliminating time from both component motions.

115737.q: How does air resistance change the path of a thrown ball compared with a parabola?
a: The descending part becomes steeper and shorter
The path stays exactly the same
The ball flies further than without air
115737.e: Air resistance mainly slows down the horizontal motion. This makes the path unsymmetrical; it is called a ballistic curve.
115737.m: With air resistance, a ball comes down more steeply at the end.

115738.q: A ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 30 degrees (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance). How high is the highest point above the launch height?
115738.e: The maximum height is v0²·sin² α divided by 2g. That gives 400 times 0.25 divided by 20, so 5 m.
115738.m: Only the vertical starting speed counts for the maximum height.

115739.q: At which launch angle does a throw with a given starting speed reach the greatest height?
115739.e: The height depends on v0·sin α. The sine is greatest at 90 degrees, in other words for a throw straight up.
115739.m: Throwing straight up gives the greatest height.

115740.q: Which scientist showed in his “Discorsi” in 1638 that the path of a thrown object is a parabola?
115740.e: In his work “Discorsi”, Galileo Galilei described the path of a throw as a combination of two motions. The parabolic shape followed from this.
115740.m: Galileo recognised the parabolic shape of a throw’s path.

115741.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 5 m/s (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance). How far has it dropped when it has travelled 2 m horizontally?
115741.e: For 2 m it needs 2 divided by 5, so 0.4 s. In this time it falls ½ times 10 times 0.16, so 0.8 m.
115741.m: In a horizontal throw, the drop grows with the square of the distance.

115742.q: Without air resistance, what is the magnitude of a ball’s velocity when it arrives back at launch height?
a: Twice as large as at launch
Half as large as at launch
115742.e: The parabola is symmetrical and no energy is lost. The vertical component has the same magnitude on impact; only the direction is reversed.
115742.m: Without friction, a ball lands as fast as it was thrown.

115743.q: What is the formula for the range of an angled throw on level ground without air resistance?
115743.e: The flight time is 2·v0·sin α divided by g. Multiplied by the horizontal speed v0·cos α, and using 2·sin α·cos α equals sin 2α, this gives the formula.
115743.m: The range depends on the sine of double the launch angle.

115744.q: A ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 60 degrees (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance, level ground). How far does it fly?
115744.e: Double the angle is 120 degrees, and sin 120° is about 0.866. 400 times 0.866 divided by 10 gives about 34.6 m.
115744.m: Steep throws go high but less far.

115745.q: A ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 45 degrees (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance, level ground). How far does it fly?
115745.e: W equals v0² times sin 90° divided by g. That gives 400 times 1 divided by 10, so 40 m.
115745.m: At 45 degrees, the range is v0 squared divided by g.

115746.q: A stone is thrown at 30 m/s at 15 degrees (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance, level ground). What is the range?
115746.e: Double the angle is 30 degrees, and sin 30° is 0.5. So 900 times 0.5 divided by 10 gives 45 m.
115746.m: The range formula contains the sine of double the angle.

115747.q: Without air resistance, to what percentage does the range fall if you reduce the launch angle from 45 to 30 degrees at the same speed?
115747.e: The range is proportional to sin 2α. At 45 degrees sin 90° equals 1, at 30 degrees sin 60° is about 0.87.
115747.m: Small deviations from the best angle only cost a little range.

115748.q: Without air resistance, how does the range change if you double the launch speed and keep the angle?
a: It becomes four times as large
It becomes eight times as large
115748.e: The range is proportional to v0². If you double v0, the range increases by a factor of 2², so 4.
115748.m: Double the launch speed gives four times the range.

115749.q: Why is the best launch angle in shot put below 45 degrees?
a: Because the shot is released above the landing point
Because the shot is heavier than a ball
Because air resistance lifts the shot
Because the Earth turns beneath the shot
115749.e: The shot leaves the hand about 2 m above the ground. If the launch point is higher than the landing point, a flatter angle is better; in addition, you can push faster at a flatter angle.
115749.m: A raised launch point calls for a flatter angle.

115750.q: How does the range change on the Moon, where g is about one sixth of the Earth’s value, at the same launch speed and angle?
a: It becomes about six times as large
It becomes about 36 times as large
It becomes about one sixth as large
115750.e: In the formula, g is in the denominator. If g is six times smaller, the range becomes six times larger.
115750.m: The smaller the gravitational acceleration, the further a throw goes.

115751.q: At what speed must you throw at 45 degrees to reach 90 m on level ground (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance)?
115751.e: At 45 degrees, W equals v0² divided by g. So v0² equals 90 times 10, which is 900, and v0 equals 30 m/s.
115751.m: For the launch speed, take the square root of range times g.

115752.q: What path does a point on the rim of a rolling bicycle wheel trace relative to the road?
115752.e: The point turns around the wheel’s axle while the axle moves forwards in a straight line. Combining the two gives a cycloid with arches.
115752.m: Circular motion plus forward motion gives a cycloid.

115753.q: Why is uniform circular motion an accelerated motion despite constant speed?
a: The direction of the velocity changes all the time
115753.e: Velocity is a vector with magnitude and direction. Even if only the direction changes, there is an acceleration.
115753.m: A change of direction is also an acceleration.

115754.q: How much work does the centripetal force do on a body in uniform circular motion?
a: None, because it acts at right angles to the motion
A great deal, because it acts all the time
Exactly as much as the weight
More and more with every lap
115754.e: Work is only done by parts of a force in the direction of motion. The centripetal force acts at right angles to the path, so the kinetic energy stays constant.
115754.m: A force at right angles to the motion does no work.

115755.q: Which force acts as the centripetal force and keeps the Moon in its orbit around the Earth?
115755.e: The Earth’s attraction constantly pulls the Moon towards the centre of the Earth. Without it, the Moon would fly straight off into space.
115755.m: Gravity steers the Moon onto a circular path.

115756.q: A stone is whirled round in a circle on a string. How does it move if the string suddenly breaks?
115756.e: Without a centripetal force there is nothing left to change the direction. According to the law of inertia, the stone flies on in a straight line in the direction it had at that moment.
115756.m: Without a centripetal force, a body flies off along the tangent.

115757.q: In which unit is the frequency of circular motion given?
115757.e: Frequency gives the number of revolutions per second. One hertz means one revolution per second.

115758.q: Which force acts as the centripetal force when a car drives round a bend on a level road?
a: Static friction between tyres and road
The engine force in the direction of travel
115758.e: The tyres press sideways against the road, and static friction steers the car towards the centre of the bend. On black ice this force is missing and the car slides straight on.
115758.m: On bends, friction keeps the car on its path.

115759.q: A 1000 kg car drives at 20 m/s round a bend with a radius of 50 m. What centripetal force is needed?
115759.e: F equals m·v² divided by r. 1000 times 400 divided by 50 gives 8000 N.
115759.m: The centripetal force depends on mass, speed and the radius of the bend.

115760.q: How is angular velocity ω defined?
a: Angle swept per unit of time
Distance covered per unit of time
Change in speed per unit of time
115760.e: Angular velocity tells you how quickly the angle of rotation changes. It is usually measured in radians per second.
115760.m: Angular velocity tells you how fast something is turning.

115761.q: A roundabout turns once in 4 seconds. What is its angular velocity?
115761.e: ω equals 2π divided by T. 6.28 divided by 4 gives about 1.57 rad/s.
115761.m: One full turn corresponds to an angle of 2π.

115762.q: Roughly what is the angular velocity of the Earth as it turns on its own axis?
115762.e: The Earth turns once on its axis in about 86,164 seconds (one sidereal day). 2π divided by this time gives about 7.3 · 10^-5 rad/s.
115762.m: The Earth turns very slowly but steadily.

115763.q: A motor turns at 3000 revolutions per minute. What is its angular velocity?
115763.e: 3000 revolutions per minute is 50 per second. ω equals 2π times 50, which gives about 314 rad/s.
115763.m: Angular velocity is 2π times the frequency.

115764.q: Which quantity is the same for all points on a rotating rigid disc?
115764.e: All points on the disc sweep the same angle in the same time. Further out, however, they are moving faster.
115764.m: On a rigid disc, all points turn at the same rate.

115765.q: A point moves at 10 m/s on a circle with a radius of 0.5 m. What is its angular velocity?
115765.e: From v equals ω times r it follows that ω equals v divided by r. 10 divided by 0.5 gives 20 rad/s.
115765.m: Angular velocity is linear speed divided by radius.

115766.q: What is the angular velocity of the second hand of a clock?
115766.e: The second hand takes 60 seconds for one round. 2π divided by 60 gives about 0.105 rad/s.
115766.m: The second hand needs one minute for the full angle of 2π.

115767.q: In which direction does the angular velocity vector point?
a: At right angles to the plane of rotation along the axis
Along the tangent to the circle
Towards the centre of the circle
115767.e: The vector lies on the axis of rotation. Its direction is found with the right-hand rule: the curled fingers point in the direction of rotation.
115767.m: The angular velocity vector lies on the axis of rotation.

115768.q: A point goes once round a circle with a radius of 0.3 m in 0.5 s. What is its linear speed?
115768.e: Linear speed is the circumference divided by the period. 2π times 0.3 m gives about 1.88 m, divided by 0.5 s gives about 3.8 m/s.
115768.m: Linear speed is circumference divided by period.

115769.q: A Ferris wheel with a diameter of 50 m turns once in 10 minutes. How fast does a cabin on the rim move?
115769.e: The circumference is π times 50 m, so about 157 m. Divided by 600 s, this gives about 0.26 m/s.
115769.m: A Ferris wheel moves more slowly at the rim than a person walking.

115770.q: A disc turns at 500 revolutions per minute. How fast does a point 6 cm from the axis move?
115770.e: 500 revolutions per minute is about 8.33 per second. Each revolution the point covers 2π times 0.06 m, so about 0.377 m, which gives about 3.1 m/s.
115770.m: Linear speed is calculated from rotation rate and radius.

115771.q: Roughly how fast does a place in Switzerland at about 47 degrees north move because of the Earth’s rotation?
115771.e: At 47 degrees latitude, the distance to the Earth’s axis is only cos 47° times the Earth’s radius, so about 0.68 times as large. 0.68 times 1670 km/h gives about 1140 km/h.
115771.m: The closer to the poles, the slower the speed due to the Earth’s rotation.

115772.q: A bicycle wheel with a radius of 0.35 m turns at 20 rad/s. How fast does a point on the tyre move around the axle?
115772.e: v equals ω times r. 20 rad/s times 0.35 m gives 7 m/s, so about 25 km/h.
115772.m: Linear speed is angular velocity times radius.

115773.q: A point on a turntable is twice as far from the axis as another. How does its linear speed compare?
a: It is four times as large
115773.e: Both points have the same angular velocity. Since v is proportional to r, the outer point is twice as fast.
115773.m: Double the radius means double the linear speed.

115774.q: Roughly at what speed does the International Space Station ISS orbit the Earth?
115774.e: The ISS flies at an altitude of about 400 km at about 7.7 km/s. That is about 28,000 km/h.
115774.m: Satellites in low orbit are extremely fast.

115775.q: How are the period T and frequency f of circular motion related?
115775.e: Frequency counts revolutions per second, and the period is the duration of one revolution. That is why one quantity is the reciprocal of the other.
115775.m: Period and frequency are reciprocals of each other.

115776.q: A wheel turns at a frequency of 50 Hz. What is the period?
115776.e: At 50 Hz the wheel makes 50 revolutions per second. One second divided by 50 gives 0.02 s, so 20 milliseconds.
115776.m: High frequency means a short period.

115777.q: Roughly how long does the Moon take for one orbit around the Earth, measured against the fixed stars?
115777.e: The Moon’s sidereal period is about 27.3 days. From full moon to full moon takes a little longer, because in the meantime the Earth has moved on around the Sun.
115777.m: The Moon circles the Earth in just under a month.

115778.q: A vinyl record turns at 33⅓ revolutions per minute. What is its period?
115778.e: There are 33⅓ revolutions per minute. 60 s divided by 33⅓ gives 1.8 s per revolution.
115778.m: The period is the total time divided by the number of revolutions.

115779.q: A Ferris wheel makes 12 revolutions in 6 minutes. What is the period?
115779.e: 6 minutes is 360 seconds. 360 s divided by 12 revolutions gives 30 s per revolution.
115779.m: For the period, divide the time by the number of rounds.

115780.q: A body turns at an angular velocity of 0.5 rad/s. What is its period?
115780.e: T equals 2π divided by ω. 6.28 divided by 0.5 gives about 12.6 s.
115780.m: The smaller the angular velocity, the longer the period.

115781.q: A planet has a semi-major axis four times as large as the Earth’s. According to Kepler’s third law, how long does its orbit around the Sun take?
115781.e: According to Kepler, T² is proportional to a³. 4³ gives 64, and the square root of 64 is 8, so the orbit takes 8 years.
115781.m: More distant planets need disproportionately longer for one orbit.

115782.q: Roughly how long is the period of a geostationary satellite?
115782.e: A geostationary satellite circles exactly as fast as the Earth turns, so once per sidereal day of about 23 hours 56 minutes. That is why it appears to stand still in the sky.
115782.m: Geostationary satellites turn along with the Earth.

115783.q: A body moves at π m/s on a circle with a radius of 2 m. What is the period?
115783.e: The circumference is 2π times 2 m, so 4π m. Divided by π m/s, this gives 4 s.
115783.m: The period is circumference divided by linear speed.

115784.q: How do you calculate centripetal acceleration from linear speed v and radius r?
115784.e: Centripetal acceleration grows with the square of the speed and falls as the radius gets larger. That is why a equals v² divided by r.
115784.m: Fast through tight bends means a large centripetal acceleration.

115785.q: What is the centripetal acceleration expressed with angular velocity ω and radius r?
115785.e: If you substitute v equals ω times r into a equals v² divided by r, you get ω² times r. At the same rotation rate, the acceleration is greater further out.
115785.m: At a fixed rotation rate, centripetal acceleration grows with the radius.

115786.q: A child sits 2 m from the axis of a roundabout that turns once in 4 s. What is the child’s centripetal acceleration?
115786.e: The linear speed is 2π times 2 m divided by 4 s, so about 3.14 m/s. Its square divided by 2 m gives about 4.9 m/s².
115786.m: On a roundabout you feel the centripetal acceleration as a pull outwards.

115787.q: A body moves at 10 m/s on a circle with a radius of 20 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
115787.e: a equals v² divided by r. 100 divided by 20 gives 5 m/s².
115787.m: For centripetal acceleration, square the speed first.

115788.q: A car drives at 72 km/h round a bend with a radius of 100 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
115788.e: 72 km/h is 20 m/s. 20² divided by 100 gives 400 divided by 100, so 4 m/s².
115788.m: Convert km/h into m/s before calculating.

115789.q: How does the centripetal acceleration change if you drive round a bend with twice the radius at the same speed?
a: It becomes four times as large
115789.e: At the same speed, centripetal acceleration is inversely proportional to the radius. Double the radius gives half the acceleration.
115789.m: Wide bends are gentler at the same speed.

115790.q: A laboratory centrifuge turns at 3000 revolutions per minute, and the sample is 10 cm from the axis. Roughly how many g does the sample experience?
115790.e: ω is 2π times 50 per second, so about 314 rad/s. ω² times 0.1 m gives about 9870 m/s², which divided by 9.81 m/s² is about 1000 g.
115790.m: Centrifuges produce many times the Earth’s gravitational acceleration.

115791.q: Roughly what is the centripetal acceleration of the Moon in its orbit around the Earth?
115791.e: With an orbital radius of about 384,000 km and a period of 27.3 days, a equals 4π²r divided by T² gives about 0.0027 m/s². Newton used this to show that the Earth’s gravity decreases with the square of the distance.
115791.m: At the distance of the Moon’s orbit, the Earth’s gravity is very weak.

115792.q: A body moves according to x(t) = 2t³ − 3t² (x in m, t in s). What is its velocity at time t = 3 s?
115792.e: The derivative is v(t) equals 6t² minus 6t. For t equals 3 s this gives 54 minus 18, so 36 m/s.
115792.m: When differentiating a power, the exponent becomes a factor and is reduced by one.

115793.q: Which quantity do you get from the second derivative of position with respect to time?
115793.e: The first derivative gives the velocity, and its derivative gives the acceleration. That is why acceleration is the second derivative of position.
115793.m: The second derivative of position is the acceleration.

115794.q: A body moves according to x(t) = 3t² + 2t (x in m, t in s). What is its velocity at time t = 2 s?
115794.e: The derivative is v(t) equals 6t plus 2. For t equals 2 s this gives 12 plus 2, so 14 m/s.
115794.m: You get the instantaneous velocity by differentiating position.

115795.q: A body moves according to x(t) = 5t³ (x in m, t in s). What is its acceleration at time t = 1 s?
115795.e: The first derivative is 15t², the second 30t. For t equals 1 s this gives 30 m/s².

115796.q: What is the derivative of acceleration with respect to time called?
115796.e: Jerk describes how quickly acceleration changes and has the unit m/s³. A large jerk can be felt, for example, when braking suddenly.
115796.m: Jerk is the rate of change of acceleration.

115797.q: What does the instantaneous velocity mean geometrically in a position-time graph?
a: The distance from the time axis
115797.e: The derivative at a point is the gradient of the tangent to the graph. In an s-t graph, that is the velocity at that moment.
115797.m: A steep tangent in an s-t graph means high velocity.

115798.q: A body oscillates according to x(t) = 4·sin(2t) (x in m, t in s). What is its velocity at time t = 0?
115798.e: The derivative is v(t) equals 8·cos(2t). At t equals 0, cos 0 equals 1, so v equals 8 m/s.
115798.m: When differentiating sin(kt), the factor k is added.

115799.q: A ball moves according to x(t) = -2t² + 8t (x in m, t in s). At what time is its velocity zero?
115799.e: The derivative is v(t) equals -4t plus 8. Setting it to zero gives t equals 2 s; that is where the ball turns round.
115799.m: Where the derivative is zero, the motion reverses.

115800.q: What does the gradient of the secant between two points in a position-time graph tell you?
115800.e: The secant connects two points; its gradient is the change in position divided by the change in time. That is the average velocity over that period.
115800.m: The secant gradient gives the average velocity.

115801.q: A cyclist rides east at 6 m/s, a runner runs north at 3 m/s. What is the magnitude of their relative velocity?
115801.e: The velocities are at right angles to each other. The magnitude of the difference is the square root of 36 plus 9, so the square root of 45, about 6.7 m/s.
115801.m: With movements at right angles, Pythagoras’ theorem helps.

115802.q: A car at 120 km/h overtakes a lorry at 90 km/h. At what relative speed does it approach the lorry?
115802.e: When travelling in the same direction, you subtract the speeds from each other. 120 minus 90 gives 30 km/h.
115802.m: In the same direction, only the difference in speed counts.

115803.q: A swimmer swims across a river at 1.2 m/s, and the current is 0.5 m/s. How fast does the swimmer move relative to the bank?
115803.e: The two velocities are at right angles to each other. By Pythagoras, the magnitude is the square root of 1.44 plus 0.25, so the square root of 1.69 equals 1.3 m/s.
115803.m: Velocities at right angles are added with Pythagoras’ theorem.

115804.q: An aeroplane flies at 800 km/h relative to the air straight into a wind of 100 km/h. How fast is it relative to the ground?
115804.e: The headwind acts against the direction of flight. 800 minus 100 gives 700 km/h over the ground.
115804.m: A headwind reduces the speed over the ground.

115805.q: A car at 30 m/s overtaking a lorry at 25 m/s has to gain 100 m on it. How long does that take?
115805.e: The relative speed is 30 minus 25, so 5 m/s. 100 m divided by 5 m/s gives 20 s.
115805.m: When overtaking, the relative speed is what counts.

115806.q: Rain falls vertically at 6 m/s, and a cyclist rides at 8 m/s. How fast do the drops hit her from her point of view?
115806.e: From the cyclist’s point of view, the rain comes at an angle from the front. The velocities are at right angles, so the square root of 36 plus 64 equals 10 m/s.
115806.m: From a moving vehicle, rain seems to fall at an angle.

115807.q: In classical mechanics, what is the conversion of positions and velocities between uniformly moving frames of reference called?
115807.e: In classical mechanics, velocities are simply added as vectors; this is described by the Galilean transformation. Only at very high speeds do you need the Lorentz transformation.
115807.m: In everyday life, velocities are simply added.

115808.q: A person walks at 1 m/s on a 30 m long escalator that moves at 0.5 m/s in the same direction. How long does it take to reach the end?
115808.e: Relative to the building, the person moves at 1 plus 0.5, so 1.5 m/s. 30 m divided by 1.5 m/s gives 20 s.
115808.m: On a moving walkway, walking speed and belt speed add up.

115809.q: A boat travels upstream at 5 m/s relative to the water, and the current is 2 m/s. How long does it take for 600 m upstream?
115809.e: Relative to the bank, the boat is only moving at 5 minus 2, so 3 m/s. 600 m divided by 3 m/s gives 200 s.
115809.m: Against the current, you subtract the speed of the current.

115810.q: Where in the chloroplast do the light reactions of photosynthesis take place?
115810.e: The photosystems and electron carriers sit in the thylakoid membranes. The Calvin cycle, by contrast, takes place in the stroma.
115810.m: The light reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes.

115811.q: Which two energy-rich products do the light reactions supply to the Calvin cycle?
115811.e: The light reactions convert light energy into chemical energy (ATP) and reducing power (NADPH). Both are used up in the Calvin cycle to make sugar.
115811.m: The light reactions supply the Calvin cycle with ATP and NADPH.

115812.q: What is the electron transport called in which electrons flow from water through both photosystems to NADP+?
115812.e: In the non-cyclic (linear) pathway, the electrons travel once from water via photosystem II and photosystem I to NADP+. This produces oxygen, ATP and NADPH.
115812.m: In non-cyclic electron transport, electrons flow from water all the way to NADP+.

115813.q: What is produced by cyclic electron transport around photosystem I?
115813.e: In the cyclic pathway, the electrons return from photosystem I to the electron transport chain. Only a proton gradient for making ATP is built up; neither NADPH nor oxygen is formed.
115813.m: Cyclic electron transport gives the cell extra ATP.

115814.q: What is the diagram called that shows the energy levels of the electrons in the light reactions as a zigzag line?
115814.e: If you plot the redox potentials of the electron carriers, you get a shape like a Z lying on its side. The two rises correspond to the excitations in the two photosystems.
115814.m: The Z-scheme shows the path of the electrons through both photosystems.

115815.q: Where do the electrons that flow through the photosystems in the light reactions come from?
115815.e: Water is split at photosystem II. This produces electrons, protons and, as a by-product, oxygen.
115815.m: The electrons of the light reactions come from water.

115816.q: What is the proton gradient that builds up across the thylakoid membrane during the light reactions used for?
a: To make ATP via ATP synthase
115816.e: The protons flow back into the stroma through the enzyme ATP synthase. This energy is used to make ATP.
115816.m: The proton gradient drives ATP synthase.

115817.q: Why is photosystem II numbered 2, even though it comes first in the electron chain?
a: It was discovered after photosystem I
It is only half the size
It only works in the dark
115817.e: The photosystems were numbered in the order in which they were discovered. Photosystem I was known first, even though the electrons pass through photosystem II first.
115817.m: The photosystems are numbered in the order of their discovery.

115818.q: Which molecule takes up CO2 in the Calvin cycle?
115818.e: The C5 molecule ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP) is joined to CO2. It then has to be regenerated at the end of the cycle.
115818.m: Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate is the CO2 acceptor in the Calvin cycle.

115819.q: Which molecule forms directly when CO2 is bound to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate?
115819.e: The C6 intermediate that forms is unstable and immediately splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (C3). That is why such plants are called C3 plants.
115819.m: CO2 fixation produces two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate.

115820.q: Into which three phases is the Calvin cycle divided?
115820.e: First CO2 is bound (fixation), then reduced to sugar using ATP and NADPH (reduction). Finally the acceptor RuBP is formed again (regeneration).
115820.m: The Calvin cycle consists of fixation, reduction and regeneration.

115821.q: How many CO2 molecules must the Calvin cycle fix to produce one molecule of glucose (C6H12O6)?
115821.e: Each CO2 supplies one carbon atom. For the six carbon atoms of glucose, six turns of the cycle, or six CO2, are therefore needed.
115821.m: The Calvin cycle fixes six CO2 for one glucose molecule.

115822.q: Where do the ATP and NADPH used by the Calvin cycle come from?
a: From the light reactions on the thylakoid membranes
From cellular respiration in the mitochondria
From the soil via the roots
115822.e: In the light reactions, light energy is converted into ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle uses these substances to build sugar from CO2.
115822.m: The light reactions supply the Calvin cycle with ATP and NADPH.

115823.q: Which C3 sugar is taken out of the Calvin cycle to make glucose or sucrose?
115823.e: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (triose phosphate) is the actual product of the cycle. Part of it leaves the cycle; the rest is used to regenerate RuBP.
115823.m: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is the sugar exported by the Calvin cycle.

115824.q: Who received the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for working out how plants fix CO2?
115824.e: Melvin Calvin and his team in Berkeley worked out the path of carbon in photosynthesis. That is why the cycle bears his name.
115824.m: Melvin Calvin was honoured for working out the carbon pathway of photosynthesis.

115825.q: Which isotope did Calvin and his colleagues use to trace the path of carbon in green algae?
115825.e: The algae were given radioactively labelled 14CO2. After short intervals, the labelled substances were separated and identified using paper chromatography.
115825.m: Radioactive carbon-14 made the Calvin cycle visible.

115826.q: Why is the Calvin cycle called “light-independent” even though it mainly takes place during the day?
a: It does not use light directly
It takes place outside the cell
115826.e: The Calvin cycle does not absorb any light itself. But it depends on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, and several of its enzymes are only activated in light.
115826.m: The Calvin cycle needs light only indirectly, through the products of the light reactions.

115827.q: In which part of the chloroplast does the Calvin cycle take place?
115827.e: The enzymes of the Calvin cycle are dissolved in the stroma, the ground substance of the chloroplast. The light reactions, by contrast, take place on the thylakoid membranes.
115827.m: The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma.

115828.q: Where in the plant cell are the photosystems of the light reactions located?
a: In the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplasts
115828.e: The photosystems are large protein complexes containing chlorophyll. They sit in the thylakoid membranes inside the chloroplasts.
115828.m: The light reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes.

115829.q: What is the light-driven splitting of water at photosystem II called?
115829.e: The oxidised P680 takes electrons from water via a metal cluster. In the process, water breaks down into oxygen, protons and electrons.
115829.m: The splitting of water in photosynthesis is called photolysis.

115831.q: What does the splitting of water at photosystem II provide?
115831.e: Photosystem II takes electrons from water, which then enter the electron transport chain. The protons help to make ATP, and the oxygen is released.
115831.m: Splitting water provides electrons, protons and oxygen.

115832.q: In which metabolic pathway do plants use CO2 to build sugar?
115832.e: In the Calvin cycle in the stroma of the chloroplasts, CO2 is built into sugar with the help of ATP and NADPH from the light reactions. The Krebs cycle, on the other hand, is part of cellular respiration.
115832.m: In the Calvin cycle, CO2 is built into sugar.

115833.q: Which two energy-rich substances do the light reactions provide for the Calvin cycle?
115833.e: In the light reactions, light energy is stored in ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle uses these substances to build sugar from CO2.
115833.m: The light reactions provide ATP and NADPH for the Calvin cycle.

115834.q: What does a herbicide that blocks electron transport in photosystem II do?
a: The plant can no longer carry out photosynthesis
The roots take up more water
115834.e: Without electron transport, neither ATP nor NADPH is made. The plant can no longer make sugar and dies. A well-known example of such a herbicide is diuron.
115834.m: Some herbicides stop photosynthesis at photosystem II.

115835.q: Why can very strong light harm a plant?
a: It damages parts of the photosynthetic machinery
It dissolves the chlorophyll in water
It makes the cell walls melt
It stops the roots taking up water
115835.e: In very strong light, reactive forms of oxygen are produced that damage proteins in photosystem II. The plant has to replace these parts constantly.
115835.m: Too much light can damage the photosynthetic machinery.

115836.q: What job does the enzyme Rubisco have in photosynthesis?
a: It binds CO2 from the air to a sugar molecule
It splits water and releases oxygen
It breaks down starch into sugar
115836.e: Rubisco is the key enzyme of the Calvin cycle. It fixes carbon dioxide, from which the plant then builds sugar.
115836.m: Rubisco fixes CO2 in the Calvin cycle.

115837.q: Which protein is considered the most abundant protein on Earth?
115837.e: Rubisco makes up a large part of the soluble proteins in leaves. Since it occurs in all green plants and algae, it is considered the most abundant protein of all.
115837.m: Rubisco is probably the most abundant protein on Earth.

115838.q: In which part of plant cells does Rubisco work?
115838.e: Rubisco is found in the stroma of the chloroplasts, where the Calvin cycle takes place. There, CO2 is processed into sugar.

115839.q: Which weakness of Rubisco leads to what is known as photorespiration?
a: It sometimes binds oxygen instead of CO2
It breaks down immediately in light
It needs nitrogen instead of CO2
115839.e: Rubisco can bind O2 as well as CO2. This produces a substance that the plant has to recycle at a cost in energy.
115839.m: Rubisco sometimes mixes up CO2 and oxygen.

115840.q: Roughly how fast does a single Rubisco molecule work?
a: Only a few reactions per second
About a thousand reactions per second
About a hundred thousand reactions per second
About a million reactions per second
115840.e: Rubisco is one of the slowest enzymes and converts only about 1 to 10 molecules per second. Plants make up for this with very large amounts of the enzyme.
115840.m: Rubisco is a very slow enzyme, so plants make a great deal of it.

115841.q: Which enzyme frees Rubisco from inhibiting sugar phosphates and so keeps it active?
115841.e: Sugar phosphates can block the active site. The ATP-dependent Rubisco activase removes them and makes the enzyme ready for work again.

115842.q: How do plants make up for Rubisco being a very slow enzyme?
a: They make very large amounts of it
They replace it with another enzyme at night
They do without the Calvin cycle
115842.e: A Rubisco molecule converts only a few CO2 per second. That is why a large part of the soluble protein in leaves is Rubisco.
115842.m: Plants make a lot of Rubisco because it works slowly.

115843.q: In plants, where is the gene for the large subunit of Rubisco stored?
115843.e: The gene rbcL lies in the circular DNA of the chloroplast, whereas the gene for the small subunit is in the nucleus. So both genomes have to work together.
115843.m: The large Rubisco subunit is encoded by the chloroplast itself.

115844.q: What drives ATP synthase in the membranes of mitochondria and chloroplasts?
a: A proton gradient across the membrane
115844.e: There are many more protons on one side of the membrane than on the other. When they flow back through ATP synthase, this provides the energy to make ATP.
115844.m: A proton gradient drives ATP synthase.

115845.q: What is the theory called which says that a proton gradient across a membrane drives the production of ATP?
115845.e: Peter Mitchell put forward the chemiosmotic theory in 1961 and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1978. It applies to mitochondria and chloroplasts.
115845.m: The chemiosmotic theory explains ATP production by a proton gradient.

115846.q: In which direction do protons flow through ATP synthase in the chloroplast?
a: From the thylakoid lumen into the stroma
From the stroma into the thylakoid lumen
From the cytoplasm into the stroma
From the stroma into the vacuole
115846.e: The proton concentration in the lumen is high. Following the gradient, the protons flow through ATP synthase into the stroma, where the ATP is also produced.
115846.m: In the chloroplast, protons flow from the lumen into the stroma.

115847.q: From which building blocks does ATP synthase make ATP?
115847.e: ATP synthase attaches another phosphate group to ADP. Exactly how this works was explained by Paul Boyer and John Walker, who received the Nobel Prize for it in 1997.
115847.m: ATP synthase joins ADP and phosphate to make ATP.

115848.q: In which membrane of the chloroplasts is ATP synthase located?
115848.e: ATP synthase sits in the thylakoid membrane, with its head part sticking out into the stroma. That is where the ATP for the Calvin cycle is made.
115848.m: In the chloroplast, ATP synthase sits in the thylakoid membrane.

115849.q: What is the production of ATP using light energy called?
115849.e: In photophosphorylation, light provides the proton gradient via the electron transport chain. In mitochondria, the corresponding process is called oxidative phosphorylation.
115849.m: Making ATP with light energy is called photophosphorylation.

115850.q: What happens if isolated thylakoids are moved from an acidic to an alkaline solution in the dark?
115850.e: It stays acidic inside and is alkaline outside. This proton gradient is enough for ATP synthase to make ATP even without light. André Jagendorf showed this in 1966.
115850.m: A proton gradient on its own is enough to make ATP.

115851.q: Why is ATP synthase called a molecular motor?
a: Part of it rotates when protons flow through
It moves the whole cell forwards
It burns fuel like a car engine
115851.e: The flow of protons sets a ring in the membrane and an axle attached to it spinning. This rotation changes the head part so that ATP is formed.
115851.m: ATP synthase is a molecular rotary motor.

115852.q: In which part of photosynthesis is NADPH produced?
115852.e: In the light reactions, light energy is used to make NADPH and ATP. Both are then used up in the Calvin cycle to build sugar.
115852.m: NADPH is produced in the light reactions.

115853.q: What job does NADPH do in the Calvin cycle?
115853.e: In the reduction phase, NADPH gives up electrons and reduces 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to a sugar. In doing so it becomes NADP+ again.
115853.m: NADPH is the reducing agent for making sugar.

115854.q: Where do the electrons stored in NADPH during photosynthesis ultimately come from?
115854.e: In the light reactions, water is split. Its electrons travel along an electron transport chain and finally end up in NADPH.
115854.m: The electrons in NADPH come from water.

115855.q: Apart from NADPH, which other energy-rich molecule is produced in the light reactions?
115855.e: The light reactions supply ATP as an energy carrier and NADPH as a reducing agent. Both drive the Calvin cycle.
115855.m: The light reactions supply ATP and NADPH.

115856.q: What happens to NADPH after it has given up electrons in the Calvin cycle?
a: It returns to the light reactions as NADP+
115856.e: NADP+ is a reusable carrier. In the light reactions it is loaded up again to make NADPH, so it shuttles between the two parts of photosynthesis.
115856.m: NADP+ and NADPH shuttle between the light reactions and the Calvin cycle.

115857.q: How does NADPH differ chemically from NADH?
115857.e: NADPH carries an extra phosphate group on the ribose part of the adenosine. This lets enzymes tell the two coenzymes apart.
115857.m: NADPH has one more phosphate group than NADH.

115858.q: On which side of the thylakoid membrane is NADPH produced?
115858.e: Ferredoxin and the enzyme that makes NADPH are on the stroma side. So NADPH is directly available to the Calvin cycle.
115858.m: NADPH is made where it is needed, on the stroma side.

115859.q: Where in the plant cell do the light reactions that produce NADPH take place?
a: On the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplasts
115859.e: Thylakoids are stacks of membranes in the chloroplast that contain chlorophyll and the electron transport chain. There, light is converted into chemical energy.
115859.m: The light reactions take place on the thylakoids.

115860.q: What are the stacks of thylakoids in the chloroplast, which look like piles of coins, called?
115860.e: A single stack is called a granum, several are called grana. Cristae, on the other hand, are the folds in mitochondria.

115861.q: What is the inner space of a thylakoid called?
115861.e: The thylakoid lumen is enclosed by the thylakoid membrane. In light, protons collect there.
115861.m: The inner space of a thylakoid is called the lumen.

115862.q: Where in the chloroplast are the thylakoids located?
115862.e: The thylakoids form a membrane system in the ground substance of the chloroplast, the stroma. The Calvin cycle also takes place in the stroma.
115862.m: Thylakoids lie in the stroma of the chloroplast.

115863.q: Which part of photosynthesis takes place on the thylakoid membranes?
115863.e: The thylakoid membranes contain chlorophyll, the photosystems and ATP synthase. There, light energy is used to make ATP and NADPH, which are needed in the stroma for the Calvin cycle.
115863.m: The light reactions take place on the thylakoids.

115864.q: What do seedlings that grow in the dark look like?
115864.e: Without light, the plastids make no chlorophyll and no finished thylakoid system. Only in light do green, working chloroplasts form within hours.
115864.m: Without light, seedlings form no finished thylakoids and stay pale.

115865.q: Which pigments are embedded in the thylakoid membrane?
115865.e: The thylakoid membrane contains chlorophyll a and b as well as carotenoids. These pigments capture light for photosynthesis.
115865.m: The leaf pigments sit in the thylakoid membranes.

115866.q: What job do the light-harvesting complexes in the thylakoid membrane have?
a: They capture light and pass the energy on
They pump water into the cell
115866.e: Light-harvesting complexes contain many chlorophyll and carotenoid molecules. They act like antennae and pass the light energy on to the reaction centres of the photosystems.
115866.m: Light-harvesting complexes are the antennae of photosynthesis.

115867.q: Which language does the word “thylakoid” come from, and what does it mean?
115867.e: The Greek word thylakos means sack or pouch. Thylakoids are flat, sac-like membrane vesicles.
115867.m: Thylakoids are named after their sac-like shape.

115868.q: What is called the stroma in the chloroplast?
a: The ground substance around the thylakoids
The inner space of the thylakoids
115868.e: The stroma is the gel-like fluid inside the inner envelope membrane. It contains the thylakoids, enzymes, DNA and ribosomes.
115868.m: The stroma is the ground substance of the chloroplast.

115869.q: Which metabolic pathway of photosynthesis takes place in the stroma?
115869.e: The enzymes for binding CO2 and making sugar are dissolved in the stroma. There, ATP and NADPH from the light reactions are used up.
115869.m: In the stroma, CO2 is turned into sugar in the Calvin cycle.

115870.q: During the light reactions of photosynthesis, where are protons pumped to from the stroma?
a: Into the inner space of the thylakoids
115870.e: In light, protons are pumped from the stroma into the thylakoid space. The resulting difference in concentration drives ATP production, and the stroma becomes slightly alkaline.
115870.m: In light, protons collect in the thylakoid space.

115871.q: What is found in the stroma that points to the bacterial origin of chloroplasts?
a: A nucleus with a nuclear envelope
115871.e: Chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and smaller 70S ribosomes, like bacteria. This supports the endosymbiotic theory.
115871.m: Their own DNA and 70S ribosomes in the stroma reveal their bacterial origin.

115872.q: Which storage substance is temporarily deposited as grains in the stroma during the day?
115872.e: If the plant makes more sugar than it can transport away, it stores it as starch grains in the stroma. At night this starch is broken down again.
115872.m: Surplus sugar is stored temporarily in the stroma as starch.

115873.q: How many envelope membranes surround a chloroplast of a land plant?
115873.e: The chloroplast is surrounded by an outer and an inner envelope membrane. The thylakoid membranes lie in addition inside.
115873.m: A chloroplast has a double membrane as its envelope.

115874.q: Which organelles of the plant cell have their own DNA, like the chloroplasts?
115874.e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and a double membrane. According to the endosymbiotic theory, both descend from bacteria that once lived freely.
115874.m: Chloroplasts and mitochondria have their own DNA.

115875.q: Apart from chlorophyll, which pigments are also found in chloroplasts?
115875.e: Carotenoids sit in the thylakoid membranes and in small fat droplets in the stroma. They help to collect light and protect against too much light. Anthocyanins, on the other hand, are in the vacuole.
115875.m: Besides chlorophyll, chloroplasts also contain carotenoids.

115876.q: In C4 plants, which molecule is the first product of CO2 fixation?
115876.e: In C4 plants, a compound with four carbon atoms, oxaloacetate, is formed first. That is where the name C4 comes from.
115876.m: The first fixation product of C4 plants is oxaloacetate.

115877.q: Which enzyme fixes CO2 in the mesophyll cells of C4 plants?
115877.e: PEP carboxylase joins phosphoenolpyruvate with a C1 unit to form oxaloacetate. It does not react with oxygen and works efficiently even when there is little CO2.
115877.m: C4 plants first fix CO2 with PEP carboxylase.

115878.q: Which weakness of the enzyme Rubisco do C4 plants get round?
a: In heat, Rubisco often binds oxygen instead of CO2
115878.e: Rubisco can bind oxygen as well as CO2, especially in heat and when CO2 is low. C4 plants concentrate CO2 around Rubisco and so reduce these losses.
115878.m: C4 plants protect Rubisco from binding oxygen.

115879.q: What is the typical leaf structure of C4 plants, with rings of cells around the vascular bundles, called?
115879.e: Mesophyll cells form a ring (German Kranz, wreath) around a layer of large bundle sheath cells. This arrangement allows the two fixation steps to be separated in space.
115879.m: C4 plants show a typical Kranz anatomy.

115880.q: In which cells of C4 plants does the Calvin cycle take place?
115880.e: The C4 acid is transported into the bundle sheath cells and decarboxylated there. The CO2 released is then fixed by Rubisco in the Calvin cycle.
115880.m: In C4 plants, Rubisco works in the bundle sheath cells.

115881.q: Which field crop common in Switzerland is a C4 plant?
115881.e: Maize comes from warmer parts of the Americas and uses the C4 pathway. Wheat, potatoes and rapeseed are C3 plants.
115881.m: Maize is the best-known C4 plant on Swiss fields.

115882.q: Which important tropical sugar crop is a C4 plant?
115882.e: Sugar cane is a grass and carries out highly productive C4 photosynthesis. Sugar beet, which is grown in Switzerland, is a C3 plant.
115882.m: Sugar cane is a particularly productive C4 plant.

115883.q: Why do C4 plants have an advantage in heat and drought?
a: They carry out no light reactions
115883.e: Thanks to pre-fixation, CO2 is strongly concentrated in the bundle sheath cells. This keeps photosynthesis efficient even when the stomata are partly closed.
115883.m: C4 plants concentrate CO2 and therefore work efficiently in heat.

115884.q: What does the abbreviation CAM stand for in plants?
115884.e: This metabolism was discovered in the stonecrop family (Crassulaceae), which gave it its name.

115885.q: When do CAM plants mainly open their stomata?
115885.e: At night it is cooler and more humid, so little water evaporates during gas exchange. During the day the stomata stay closed.
115885.m: CAM plants take in CO2 at night.

115886.q: In which form do CAM plants store the CO2 they take in at night?
a: As malic acid in the vacuole
As gas in the intercellular spaces
115886.e: The CO2 is bound to a C3 molecule and collected as malate (malic acid) in the large vacuole. That is why the leaves are noticeably more acidic in the morning.
115886.m: CAM plants store CO2 at night as malic acid.

115887.q: Which crop plant is a CAM plant?
115887.e: The pineapple is a bromeliad from dry regions and uses CAM metabolism. Maize is a C4 plant, wheat and sunflowers are C3 plants.
115887.m: The pineapple carries out CAM photosynthesis.

115888.q: What is the basic difference between CAM plants and C4 plants?
a: Separation in time instead of in space
Separation in space instead of in time
115888.e: C4 plants split pre-fixation and the Calvin cycle between different cells. CAM plants do both in the same cell, but at different times of day.
115888.m: CAM plants separate the steps in time, C4 plants in space.

115889.q: Which plant native to the Swiss Alps belongs to the stonecrop family, after which CAM is named?
115889.e: The houseleek (Sempervivum) grows on rocks and walls and stores water in its thick leaves. Like stonecrop, it belongs to the Crassulaceae.
115889.m: The houseleek is an Alpine member of the stonecrop family.

115890.q: What is the most important advantage of CAM metabolism?
a: It saves a great deal of water
It makes the plant grow faster
115890.e: Because the stomata stay closed during the day, CAM plants lose much less water per CO2 bound. In return, they usually grow slowly.
115890.m: CAM is an adaptation to water shortage.

115891.q: Where does the Calvin cycle of a CAM plant get its CO2 from during the day?
a: From the soil via the roots
115891.e: During the day, the acid stored at night is taken from the vacuole and decarboxylated. With the stomata closed, the released CO2 goes into the Calvin cycle.
115891.m: During the day, CAM plants release the stored CO2 again.

a: Rubisco binds O2 instead of CO2
The plant only respires at night
115892.e: The oxygenase reaction of Rubisco produces a molecule that the plant has to recycle at great effort. This recovery pathway is called photorespiration.
115892.m: Photorespiration begins when Rubisco binds oxygen instead of CO2.

115893.q: Which enzyme binds CO2 in photosynthesis and is considered the most abundant protein on Earth?
115893.e: In the Calvin cycle, Rubisco builds CO2 into organic molecules. Because it works slowly, plants make huge amounts of it. But it can also bind O2, which leads to photorespiration.
115893.m: Rubisco binds CO2 and is the most abundant protein on Earth.

115894.q: In which three organelles does photorespiration take place?
115894.e: Glycolate moves from the chloroplast to the peroxisome and, as glycine, on into the mitochondrion. The carbon returns to the chloroplast via the peroxisome.
115894.m: Chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion are involved in photorespiration.

115895.q: Which gas is released in the mitochondria during photorespiration and lost to the plant?
