116142.m: Bodies of equal mass swap velocities in an elastic collision.

116143.q: A 2 kg body hits a stationary 1 kg body head-on and elastically at 3 m/s. How fast is the lighter body afterwards?
116143.e: For the body that is hit, v equals 2 times m1 divided by the sum of the masses times 3 m/s. That is 4 divided by 3 times 3 m/s, which equals 4 m/s.
116143.m: In an elastic collision, the lighter partner can become faster than the body that hits it.

116144.q: A very heavy body hits a very light stationary body head-on and elastically. Roughly how fast does the light body become?
a: About twice as fast as the heavy one
About as fast as the heavy one
About half as fast as the heavy one
116144.e: In the limiting case of very unequal masses, the heavy body moves on almost unchanged. The light body gains about double the speed.
116144.m: A heavy collision partner flings a light one away at almost double speed.

116145.q: What is the coefficient of restitution, the ratio of separation speed to approach speed, in a perfectly elastic collision?
116145.e: In a perfectly elastic collision, the bodies move apart with the same relative speed at which they approached. The ratio is therefore 1.
116145.m: The coefficient of restitution of a perfectly elastic collision is one.

116146.q: A ball bounces perfectly elastically head-on off a very heavy stationary wall. What is its velocity afterwards?
a: The same size, but in the opposite direction
116146.e: Because of its huge mass, the wall takes up practically no energy. The ball keeps its speed and flies back.
116146.m: At an elastic obstacle, only the direction is reversed.

116147.q: Why are substances containing hydrogen, such as water, particularly good at slowing down fast neutrons in nuclear reactors?
a: Hydrogen nuclei are almost as heavy as neutrons
Hydrogen is electrically charged like neutrons
116147.e: In an elastic collision, the most energy is transferred when both masses are about the same. A proton has almost the mass of a neutron.
116147.m: Collision partners of equal mass slow each other down most effectively.

116148.q: At what angle do two balls of equal mass move apart after an oblique elastic collision if one was at rest beforehand?
116148.e: For equal masses, conservation of momentum and energy give a right angle between the paths. You can see this in snooker with off-centre shots.
116148.m: Balls of equal mass move apart at right angles after an oblique elastic collision.

116149.q: What characterises a perfectly inelastic collision?
a: The bodies move on together afterwards
The bodies bounce off at the same speed
116149.e: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies stick together and afterwards have the same velocity. Some of the kinetic energy is converted.
116149.m: After a perfectly inelastic collision, both bodies have the same velocity.

116150.q: A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s runs into a stationary 500 kg car, and the two get wedged together. How fast do they move immediately afterwards?
116150.e: The momentum before is 30,000 kg·m/s. Shared over 2000 kg, this gives a common velocity of 15 m/s.
116150.m: In an inelastic collision, total momentum is shared over the combined mass.

116151.q: A body hits a stationary body of equal mass in a perfectly inelastic collision. What share of the kinetic energy is lost?
116151.e: The common velocity is half as large, and double the mass moves on. The kinetic energy afterwards is only half.
116151.m: In an inelastic collision of equal masses, half the kinetic energy remains.

116152.q: A 2 kg body at 6 m/s hits a stationary 4 kg body in a perfectly inelastic collision. How much kinetic energy is converted?
116152.e: Before, it is 0.5 times 2 kg times 36 m²/s², which equals 36 J. The common velocity is 2 m/s, so afterwards 12 J; the loss is 24 J.
116152.m: In an inelastic collision, some of the kinetic energy is converted into other forms of energy.

116153.q: What is a ballistic pendulum used for?
a: To measure the speed of projectiles
116153.e: The projectile gets stuck in the pendulum body, which then swings out. The projectile’s speed can be calculated from the height reached and the conservation of momentum.
116153.m: The ballistic pendulum makes high projectile speeds measurable.

116154.q: A 10 g bullet gets stuck in a stationary 990 g block of wood. Both then move at 2 m/s. How fast was the bullet?
116154.e: After the collision, the momentum is 1 kg times 2 m/s, which is 2 kg·m/s. This came from the bullet, so 2 divided by 0.01 kg equals 200 m/s.
116154.m: From the shared momentum after the collision, you get the speed of the bullet.

116155.q: Where does the kinetic energy go that is lost in an inelastic collision?
a: Into the mass of the bodies
116155.e: Energy is never lost, only converted. In a car crash, the crumple zone deforms and heats up.
116155.m: In an inelastic collision, kinetic energy is converted into work of deformation and heat.

116156.q: Two balls of modelling clay of equal mass fly towards each other at the same speed and stick together. What share of the kinetic energy is kept?
116156.e: Total momentum beforehand is zero, so the lump is at rest afterwards. All the kinetic energy has been converted into other forms of energy.
116156.m: With equal and opposite momenta, a sticking lump comes to a standstill.

116157.q: A ball falls from a height of 1 m onto the floor and then bounces up 0.64 m. What is the coefficient of restitution of this partly elastic collision?
116157.e: The coefficient of restitution is the ratio of the speeds after and before impact. Because speed grows with the square root of height, the square root of 0.64 gives 0.8.
116157.m: The coefficient of restitution can be calculated from drop and bounce height using a square root.

116158.q: Which conservation law is the recoil principle based on?
116158.e: If mass is expelled in one direction, the rest gains an equal momentum in the opposite direction. Total momentum stays unchanged.
116158.m: Recoil is a direct consequence of the conservation of momentum.

116159.q: A 4 kg rifle fires a 10 g bullet at 800 m/s. At what speed does the rifle recoil?
116159.e: The bullet’s momentum is 0.01 kg times 800 m/s, which is 8 kg·m/s. The rifle gains the same momentum, so 8 divided by 4 equals 2 m/s.
116159.m: The heavy rifle recoils much more slowly than the light bullet flies.

116160.q: Two ice skaters of 60 kg and 40 kg stand still and push off from each other. The heavier one glides away at 2 m/s. How fast is the lighter one?
116160.e: The two momenta must add up to zero. 60 kg times 2 m/s equals 120 kg·m/s, and divided by 40 kg this gives 3 m/s.
116160.m: After pushing off, both partners have equal and opposite momenta.

116161.q: How do squid move when fleeing quickly?
a: By expelling water using the recoil principle
By beating their pectoral fins quickly
By pushing off from the sea floor
116161.e: Squid suck water into their mantle and squeeze it out through a funnel. The recoil drives them in the opposite direction.
116161.m: Squid use recoil like a jet engine.

116162.q: Why do firefighters have to hold a nozzle with a high water flow firmly?
a: The jet of water coming out produces a recoil
The water in the hose is very hot
The hose contracts because of the cold
The air presses on the nozzle
116162.e: The water is accelerated forwards at high speed. According to the conservation of momentum, an equal force acts backwards on the nozzle.
116162.m: A fast jet of water pushes the nozzle backwards.

116163.q: Why does a lawn sprinkler with curved nozzle arms turn by itself?
a: The water coming out produces a recoil
A small motor inside drives it
The water pulls the arms forwards
116163.e: The water is expelled backwards from the curved arms. According to the conservation of momentum, a force acts on the arms in the opposite direction, and the sprinkler turns.
116163.m: A lawn sprinkler turns because of recoil.

116164.q: A 100 kg astronaut is floating at rest in space and throws a 2 kg tool away at 5 m/s. How fast does she move afterwards?
116164.e: The tool gains 2 kg times 5 m/s, which is 10 kg·m/s. The astronaut gains the same momentum in the opposite direction, so 10 divided by 100 equals 0.1 m/s.
116164.m: If you throw something away in space, you move in the opposite direction.

116165.q: How does an aircraft’s jet engine produce its thrust?
a: It expels gas backwards at high speed
It sucks the aircraft forwards with low pressure
It pushes air against the wings
116165.e: The engine strongly accelerates air and combustion gases backwards. The change in momentum of the gas stream gives a thrust force forwards.
116165.m: A jet engine works by the recoil principle.

116166.q: Which scientist published the rocket equation named after him in 1903?
116166.e: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky is regarded as a pioneer of space flight theory. The rocket equation is therefore also called the Tsiolkovsky equation.
116166.m: The rocket equation goes back to Konstantin Tsiolkovsky.

116167.q: According to the rocket equation, which two quantities does the achievable change in velocity of a rocket without external forces depend on?
a: Burn time and launch mass alone
Type of fuel and air pressure
116167.e: The change in velocity is the exhaust velocity times the natural logarithm of the ratio of launch mass to final mass. The burn time plays no part.
116167.m: A rocket’s final velocity depends on the mass ratio and the exhaust velocity.

116168.q: A rocket has an exhaust velocity of 3000 m/s and a mass ratio of 4. Roughly what change in velocity does it reach without external forces?
116168.e: This is 3000 m/s times ln 4. Because ln 4 is about 1.386, the result is about 4160 m/s.
116168.m: The final velocity only grows with the logarithm of the mass ratio.

116169.q: Roughly what mass ratio does a rocket need to reach a change in velocity of twice its exhaust velocity?
116169.e: From ln of m0 divided by m1 equals 2, it follows that m0 divided by m1 equals e to the power of 2. That is about 7.39.
116169.m: For each additional exhaust velocity of final speed, the required mass ratio grows by a factor of e.

116170.q: From what mass ratio does a rocket become faster than its own exhaust velocity?
116170.e: The change in velocity exceeds the exhaust velocity as soon as the logarithm is greater than 1. This is the case from Euler’s number e upwards.
116170.m: A rocket can become faster than its exhaust jet.

116171.q: Why are rockets for reaching orbit usually built with several stages?
a: Empty tanks are dropped, improving the mass ratio
Each stage has an exhaust velocity higher than light
Several stages reduce air resistance to zero
The Earth’s gravity only acts on the first stage
116171.e: Empty tanks and engines would otherwise be dead weight that would have to be accelerated further. By dropping them, each stage achieves a better mass ratio.

116172.q: A rocket expels 100 kg of gas per second at 2500 m/s. What is its thrust?
116172.e: Thrust is the mass flow times the exhaust velocity. 100 kg/s times 2500 m/s gives 250,000 N.
116172.m: Thrust is the product of mass expelled per second and exhaust velocity.

116173.q: Which mathematical function links the mass ratio with the change in velocity in the rocket equation?
116173.e: Because the rocket keeps getting lighter while it burns, you have to integrate over the mass. This gives the natural logarithm.
116173.m: The rocket equation contains a natural logarithm.

116174.q: Roughly what exhaust velocity do chemical rocket engines running on hydrogen and oxygen reach in a vacuum?
116174.e: Hydrogen-oxygen engines are among the most powerful chemical propulsion systems. Their gas jet leaves the nozzle at a good 4 km/s.
116174.m: Chemical rockets expel their gases at a few kilometres per second.

a: The product of force and the time it acts
The product of force and distance
116175.e: Impulse is the integral of force over time; for a constant force, simply force times time. It equals the change in momentum of the body.
116175.m: An impulse causes an equal change in momentum.

116176.q: A constant force of 200 N acts for 0.05 s. What is the impulse?
116176.e: The impulse is 200 N times 0.05 s. That gives 10 N·s.
116176.m: Force times the time it acts gives the impulse.

116177.q: How does an airbag protect the occupants in a crash?
a: It lengthens the stopping time and so reduces the force
It reduces the change in momentum to zero
It increases the mass of the head
116177.e: The change in momentum when stopping is fixed. If it is spread over a longer time, the average force is correspondingly smaller.
116177.m: A longer stopping time means a smaller force.

116178.q: A 0.4 kg ball is kicked from rest to 25 m/s, and contact with the foot lasts 0.01 s. What is the average force?
116178.e: The change in momentum is 0.4 kg times 25 m/s, which is 10 kg·m/s. Divided by 0.01 s, this gives 1000 N.
116178.m: Short contact times lead to large forces.

116179.q: How can the impulse be found from a force-time graph?
a: As the area under the curve
As the gradient of the curve
As the point where it crosses the time axis
116179.e: Impulse is the integral of force over time. Geometrically, this is the area between the curve and the time axis.
116179.m: In a force-time graph, the impulse is the area under the curve.

116180.q: A 1000 kg car travelling at 15 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s in a crash. What is the average force?
116180.e: The change in momentum is 15,000 kg·m/s. Divided by 0.1 s, this gives 150,000 N, which is 150 kN.
116180.m: The shorter the impact, the greater the average force.

116181.q: An impulse of 6 N·s acts without friction on a stationary 2 kg body. How fast is it afterwards?
116181.e: The impulse equals the change in momentum, so 6 kg·m/s. Divided by 2 kg, this gives 3 m/s.
116181.m: The impulse determines a body’s change in velocity.

116182.q: In sports such as tennis or golf, why do you follow through and keep contact with the ball for as long as possible?
a: Longer contact gives a larger impulse
Longer contact reduces the mass of the ball
Longer contact slows down the racket or club
116182.e: If the striking force acts for longer, more momentum is transferred to the ball. The ball therefore flies off faster.
116182.m: More contact time with the same force means more momentum for the ball.

116183.q: A force-time graph shows a triangular force curve with a peak of 400 N lasting 0.02 s. What is the impulse?
116183.e: The impulse equals the area of the triangle, so one half times 400 N times 0.02 s. That gives 4 N·s.
116183.m: With a triangular force curve, the impulse is half of peak force times duration.

116184.q: In which direction does the inertial force point in an accelerated frame of reference?
a: Against the acceleration of the frame
In the direction of the acceleration
Always towards the centre of the Earth
116184.e: According to d’Alembert, the inertial force is minus mass times acceleration. It therefore acts against the acceleration of the frame of reference.
116184.m: The inertial force acts against the acceleration.

116185.q: A bus brakes hard. What do the standing passengers in the bus feel?
116185.e: In the braking bus, an inertial force acts forwards. Seen from outside, the passengers simply carry on moving at their previous speed.
116185.m: When braking, you seem to be pulled forwards.

116186.q: A lift is going down and slows down. How does a person in the lift feel while it is braking?
116186.e: When a downward journey slows down, the acceleration is directed upwards. The inertial force points downwards and adds to the weight.
116186.m: When a lift going down brakes, you feel heavier.

116187.q: What does a set of bathroom scales show in a freely falling lift?
116187.e: In a freely falling system, the inertial force cancels the weight exactly. The person and the scales fall at the same rate, so the scales carry no load.
116187.m: In free fall there is weightlessness.

116188.q: What is the inertial force called that you feel outwards on a turning roundabout?
116188.e: In the rotating frame of reference, a force seems to act outwards. Seen from outside, however, a centripetal force inwards is needed to keep you on the circular path.
116188.m: Centrifugal force is an inertial force in a rotating frame.

116189.q: A car accelerates at 3 m/s². Roughly by what angle does a freely hanging pendulum in the car deviate from the vertical (g equals 9.81 m/s²)?
116189.e: For the angle, tan alpha equals a divided by g, so 3 divided by 9.81. That gives about 17°, and the pendulum hangs backwards.
116189.m: A pendulum in an accelerating car shows the acceleration by its tilt.

116190.q: What distinguishes an inertial force from an ordinary force such as the gravitational force?
a: It has no counterforce under the third law
It is always greater than the weight
It only acts on charged bodies
116190.e: Inertial forces do not arise from an interaction with another body. That is why there is no counterforce to them.
116190.m: There is no counterforce to an inertial force.

116191.q: How does an observer on the platform explain that a passenger is pressed into the seat when the train pulls away?
a: The seat accelerates the body, which has inertia, forwards
A force pushes the passenger backwards
The airflow pushes through the windows
The Earth’s rotation pushes the passenger back
116191.e: In the frame of reference at rest, no inertial force is needed. The body tends to stay at rest, and the back of the seat exerts the force that accelerates it.
116191.m: If you watch from outside, you need no inertial force to explain it.

116192.q: Which fictitious force in a rotating frame of reference acts only on bodies moving relative to that frame?
116192.e: The Coriolis force only arises with motion relative to the rotating frame. The centrifugal force, on the other hand, also acts on bodies at rest.
116192.m: The Coriolis force only acts on moving bodies in a rotating frame.

116193.q: At the North Pole, roughly how long does the plane of swing of a Foucault pendulum take for a full turn?
116193.e: At the pole, the Earth turns once beneath the pendulum per sidereal day, so in just under 24 hours. At lower latitudes it takes longer.
116193.m: At the pole, the plane of the pendulum turns once in about a day.

116194.q: What did Léon Foucault prove in 1851 with his pendulum in the Panthéon in Paris?
a: The Earth’s rotation on its own axis
The Earth’s orbit around the Sun
The flattening of the Earth at the poles
116194.e: The plane of swing of the Foucault pendulum appears to turn during the day. In reality, the Earth is turning away beneath the pendulum.
116194.m: The Foucault pendulum shows the Earth’s rotation.

116196.q: Where on Earth is the horizontal deflection due to the Coriolis force zero?
116196.e: The horizontal component of the Coriolis force is proportional to the sine of the latitude. At the equator this sine is zero.
116196.m: At the equator, the Coriolis force causes no horizontal deflection.

116197.q: A projectile is fired southwards from the North Pole. In which direction does it deviate as seen from the Earth?
116197.e: During the flight, the Earth turns away eastwards beneath the projectile. Seen from the Earth, it therefore seems to be deflected to the west.
116197.m: The Earth’s rotation makes bodies flying south in the northern hemisphere deviate to the west.

116198.q: How does the size of the Coriolis force depend on the speed of the body relative to the rotating frame?
a: It is proportional to the speed
It is proportional to the square of the speed
It does not depend on the speed
It is inversely proportional to the speed
116198.e: The Coriolis force equals two times mass times the cross product of velocity and angular velocity. It therefore grows linearly with speed.
116198.m: Double the speed means double the Coriolis force.

116199.q: Which French scientist described in 1835 the fictitious force in rotating frames of reference that is named after him?
116199.e: Gaspard Gustave de Coriolis studied motion in rotating systems, for example in machines with turning parts. His work of 1835 gave the Coriolis force its name.
116199.m: The Coriolis force is named after Gaspard Gustave de Coriolis.

116200.q: A 0.5 kg stone is whirled round on a 1 m string at 2 revolutions per second. Roughly what is the centrifugal force in the rotating frame?
116200.e: The angular velocity is 2 times 2 pi, which is about 12.6 per second. With m times omega squared times r, this gives 0.5 times 158 times 1, which is about 79 N.
116200.m: Centrifugal force can be calculated from mass, angular velocity and radius.

116201.q: How does the centrifugal force on a bend change if you drive twice as fast with the same radius?
116201.e: Speed appears squared in the formula. Double the speed therefore gives four times the force.
116201.m: Centrifugal force grows with the square of the speed.

116202.q: How does the centrifugal force change if the radius is doubled at the same angular velocity?
116202.e: In the form m times omega squared times r, the force is proportional to the radius. Double the radius gives double the force.
116202.m: At the same rotation rate, centrifugal force grows with the distance from the axis.

116203.q: How does a spin dryer remove water from washing?
a: The water flies outwards through the holes in the drum
The water is sucked into the middle
The washing squeezes the water upwards
116203.e: The drum keeps the washing on its circular path, but the water can escape through the holes. In the rotating frame, the centrifugal force drives it outwards.
116203.m: In a spin dryer, water is flung outwards by the spinning.

116204.q: In an inertial frame, which real force keeps a body on a circular path?
a: The centripetal force towards the centre
The Coriolis force across the path
116204.e: Without a force, the body would carry on in a straight line. A circular path needs a force directed towards the centre, such as rope tension or friction.
116204.m: Circular motion needs a force towards the centre.

116205.q: Why is the Earth flattened at the poles?
a: Because of the centrifugal effect of its rotation
Because of the masses of ice at the poles
116205.e: At the equator the speed of rotation is greatest, and the Earth bulges outwards there. The equatorial radius is about 21 km larger than the polar radius.
116205.m: Rotation makes the Earth thicker at the equator.

116206.q: On a chair swing ride, a seat circles at 5 m/s on a path with a radius of 5 m. Roughly by what angle is the chain tilted from the vertical (g equals 9.81 m/s²)?
116206.e: tan alpha equals v squared divided by r times g, so 25 divided by 49.05, which is about 0.51. That gives about 27°.
116206.m: The faster the ride turns, the further out the seats swing.

116207.q: What is the minimum speed a car must have at the top of a loop with a radius of 10 m so that it does not fall off the track (g equals 9.81 m/s²)?
116207.e: At the top, the centrifugal force must be at least as large as the weight. From v squared equals g times r, the square root of 98.1 gives about 9.9 m/s.
116207.m: In a loop, the speed at the top must not fall below a minimum value.

116208.q: Why can plants hardly take up any water from very dry soil?
a: The remaining water clings tightly to the soil particles
Dry soil contains no water at all
The roots go to sleep in drought
116208.e: The drier the soil, the more tightly the remaining water is bound to soil particles. The root can then no longer draw it in, and the plant wilts.
116208.m: In dry soil, the water is tightly bound.

116209.q: By definition, what is the water potential of pure water at normal pressure and the same height?
116209.e: Pure, free water under standard conditions is the reference point and has a water potential of zero.
116209.m: Pure water has a water potential of zero; solutions have negative values.

116210.q: In which direction does water move by itself in a plant?
a: From higher to lower water potential
From lower to higher water potential
Always from the phloem into the xylem
116210.e: Water flows passively to where its water potential is lower, that is, more negative. This is how it travels from the soil through the root into the atmosphere.
116210.m: Water always flows towards the more negative water potential.

116211.q: Why do plants wilt if you water them with very salty water?
a: The water potential of the soil falls below that of the root
Salt immediately blocks all the stomata
Salt destroys the chlorophyll within minutes
116211.e: Dissolved salt makes the water potential of the soil water very negative. If it is lower than in the root, the plant can no longer take up water or even loses some.
116211.m: Salty soil takes water away from the root instead of supplying it.

116212.q: Which process mainly pulls water up a tall tree?
116212.e: When water evaporates from the leaves, it creates suction. Because water molecules stick together, an unbroken column of water is pulled from the root up to the crown.
116212.m: The pull of evaporation draws water up the tree.

116213.q: What is the water potential of a cell with an osmotic potential of -0.8 MPa and a pressure potential of 0.5 MPa?
116213.e: The water potential is the sum of its components. -0.8 MPa + 0.5 MPa = -0.3 MPa.
116213.m: Water potential is the sum of osmotic potential and pressure potential.

116214.q: What happens to a plant cell that is placed in pure water?
a: It takes up water and becomes firm
116214.e: Many substances are dissolved in the cell sap, so water flows into the cell by osmosis. The rigid cell wall stops it from bursting, and the cell becomes firm.
116214.m: In pure water, a plant cell takes up water by osmosis.

116215.q: In which weather do plants lose the most water through evaporation?
116215.e: Dry, warm air takes up a lot of water vapour, and wind carries the damp air away from the leaf. That is when water loss is greatest.
116215.m: Warmth, dry air and wind increase evaporation.

116216.q: Why do trees not grow upwards without limit?
a: Water can only be pulled up to a certain height
The air gets too warm at the top
116216.e: The taller the tree, the stronger the suction must be to pull water up against gravity. Above 100 metres the water column breaks easily, which is why there are hardly any taller trees.
116216.m: Water transport limits the height of trees.

116217.q: According to the cohesion theory, what pulls water up a tree?
a: The suction caused by evaporation from the leaves
116217.e: Henry Dixon and John Joly explained in 1894 that when water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls the continuous column of water in the xylem after it. The cohesion of the water molecules stops it from breaking.
116217.m: Evaporation from the leaves pulls water up the tree.

116218.q: Which bonds are responsible for the cohesion between water molecules?
116218.e: Water molecules are dipoles and attract each other through hydrogen bonds. This cohesion keeps the water column in the xylem from breaking.
116218.m: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules together as a column.

116219.q: What is the sticking of water molecules to the walls of the transport vessels called?
116219.e: Adhesion is the attraction between different substances, here between water and the cell wall. It helps to stabilise the water column.
116219.m: Adhesion binds water to other surfaces such as the vessel wall.

116220.q: Under what pressure is the water column in the xylem of a transpiring plant?
116220.e: The water column is pulled from above and is therefore under negative pressure. If you pierced a vessel, air would be sucked in rather than water pushed out.
116220.m: In the xylem, water is pulled, not pushed.

116221.q: What is the breaking of the water column in the xylem, in which gas bubbles form, called?
116221.e: Under very strong tension the water column can break and a gas bubble forms (embolism). The affected vessel element then stops working for transport.
116221.m: Cavitation breaks the water column with a gas bubble.

116222.q: Why can air pressure alone not lift water into the crown of a 30-metre-tall tree?
a: It can only support a column of water about 10 metres high
It only acts on the plant at night
It is cancelled out in the roots
116222.e: Air pressure of about 1 bar corresponds to a column of water about 10 metres high. Taller trees need the pull from above through cohesion.
116222.m: Air pressure can only lift water about 10 metres.

116223.q: Which tree species does the tallest known living tree on Earth belong to?
116223.e: The coast redwood “Hyperion” in California is almost 116 metres tall. Even to that height, water is pulled up by cohesion. The tallest eucalyptus reaches about 100 metres.
116223.m: The tallest known tree is a coast redwood in California.

116224.q: In which tissue does the continuous column of water rise from the root to the leaf?
116224.e: The xylem (woody part) carries water and minerals upwards. The phloem, on the other hand, mainly transports sugar.
116224.m: Water rises in the xylem from the root to the leaves.

116225.q: Why can capillarity alone not lift water into the crown of a tall tree?
a: In such fine tubes it only lifts water a few metres
It only works in glass tubes
116225.e: In vessels a few micrometres in radius, water rises by capillarity only about one to two metres. Tall trees need the pull of evaporation and cohesion.
116225.m: Capillarity only lifts water a few metres in plant vessels.

116226.q: Where does the transpiration pull mainly start?
a: At the cell walls of the mesophyll in the leaf
In the cambium of the trunk
In the sieve tubes of the bark
116226.e: Water evaporates from the moist cell walls of the mesophyll into the air spaces and escapes through the stomata. This draws more water up from the xylem.
116226.m: The pull begins where water evaporates in the leaf.

116227.q: What proportion of the water taken up by the root does a plant typically transpire again?
116227.e: Only a small part of the water is used for photosynthesis and growth. By far the largest part, usually over 90 per cent, evaporates through the leaves.
116227.m: Almost all the water taken up evaporates again through the leaves.

116228.q: In which weather conditions is transpiration strongest?
116228.e: Warmth and dry air increase the water potential gradient to the air, and light opens the stomata. Wind carries away the layer of damp air on the leaf.
116228.m: Warm, dry, moving air drives transpiration.

116229.q: By which route does most of the transpired water leave a leaf?
116229.e: The leaf surface is almost watertight thanks to a waxy layer. Most of the water escapes as stomatal transpiration.
116229.m: Most transpiration happens through the stomata.

116230.q: Which device measures the water uptake of a cut shoot as a measure of transpiration?
116230.e: In a potometer, the shoot is placed in a tube filled with water. The movement of an air bubble shows how much water is taken up.
116230.m: A potometer measures how much water a shoot takes up.

116231.q: Why does wind increase the transpiration of a leaf?
a: It removes the damp boundary layer above the leaf
116231.e: A thin layer of damp, still air forms above the leaf. Wind carries it away, so the gradient to the dry air stays large.
116231.m: Wind thins the damp layer of air and so speeds up evaporation.

116232.q: How does transpiration benefit the temperature of the leaf?
a: It warms the leaf at night
It stores heat in the xylem
116232.e: Water needs a lot of energy to evaporate, and this energy is taken from the leaf. So leaves overheat less in the sun.
116232.m: Transpiration cools leaves just as sweating cools the body.

116233.q: Why does the root take up water from moist soil when the plant is transpiring?
a: The water potential in the root is lower than in the soil
The soil actively presses the water in
The root uses ATP for every water molecule
116233.e: The pull from the leaves lowers the water potential in the xylem all the way down to the root. Water passively follows the gradient from the soil into the root.
116233.m: The root takes up water passively along the water potential gradient.

a: Giving off liquid water as droplets
Giving off water vapour through the stomata
Taking up dew through the leaves
Releasing sugar into the sieve tube
116234.e: In guttation, the plant presses out water in liquid form through special openings. Droplets form at the tips and edges of the leaves.
116234.m: In guttation, the plant gives off droplets of water.

116235.q: Through which structures is water given off during guttation?
116235.e: Hydathodes are water pores at the ends of vascular bundles, usually at the teeth and tips of leaves. Unlike stomata, they cannot close.
116235.m: Hydathodes are the water pores used for guttation.

116236.q: What is the sap called that flows from freshly cut vines in spring and, like guttation, is caused by root pressure?
116236.e: Before the leaves come out, there is no transpiration pull, but the roots are already pushing water upwards. Xylem sap then drips from cut surfaces, and the vine is said to “bleed”.
116236.m: Bleeding vines show root pressure in spring.

116237.q: Under which conditions is guttation especially often seen?
a: At night and early in the morning with humid air and wet soil
At midday in heat and drought
In winter when the ground is frozen
In strong wind in the afternoon
116237.e: When the air is humid, hardly any water can evaporate and there is no transpiration pull. Then the pressure from the root wins and water comes out as liquid.
116237.m: Guttation is seen mainly on humid nights.

116238.q: In which meadow plant are silvery guttation droplets on the leaf edges a well-known feature?
116238.e: In the morning, lady's mantle (Alchemilla) often has beads of water on the teeth of its leaves. Many people think it is dew, but it is water given off by the plant.
116238.m: The beads on lady's mantle are usually guttation droplets, not dew.

116239.q: How can you tell guttation droplets from dew drops?
a: They sit specifically at leaf tips and edges
They are always larger than a centimetre
116239.e: Dew settles evenly over the whole surface. Guttation droplets, by contrast, only come out at the hydathodes, that is, at the tips and teeth of the leaves.
116239.m: Guttation droplets hang from leaf tips; dew spreads over the surface.

116240.q: Why do dried guttation droplets often leave white crusts?
a: They contain dissolved salts and organic substances
They consist of pure distilled water
They contain starch grains from the plastids
116240.e: Guttation water comes from the xylem and contains mineral salts as well as some sugar and amino acids. When it evaporates, these substances are left behind.
116240.m: Guttation water is not pure water; it contains dissolved substances.

116241.q: Why can guttation droplets from maize plants grown from treated seed be dangerous for bees?
a: They can contain insecticides from the seed treatment
They are strongly acidic like battery acid
They contain a lot of alcohol
They are always poisonous fungal spores
116241.e: Systemic seed treatments such as neonicotinoids are taken up by the plant and distributed in the xylem. Studies found them in guttation droplets, which bees may use as a source of water.
116241.m: Systemic pesticides can also turn up in guttation water.

116242.q: What belongs to the apoplast of a plant?
a: Cell walls, intercellular spaces and dead vessel elements
The cytoplasm of all living cells
Only the vacuoles of the cells
116242.e: The apoplast includes everything outside the plasma membranes. This includes the cell walls, the spaces between cells and the dead cells of the xylem.
116242.m: The apoplast is the space outside the living protoplasts.

116243.q: What is a feature of the apoplastic route of water through the root cortex?
a: Water flows through cell walls without crossing membranes
Water moves from cytoplasm to cytoplasm
Water is actively pumped using ATP
116243.e: On the apoplastic route, water moves through the network of cell walls and spaces between cells. It does not have to pass through any plasma membrane.
116243.m: In the apoplast, water flows through the cell walls.

116244.q: Which layer seals the apoplast of leaves from the outside against evaporation?
116244.e: The cuticle is a waxy layer on the outer walls of the epidermis. Without it, water would evaporate freely from the cell walls.
116244.m: The cuticle seals the cell walls of the leaf surface.

116245.q: Why do the vessel elements of the xylem count as part of the apoplast?
a: When mature, they are dead cells without a protoplast
They contain a particularly large number of chloroplasts
116245.e: Vessels and tracheids die as they mature, leaving only their lignified cell walls. So they lie outside all living protoplasts.
116245.m: The water-conducting xylem consists of dead cells and belongs to the apoplast.

116246.q: Why is the liquid in plant cell walls usually slightly acidic?
a: Proton pumps move H⁺ ions out of the cells
Rainwater contains a lot of hydrochloric acid
Cell walls are made of citric acid
116246.e: Proton pumps in the cell membrane move H⁺ ions to the outside. That is why the pH in the apoplast is usually about 5 to 6.
116246.m: Proton pumps make the apoplast slightly acidic.

116247.q: What is mainly transported in the phloem of a plant?
116247.e: The phloem distributes the sugar made in the leaves around the plant. Water and mineral salts, on the other hand, rise in the xylem.
116247.m: The phloem carries sugar, the xylem carries water.

116248.q: Which layer in the root stops water flowing through the cell walls and forces it through living cells?
a: The endodermis with the Casparian strip
116248.e: The Casparian strip is a watertight band in the cell walls of the endodermis. There, water has to pass through membranes, so the plant can control which substances get in.
116248.m: The Casparian strip blocks the route through the cell walls.

116249.q: Why is water transport in the apoplast particularly fast?
a: It has low resistance to flow
It is speeded up by ATP
It only runs through living cells
It uses the power of the nucleus
116249.e: Cell walls are porous, and water does not have to cross any membranes. So it flows there with little resistance.
116249.m: With no membranes in the way, water flows easily in the apoplast.

116250.q: What is meant by the symplast?
a: All the protoplasts connected by plasmodesmata
The network of all cell walls
All the dead cells of the wood
The air spaces in the leaf
116250.e: Living plant cells are connected to each other by cytoplasmic channels. This creates a continuous cytoplasmic space, the symplast.
116250.m: The symplast is the connected cytoplasm of many cells.

116251.q: What are the cytoplasmic channels that connect neighbouring plant cells called?
116251.e: Plasmodesmata pass through the cell walls and connect the cytoplasm of two cells. Water, sugar and signalling substances travel through them.
116251.m: Plasmodesmata connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring plant cells.

116252.q: Why do plant cells need plasmodesmata to connect their cytoplasm?
a: Because each cell is surrounded by a rigid cell wall
Because they have no cell membrane
116252.e: The rigid cell wall separates neighbouring plant cells. Plasmodesmata are channels through this wall and connect the cytoplasm of the cells.
116252.m: Plasmodesmata pass through the rigid cell wall of plant cells.

116253.q: What does a plant cell achieve when it narrows its plasmodesmata?
a: It slows down exchange with neighbouring cells
116253.e: Plasmodesmata are narrowed by depositing the polysaccharide callose. This lets the plant control the exchange of substances and, for example, slow the spread of viruses.
116253.m: Narrowed plasmodesmata slow the exchange between cells.

116254.q: How do many plant viruses spread from cell to cell?
a: Through plasmodesmata with the help of movement proteins
Through the root hairs into the soil
116254.e: Viruses make special movement proteins that widen plasmodesmata. This way the virus passes through the symplast into neighbouring cells.
116254.m: Plant viruses use plasmodesmata as passageways.

116255.q: What is needed on the symplastic route of water through the root cortex?
a: Crossing a plasma membrane once on entry
Crossing every cell wall using ATP
A route only through dead cells
116255.e: Water enters a cell once through the plasma membrane. After that it moves via plasmodesmata from cytoplasm to cytoplasm.
116255.m: In the symplast, water stays inside the cells after entering.

116256.q: Which membrane proteins form channels through which water quickly enters cells?
116256.e: Aquaporins are water channels in membranes. Plants can adjust their number and opening and so control how well water is conducted.
116256.m: Aquaporins are the water channels of membranes.

116257.q: In which form is sugar transported in the phloem of most plants?
116257.e: Sucrose is highly soluble in water and unreactive, which makes it suitable for long-distance transport. Starch and cellulose are insoluble, and glycogen occurs in animals and fungi.
116257.m: In the phloem, sugar is mostly transported as sucrose.

116258.q: In which cell layer of the root is the Casparian strip found?
116258.e: The endodermis is the innermost layer of the root cortex. Its cell walls carry a sealing band, the Casparian strip.
116258.m: The Casparian strip lies in the endodermis.

116259.q: Which deposited substance makes the Casparian strip impermeable to water?
116259.e: Water-repellent substances, mainly lignin, are deposited in the cell wall of the strip. As a result, water can no longer seep through between the cells.
116259.m: Deposited lignin seals the Casparian strip.

116260.q: In which cell walls of the endodermis cells is the Casparian strip located?
a: In the radial and transverse walls
Only in the outer wall facing the cortex
Only in the inner wall facing the xylem
In no wall, but in the cytoplasm
116260.e: The strip runs round each endodermis cell like a belt in the side walls. This seals the gaps between the cells.
116260.m: The Casparian strip seals the side walls between endodermis cells.

116261.q: What is the main function of the Casparian strip?
a: It forces water and ions to pass through living cells
It stores starch for the winter
It carries sugar to the root tip
116261.e: The strip blocks the route through the cell walls. Substances have to pass through a membrane, where the plant controls which ions get in.
116261.m: The Casparian strip turns the root into a selective filter.

116262.q: Why is the Casparian strip important for building up root pressure?
a: It stops ions flowing back out of the central cylinder
It opens the stomata at night
116262.e: Ions are pumped into the central cylinder and, because of the seal, cannot escape through the cell walls. So the water potential there stays low and water flows in after them.
116262.m: Without the endodermis seal, no root pressure could build up.

116263.q: Which transport route through the root cortex is interrupted by the Casparian strip?
a: The route through the cell walls (apoplast)
116263.e: In the cortex, water can flow through the cell walls. At the endodermis this route is blocked, and substances have to move into the cytoplasm.
116263.m: The Casparian strip blocks the route through the cell walls.

116264.q: Which tissue does the endodermis, with its Casparian strip, enclose?
a: The central cylinder with the vascular tissues
The whole cortex from the outside
116264.e: The endodermis forms a ring around the central cylinder, which contains the pericycle, xylem and phloem. It separates it from the root cortex.
116264.m: The endodermis is a control sheath around the central cylinder of the root.

116265.q: How can you make the Casparian strip visible in a cross-section of a root?
a: With a light microscope after staining
116265.e: The strip is only a few micrometres wide. In a thin, stained cross-section you can see it in the walls of the endodermis under a light microscope.
116265.m: You can see the Casparian strip under a microscope.

116266.q: According to the pressure flow theory, what is transported in the phloem?
a: Sugar solution from the leaves to where it is used
Water from the roots to the leaves
Air from the stomata to the roots
Soil water with mineral salts into the flowers
116266.e: Ernst Münch's pressure flow theory (1930) explains how sugar travels in the phloem from the leaves to roots, fruits and tubers. Water and mineral salts from the soil, on the other hand, rise in the xylem.
116266.m: The phloem carries sugar solution from source to sink.

116267.q: According to the pressure flow theory, how does the high pressure at the source build up?
a: Loading sugar lowers the water potential and water flows in by osmosis
The root presses air into the sieve tubes
The sun heats the sieve tubes
116267.e: In leaves, sucrose is loaded into the sieve tubes. Water follows from the xylem by osmosis and the turgor pressure rises.
116267.m: At the source, sugar draws in water and builds up pressure.

116268.q: Which part of a plant typically acts as a sink for sugar?
a: A fully developed leaf in the light
116268.e: Sinks use up or store sugar, for example tubers, fruits, roots and young leaves. A fully grown leaf in the light, on the other hand, is a source.
116268.m: Storage organs such as tubers are sugar sinks.

116269.q: According to the pressure flow theory, where does phloem transport mainly need metabolic energy?
a: When actively loading sugar at the source
For pumps in every single sieve tube element
116269.e: The flow itself is passive and follows the pressure gradient. Energy is needed mainly to load sugar into the phloem against a concentration gradient.
116269.m: The pressure flow is passive; only loading costs energy.

116270.q: Where does the water that flows into the sieve tubes at the source come from?
a: From the rain on the leaf
From respiration in the mitochondria alone
116270.e: Xylem and phloem lie side by side in the vascular bundle. Water flows by osmosis from the xylem into the phloem and partly back again at the sink.
116270.m: The phloem borrows its water from the xylem.

116271.q: According to the pressure flow theory, what happens at the sink?
a: Sugar is unloaded, water leaves and the pressure falls
The pressure rises to its maximum
Water evaporates through the sieve plates
116271.e: In the sink, sucrose is used up or stored. The water potential rises, water leaves the sieve tube and the pressure falls.
116271.m: The pressure difference between source and sink drives the phloem flow.

116272.q: How does the direction of transport in the phloem differ from that in the xylem?
a: In the phloem, transport upwards and downwards is possible
In the phloem, everything flows only upwards
In the phloem, the sap always stands still
In the phloem, everything flows only into the leaves
116272.e: The direction depends on where the sources and sinks are, for example towards roots or towards fruits. In the xylem, by contrast, water flows almost only upwards.
116272.m: Phloem sap always flows from source to sink, whatever the direction.

116273.q: How do researchers collect pure phloem sap to test the pressure flow theory?
a: Using the severed mouthparts of an aphid
116273.e: Aphids pierce a sieve tube precisely. If the insect is cut away from its mouthparts, phloem sap keeps flowing out of them.
116273.m: Aphids serve as a tool for collecting phloem sap.

116274.q: Which meristem in a tree trunk continuously produces new sieve tubes?
116274.e: The cambium is a ring of dividing cells between the wood and the bark. It produces new phloem towards the outside and new wood towards the inside.
116274.m: The cambium makes phloem outwards and wood inwards.

116275.q: Under what pressure are the contents of working sieve tubes?
116275.e: If a sieve tube is cut, the sap oozes out. The turgor created by osmosis pushes the phloem sap forwards.
116275.m: Working sieve tubes are under positive pressure.

116276.q: What are the perforated cross walls between two sieve tube elements called?
116276.e: The cross walls are pierced by large pores, rather like a sieve. The phloem sap flows through them from one element to the next.
116276.m: Sieve plates connect the elements of a sieve tube.

116277.q: On which side of a vascular bundle is the phloem in a typical leaf?
a: Towards the underside of the leaf
Towards the upper side of the leaf
116277.e: In the leaf, the xylem lies at the top of the vascular bundle and the phloem at the bottom. This matches the position in the stem, where the phloem lies on the outside.
116277.m: In a leaf, the phloem lies on the lower side of the veins.

116278.q: What are the proteins called that also quickly block sieve tubes when they are injured?
116278.e: P-proteins are found in the sieve tubes and collect at the pores between the elements when the pressure drops. They act like a quick emergency seal.
116278.m: P-proteins form a quick plug in injured sieve tubes.

116279.q: Which conducting cells do conifers have instead of sieve tubes?
116279.e: Gymnosperms have sieve cells without true sieve plates. They are supplied by albuminous cells, known as Strasburger cells.
116279.m: Conifers carry sugar in sieve cells instead of sieve tubes.

116280.q: Why does a tree usually die if a ring of bark is removed all round the trunk?
a: The roots no longer receive sugar from the leaves
The leaves lose their chlorophyll immediately
The trunk breaks under its own weight
116280.e: Removing the bark cuts through the sieve tubes, while the wood stays intact. The roots slowly starve and die, and then the tree dies too.
116280.m: A ring of removed bark cuts off the sugar supply to the roots.

116281.q: In which part of a tree trunk are the working sieve tubes?
a: In the bast of the inner bark
116281.e: The living phloem lies as a thin layer directly under the outer bark; older sieve tubes get crushed.
116281.m: A tree's sieve tubes lie in the bast under the outer bark.

a: A long, dead cell with pointed ends and pits
A living cell without a nucleus with sieve plates
A short cell with many chloroplasts
A round cell with starch grains
116282.e: Tracheids are long water-conducting cells that are dead when mature. Water flows from cell to cell through pits in the walls.
116282.m: Tracheids are dead, spindle-shaped water-conducting cells.

116283.q: How do vessels differ from tracheids?
116283.e: In vessels, the cross walls have dissolved completely or partly, forming long tubes. Tracheids remain closed individual cells.
116283.m: Vessels are open tubes, tracheids closed individual cells.

116284.q: In which group of plants does the wood consist mainly of tracheids?
a: In broadleaf trees such as oak
116284.e: Softwoods such as spruce and fir have almost no vessels. Over 90 per cent of their wood is made of tracheids, which conduct water and provide support.
116284.m: Softwood is made up mainly of tracheids.

116285.q: How does water get from one tracheid to the next?
a: Through pits in the cell walls
116285.e: Tracheids are closed cells. Water flows through thin areas in the wall, the pits. In softwoods, a thickened torus in the pit works like a valve.
116285.m: Water flows through pits from tracheid to tracheid.

116286.q: Which substance makes the walls of tracheids woody and resistant to pressure?
116286.e: Lignin is deposited in the cellulose walls and makes them firm. This stops the tracheids collapsing under the tension of the water.
116286.m: Lignin makes the walls of water-conducting cells woody.

116287.q: Why are tracheids safer from embolisms than wide vessels?
a: A gas bubble stays confined to one small cell
They only conduct water at night
116287.e: Tracheids are short, narrow and connected only by pits. A gas bubble can therefore hardly spread.
116287.m: Narrow, short conducting cells limit embolisms to small areas.

116288.q: Why do tracheids in softwood form visible annual rings?
a: Late wood tracheids are thick-walled with a narrow lumen
No cells with walls form in autumn
Early wood consists only of resin
Tracheids grow most strongly in winter
116288.e: In spring the tree forms wide, thin-walled tracheids, in summer thick-walled, narrow ones. The change to the light early wood of the following year creates the boundary.
116288.m: Annual rings form from the change between early wood and darker late wood.

116289.q: Which two jobs do tracheids in softwood do at the same time?
116289.e: Because softwood has hardly any fibres, the tracheids also carry the weight of the tree. Late wood tracheids are particularly strong.
116289.m: In softwood, the tracheids conduct and support at the same time.

116290.q: How many guard cells make up a typical stoma?
116290.e: Two curved guard cells surround the pore. When their turgor changes, the opening opens or closes.
116290.m: Two guard cells together form a stoma.

116291.q: Which ions do guard cells mainly take up when the stoma opens?
116291.e: Proton pumps create a gradient, then K+ ions flow in. Water follows by osmosis, the turgor rises and the pore opens.
116291.m: Potassium draws water into the guard cells and opens the pore.

116292.q: Which plant hormone makes the stomata close during drought?
116292.e: When water is short, the plant makes abscisic acid (ABA). It causes the guard cells to lose ions and water, and the pore closes.
116292.m: Abscisic acid is the plant's drought stress hormone.

116293.q: Which light is a particularly effective signal for opening the stomata?
116293.e: Blue light receptors in the guard cells activate proton pumps. This starts the uptake of ions and the opening in the morning.
116293.m: Blue light signals guard cells to open.

116294.q: How do guard cells usually differ from the other cells of the leaf epidermis?
116294.e: Most epidermis cells are colourless and transparent. Guard cells, by contrast, contain chloroplasts.
116294.m: Guard cells are usually the only cells in the epidermis with chloroplasts.

116295.q: Why do guard cells bend when they swell and so open the pore?
a: Their cell walls are unevenly thickened and built
They lose water in the process
116295.e: The wall facing the pore is thicker and less stretchy, and the cellulose fibres run outwards from the pore like rays (radial micellation). When turgor rises, the cells stretch unevenly and move apart.
116295.m: Unevenly built walls make guard cells bend when they swell.

116296.q: How do guard cells react to a greatly increased CO2 concentration in the leaf?
116296.e: If there is enough CO2 in the leaf, the plant does not need a wide-open pore. It narrows the opening and so saves water.
116296.m: A lot of CO2 in the leaf makes the stomata narrower.

116297.q: What are the epidermis cells called that accompany the guard cells in many plants and support their movement?
116297.e: Subsidiary cells lie directly next to the guard cells and differ from ordinary epidermis cells. They exchange ions with the guard cells.
116297.m: Subsidiary cells form the stomatal complex together with the guard cells.

116298.q: What shape are the guard cells of grasses such as wheat and maize?
116298.e: Grasses have dumbbell-shaped guard cells with a thick middle and thin ends. This lets them open very quickly.

116299.q: What does the water use efficiency of a plant indicate?
a: Biomass produced per amount of water used
Amount of water per square metre of soil
116299.e: Water use efficiency compares production with water consumption. It is given, for example, in grams of dry matter per kilogram of water.
116299.m: High water use efficiency means a lot of growth with little water.

116300.q: Which type of photosynthesis generally reaches the highest water use efficiency?
116300.e: CAM plants open their stomata at night, when it is cool, and store CO2 as malic acid. During the day the pores stay closed.
116300.m: CAM plants save water by taking in CO2 at night.

116301.q: Why do C4 plants such as maize usually have a higher water use efficiency than C3 plants?
a: PEP carboxylase binds CO2 well even with narrow stomata
They have no stomata at all
They take up water through their leaves
116301.e: PEP carboxylase has a high affinity for CO2 and does not react with oxygen. So the plant can fix enough CO2 with less open pores.
116301.m: C4 plants get more CO2 per unit of water evaporated.

116302.q: Which leaf feature helps plants in dry places lose less water per unit of CO2 taken in?
a: Stomata only on the upper side
116302.e: In hollows, a still, damp layer of air stays over the stomata. This slows the loss of water more than the uptake of CO2.
116302.m: Sunken stomata are a typical water-saving feature of dry-land plants.

116303.q: Roughly how many grams of water does a typical C3 plant transpire to produce 1 gram of dry matter?
116303.e: Textbook values for C3 plants are several hundred grams of water per gram of dry matter. C4 plants need about half that, CAM plants much less.
116303.m: C3 plants evaporate hundreds of grams of water for one gram of biomass.

116304.q: A plant produces 2 kg of dry matter and uses 600 kg of water in the process. What is its water use efficiency?
a: About 3.3 g per kg of water
About 0.3 g per kg of water
About 30 g per kg of water
About 300 g per kg of water
116304.e: 2000 g of dry matter divided by 600 kg of water gives 3.33 g per kg. Put the other way round, the plant needs 300 kg of water per kg of dry matter.
116304.m: Water use efficiency divides the biomass by the amount of water used.

116305.q: How does a higher CO2 concentration in the air usually affect the water use efficiency of plants?
a: It rises, because the stomata can be narrower
It always stays exactly the same
It falls, because more water evaporates
116305.e: With more CO2 in the air, more CO2 gets into the leaf for the same opening time. Plants often narrow their pores and lose less water.
116305.m: More CO2 in the air usually improves water use efficiency.

116306.q: Through which openings does a plant lose most of its water?
116306.e: The plant takes in CO2 through the stomata, but also gives off water vapour. That is why it always has to balance photosynthesis against saving water.
116306.m: CO2 gets in and water gets out through the stomata.

116307.q: Which irrigation method particularly improves water use efficiency in farming?
a: Drip irrigation directly at the roots
116307.e: With drip irrigation, water goes straight to the roots. Little unused water is lost through evaporation or seeping away.
116307.m: Drip irrigation delivers water sparingly right to the roots.

116408.q: In which layer of the skin are melanocytes mainly found?
a: In the lowest layer of the epidermis
In the subcutis near the fat tissue
116408.e: Melanocytes sit in the basal layer, the lowest layer of the epidermis. From there their extensions reach the skin cells above.
116408.m: Melanocytes lie in the lowest layer of the epidermis.

116410.q: In which organelles do melanocytes make the pigment melanin?
116410.e: Melanin forms in special membrane-bound organelles, the melanosomes. These are then passed on to the surrounding skin cells.

116411.q: Which hereditary condition occurs when melanocytes cannot make melanin?
116411.e: In albinism the enzyme tyrosinase, which starts melanin production, is usually missing. Skin, hair and eyes then have hardly any pigment. In vitiligo, by contrast, melanocytes are only lost later.
116411.m: In albinism the pigment melanin is missing.

116412.q: How do melanocytes pass their pigment on to the keratinocytes?
116412.e: Melanocytes have dendritic extensions through which they hand melanosomes directly to neighbouring keratinocytes. In this way one melanocyte supplies many skin cells at once.
116412.m: Melanocytes distribute their pigment through their dendrites.

116413.q: Why do people with dark skin not have clearly more melanocytes than people with light skin?
a: What matters is the amount and type of melanosomes
Their melanocytes lie deeper in the dermis
116413.e: The number of melanocytes is similar for all skin colours. Differences come from the size, number and melanin type of the melanosomes and how they are spread in the keratinocytes.
116413.m: Skin colour depends on how active the melanocytes are, not on their number.

116414.q: Why do you only get properly tanned a few days after sunbathing?
a: The melanocytes first have to make new melanin and pass it on
The skin first has to peel
The blood first has to bring the pigment
The sun cream first has to break down
116414.e: UV radiation stimulates the melanocytes to make more melanin. It takes a few days for it to be made and spread to the skin cells.
116414.m: A tan develops because melanocytes make new pigment.

116415.q: Which skin disease is caused by the loss of melanocytes in sharply defined patches of skin?
116415.e: In vitiligo, melanocytes are usually destroyed by an autoimmune reaction. The affected areas lose their pigment and become white.
116415.m: In vitiligo, melanocytes are missing in white patches.

116416.q: How do the melanosomes in keratinocytes protect the DNA in a particularly targeted way?
a: They settle like a cap over the cell nucleus
They build themselves into the cell membrane
They move into the cell nucleus
116416.e: In keratinocytes the melanosomes gather on the side of the nucleus facing the sun. This nuclear cap absorbs UV radiation before it reaches the DNA.
116416.m: Melanin forms a sunshade for the DNA over the cell nucleus.

116417.q: How does UVA radiation differ from UVB radiation?
a: UVA has a longer wavelength and less energy
UVA has a shorter wavelength and more energy
UVA is part of visible light
UVA is completely filtered out by the ozone layer
116417.e: UVA ranges from 315 to 400 nanometres and borders on visible violet. UVB has a shorter wavelength and so more energy.
116417.m: UVA is the UV radiation with the longest wavelength.

116418.q: Roughly what share of the UV radiation reaching the ground is UVA?
116418.e: The ozone layer strongly filters short-wave UV radiation but hardly filters long-wave UVA. That is why most UV radiation at ground level is UVA.
116418.m: Almost all UV radiation at ground level is UVA.

116419.q: Down to which layer of the skin does UVA radiation mainly penetrate?
116419.e: Because of its longer wavelength, UVA gets deeper into the skin than UVB and reaches the dermis. There it damages collagen and elastic fibres.
116419.m: UVA penetrates down to the dermis.

116420.q: Which skin change is mainly caused by UVA radiation?
116420.e: UVA destroys collagen and elastic fibres in the dermis. In the long term this leads to wrinkles and leathery skin, known as photoageing.
116420.m: UVA makes the skin age prematurely.

116421.q: Why can you still get UV damage behind an ordinary window pane?
a: Normal glass lets through a lot of UVA
116421.e: Window glass largely blocks UVB but lets a large part of UVA radiation through. That is why behind glass sunburn is unlikely but skin ageing is possible.
116421.m: Behind normal glass, UVA still has an effect.

116422.q: How does UVA radiation mainly damage DNA?
116422.e: DNA absorbs UVA only weakly. However, UVA produces free radicals and other reactive oxygen compounds that damage the genetic material by oxidation.
116422.m: UVA damages DNA mainly through free radicals.

116423.q: Which type of radiation is dominant in the lamps of most sunbeds?
116423.e: Sunbeds tan mainly with UVA radiation, often with a small amount of UVB. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies sunbed use as carcinogenic.

116424.q: Which rule applies in the EU to sunscreens with the circled UVA logo?
a: The UVA protection is at least one third of the SPF
The UVA protection is as high as the SPF
The product protects only against UVA
The product contains no chemical filters
116424.e: According to an EU recommendation, only products whose UVA protection reaches at least one third of the stated sun protection factor may carry the UVA logo. This ensures balanced protection.
116424.m: The UVA logo guarantees balanced UVA protection.

116425.q: Which UV radiation is largely, but not completely, held back by the ozone layer?
116425.e: UVB, at 280 to 315 nanometres, is strongly weakened by the ozone layer, but some of it reaches the ground. UVC is completely absorbed, UVA hardly at all.

116426.q: Which acute skin reaction is mainly triggered by UVB radiation?
116426.e: UVB has more energy than UVA and is strongly absorbed in the epidermis. There it triggers inflammation with redness: sunburn.
116426.m: Sunburn is mainly a result of UVB.

116427.q: Which DNA damage is typical of the direct effect of UVB?
116427.e: UVB is absorbed directly by DNA. Neighbouring pyrimidine bases such as thymine join together into dimers, which can cause mutations when the DNA is copied.
116427.m: UVB sticks neighbouring DNA bases together into dimers.

116428.q: Which protective reaction of the epidermis is triggered by repeated UVB exposure?
116428.e: UVB stimulates keratinocytes to divide and the horny layer becomes thicker. This so-called light callus scatters and absorbs part of the radiation.
116428.m: Repeated sun makes the horny layer thicker.

116429.q: What is the job of the protective protein p53, which is often damaged by UVB in skin cancer cells?
a: It stops cell division when DNA is damaged
It makes the skin pigment melanin
It transports oxygen into the skin
It builds collagen in the dermis
116429.e: p53 is considered the guardian of the genome: when DNA is damaged it halts cell division or makes the cell die. If it fails because of mutations, damaged cells can divide unchecked.
116429.m: The protective gene p53 is often damaged by UVB.

116430.q: How can researchers tell that a skin tumour was caused by UV radiation?
a: From typical mutation patterns in the DNA
From the colour of the tumour cells
From the temperature of the tumour
From the size of the cell nuclei
116430.e: UVB joins neighbouring DNA bases. During repair or copying, typical errors often occur, for example cytosine is replaced by thymine. This “UV signature” reveals the origin.
116430.m: Cytosine-to-thymine mutations are a fingerprint of UV radiation.

116431.q: When does the redness of sunburn typically reach its peak?
116431.e: The inflammation takes time, because messenger substances widen the blood vessels only gradually. The redness begins after a few hours and is usually strongest after about half a day to a full day.
116431.m: Sunburn only shows its full extent hours later.

116432.q: How is the UV index calculated from solar radiation?
a: From the irradiance weighted by its sunburn effect
From the air temperature at midday
From the number of hours of sunshine per day
From the brightness of visible light
116432.e: The UV radiation is weighted with the erythema action spectrum, in which UVB counts especially strongly. One index level corresponds to 25 milliwatts of erythemally effective radiation per square metre.
116432.m: The UV index measures radiation that causes sunburn.

116433.q: Why is a single UVB photon more dangerous for DNA than a UVA photon?
a: It carries more energy because of its shorter wavelength
It only has an effect at night
116433.e: The energy of a photon is inversely proportional to its wavelength. The more energetic UVB photons are also absorbed right in the range where DNA absorbs light.
116433.m: The shorter the wavelength, the more energetic the photon.

116434.q: Which skin cancer is the most common type of cancer of all in people with fair skin?
116434.e: Basal cell carcinoma, also called basalioma, is the most common malignant tumour in people with fair skin. It usually grows slowly.
116434.m: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common cancer in people with fair skin.

116435.q: What is typical of the way a basal cell carcinoma grows?
a: It destroys locally but rarely forms metastases
It spreads to the lungs very early
It grows only in mucous membranes
116435.e: Basal cell carcinoma can destroy surrounding tissue down to the bone. However, it only very rarely forms secondary tumours, which is why it is sometimes called semi-malignant.
116435.m: A basalioma grows destructively but hardly spreads.

116436.q: On which part of the body do basal cell carcinomas occur most often?
116436.e: Most basaliomas develop in places that get a lot of sun over decades, especially the face. The nose, forehead and ears are typical.
116436.m: Basaliomas usually develop on the sun-exposed face.

116437.q: What does a nodular basal cell carcinoma typically look like?
a: A glassy lump with a pearly edge and fine little blood vessels
A black spot with a ragged edge
116437.e: Typical are a skin-coloured to reddish, glassy shiny lump and a raised edge like a string of pearls. Widened blood vessels are often visible on the surface.
116437.m: A basalioma often shows a pearly raised edge.

116438.q: Which kind of UV exposure is considered the most important risk factor for basal cell carcinoma?
a: The UV dose built up over a lifetime
116438.e: The risk rises with the UV dose added up over a lifetime. That is why older people and people who work outdoors a lot are especially affected.
116438.m: For basalioma, the total UV dose of a lifetime counts.

116439.q: What does UV radiation do in skin cells that can lead to skin cancer such as basal cell carcinoma?
a: It fills the cells with water
It uses up all the melanin
116439.e: UV radiation changes building blocks of DNA. If the damage is not repaired, mutations arise and a cell can divide uncontrollably.
116439.m: Skin cancer is caused by UV damage to DNA.

116440.q: What is the standard treatment for a basal cell carcinoma?
116440.e: The basalioma is usually cut out completely. Microscopic examination of the cut edges checks whether the tumour has been fully removed.

116441.q: Why are the cut edges examined under the microscope after a basal cell carcinoma has been cut out?
a: To check whether the tumour has been completely removed
To count bacteria in the wound
116441.e: If tumour cells remain at the edge, the cancer can grow back. That is why more is cut away until the edges are free of tumour.
116441.m: Tumour-free edges show that the cancer has been completely removed.

116442.q: Why is a melanoma that grows quickly downwards particularly dangerous?
a: It quickly reaches blood and lymph vessels
It grows only on the scalp
It can never be operated on
116442.e: Blood and lymph vessels lie in the deeper dermis. The deeper a melanoma reaches, the more easily tumour cells can travel through them to other organs.
116442.m: The deeper a melanoma grows, the more dangerous it is.

116443.q: What does the “E” stand for in the ABCDE rule for assessing moles?
116443.e: The rule checks asymmetry, border, colour, diameter and evolution. A mole that changes in size, shape or colour should be examined by a doctor.
116443.m: A mole that changes should be checked by a doctor.

116444.q: From which cells does a melanoma develop?
a: From the pigment cells of the skin
From the fat cells of the subcutis
116444.e: A melanoma is a malignant tumour of the melanocytes, the cells that make the pigment melanin. That is why it is often dark in colour.
116444.m: A melanoma is a tumour of the pigment cells.

116445.q: Why is melanoma also called “black skin cancer” in German?
a: Because it is usually darkly pigmented
Because it occurs only on dark skin
Because it grows mainly at night
116445.e: Melanomas develop from pigment cells and often make a lot of melanin. That is why they usually look brown to black, unlike the light-coloured skin cancers.
116445.m: Melanomas are usually dark because they develop from pigment cells.

116446.q: Why should you also check the soles of your feet and your nails for unusual dark spots?
a: Melanomas can also develop in places that get little sun
There are no pigment cells there
The skin there is immune to cancer
116446.e: Not every melanoma is caused by the sun. One form grows on the palms, soles or under the nails, and in people with dark skin it is even the most common.
116446.m: Melanomas can also develop on the soles of the feet and under the nails.

116447.q: What lies behind the development of a melanoma at the level of the cell?
a: Changes in the DNA of the pigment cells
Too much melanin in the blood
116447.e: UV radiation can damage the DNA of pigment cells. If such mutations build up, for example in the BRAF gene, the cells divide uncontrollably.
116447.m: Melanomas are caused by DNA damage, often from UV radiation.

116448.q: Which treatment has greatly improved the chances in melanoma that has spread since the 2010s?
a: Immunotherapies that activate the immune system against the tumour
116448.e: New immunotherapies release a brake on the immune system. This allows T cells to attack the tumour cells more effectively.
116448.m: Immunotherapies help the immune system fight melanoma cells.

116449.q: What is a sentinel lymph node biopsy for in melanoma?
a: To check whether tumour cells have spread into the lymph system
116449.e: The sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node in the area that drains the tumour. If it is free of tumour cells, spread through the lymph is unlikely.
116449.m: The sentinel lymph node shows whether a melanoma has spread.

116450.q: Which factor raises the risk of melanoma particularly clearly?
a: Many moles and sunburns in childhood
Swimming often in an indoor pool
116450.e: A high number of moles and bad sunburns at a young age are among the most important risk factors. Fair skin and cases in the family also raise the risk.
116450.m: Sunburns in childhood raise the risk of melanoma.

116451.q: Which instrument do dermatologists use to examine moles magnified and lit up?
116451.e: The dermatoscope works with magnification and incident light. This makes structures in the skin visible that cannot be seen with the naked eye.
116451.m: With a dermatoscope you can see moles more closely.

116452.q: What does the “ugly duckling sign” mean when checking the skin?
a: A mole that looks different from all the others is suspicious
Moles on the hands are harmless
116452.e: Most of a person's moles look alike. A mole that does not fit the pattern, an ugly duckling, should be examined more closely.
116452.m: A mole that stands out from the rest should be checked.

116453.q: Which form of prevention does early detection of skin cancer belong to?
116453.e: Early detection means finding a disease that has already developed as early as possible. At this stage it can usually be treated well.

116454.q: Which measure belongs to the primary prevention of skin cancer?
a: Protection with clothing, a hat and shade
116454.e: Primary prevention aims to stop a disease from developing at all. For skin cancer this mainly means reducing UV exposure.
116454.m: The best protection against skin cancer is less UV radiation.

a: Specialists assessing skin images from a distance
Treating the skin with television light
A skin check only by phone without images
Measuring skin temperature from a distance
116455.e: In teledermatology, photos or dermatoscope images are sent electronically to specialists. They can then judge whether an examination in person is needed.
116455.m: Teledermatology assesses skin images from a distance.

116456.q: Which simple shadow rule helps you recognise the time of high UV exposure?
a: If your shadow is shorter than you are, look for shade
If your shadow is longer than you are, put on cream
Without a shadow there is no UV radiation
116456.e: A short shadow means the sun is high. Then the path through the atmosphere is short and UV radiation is correspondingly strong.
116456.m: A short shadow warns of strong UV radiation.

116457.q: After removal, how is a suspicious skin finding reliably confirmed or ruled out as cancer?
116457.e: The removed tissue is examined under the microscope in histology. Only this finding gives a confirmed diagnosis.
116457.m: Histology confirms the diagnosis of skin cancer.

116458.q: Why is a mirror or a second person useful when checking your own skin?
a: Because the back and scalp are otherwise hard to see
Because moles look bigger in the mirror
Because light would otherwise change the moles
Because it shows your blood group
116458.e: Skin cancer can develop anywhere, including places that are hard to see. With a mirror or help, you can check your back, neck and scalp.
116458.m: Self-checks should include places that are hard to see.

116459.q: Why should an actinic keratosis be treated?
a: It can develop into skin cancer
116459.e: Actinic keratoses are precancerous lesions. Without treatment they can turn into a light-coloured skin cancer.
116459.m: An actinic keratosis is a precancerous lesion.

116460.q: How does an actinic keratosis typically feel?
116460.e: The patches are often scaly and horny. They can often be felt better than seen.

116461.q: Where do actinic keratoses occur particularly often?
a: On a bald head, the forehead and the backs of the hands
On the soles of the feet
116461.e: The changes develop where the skin gets a lot of UV radiation over years. Typical places are a hairless scalp, the face, ears and the backs of the hands.
116461.m: Actinic keratoses grow in places plagued by the sun.

116462.q: What is the main trigger of actinic keratoses?
a: Chronic UV exposure over many years
A virus from the swimming pool
116462.e: The word actinic means caused by radiation. Years of sun exposure damage the DNA of the keratinocytes.
116462.m: Actinic keratoses are the result of years of sun exposure.

116463.q: Which treatment is often used for single actinic keratoses?
116463.e: In cryotherapy the patch is frozen with liquid nitrogen. The damaged cells die and healthy skin grows back.
116463.m: Single keratoses can be frozen off.

116464.q: What does the term “field cancerisation” mean for actinic keratoses?
a: The whole sun-damaged area of skin is altered
The cancer only grows on fields
Only one single spot is affected
116464.e: Besides the visible patches, the whole surrounding skin is often already UV-damaged. That is why whole areas are often treated instead of just single spots.
116464.m: In field cancerisation a whole area of skin is damaged.

116465.q: How does photodynamic therapy work for actinic keratoses?
a: An applied substance makes diseased cells sensitive to light, and light destroys them
UVB light turns the keratoses brown
116465.e: A cream with aminolevulinic acid builds up in the altered cells. When light is shone on them, reactive oxygen compounds form that kill these cells.
116465.m: In photodynamic therapy, light destroys marked precancerous cells.

116466.q: Which occupational group has a particularly high risk of actinic keratoses?
a: People who work outdoors a lot
People who work in an office at night
People who work in a laboratory
116466.e: Anyone who works, for example, in construction, farming or as a mountain guide is exposed to strong sunlight for years. In Germany, multiple actinic keratoses and squamous cell carcinomas caused by UV radiation have therefore been recognised as an occupational disease since 2015.
116466.m: People who work outdoors need especially good sun protection.

116467.q: How do mineral UV filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide work?
a: They scatter, reflect and absorb UV radiation
116467.e: Mineral filters are fine particles that reflect, scatter and partly absorb UV radiation. They are considered well tolerated but can leave a white film.
116467.m: Mineral filters protect with tiny particles on the skin.
