117751.e: The tensile strength of concrete is only about a tenth of its compressive strength; so the reinforcing steel takes the tensile forces.
117751.m: In reinforced concrete, the steel carries the tensile forces.

117752.q: The breaking length is the length at which a freely hanging wire breaks under its own weight. How long is it for steel with a tensile strength of 500 N/mm² and a density of 7850 kg/m³ (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117752.m: The breaking length depends on strength and density, not on the cross-section.

117753.q: Why is the practical tensile strength of glass far below the theoretical value?
a: Tiny surface cracks act as notches
117753.e: Stress concentrates at fine cracks, and brittle materials cannot reduce these peaks by flowing.
117753.m: Small cracks greatly reduce the strength of brittle materials.

117754.q: What is typical of plastic deformation?
a: It remains after the load is removed
It disappears completely after the load is removed
117754.e: Unlike with elastic deformation, a plastically deformed body does not return to its original shape.

117755.q: What is the permanent extension of a tensile sample after fracture, relative to its original length, called?
117755.e: Elongation at break is given as a percentage and measures how much a material can be deformed plastically before it breaks.
117755.m: A large elongation at break marks a material that is easy to deform.

117756.q: What happens inside a metal during plastic deformation?
a: Layers of atoms slide past each other
117756.e: Under a large load, whole planes of atoms in the crystal slide past each other. This is made possible by small defects in the lattice, called dislocations, which move through the crystal.
117756.m: Plastic deformation is based on layers of atoms slipping.

117757.q: Why does a copper wire get stiffer when you bend it back and forth several times?
117757.e: The deformation creates many dislocations that get in each other's way; the material becomes stronger but more brittle.

117758.q: In a tensile test, a steel sample is slowly stretched. What does the yield point show?
a: The stress at which the deformation becomes permanent
The stress at which the sample breaks
117758.e: Up to the yield point, the steel springs back after the load is removed. Above it, it starts to flow and stays plastically deformed.
117758.m: Above the yield point a material deforms permanently.

117759.q: Which material breaks at room temperature with practically no plastic deformation?
117759.e: Glass is brittle: it only deforms elastically until it breaks, whereas metals such as copper are ductile.
117759.m: Brittle materials such as glass break without permanent deformation.

117760.q: What is the crumple zone of a car for?
a: It absorbs impact energy through plastic deformation
117760.e: As it crumples, kinetic energy is turned into deformation work and the deceleration of the passengers is softened.
117760.m: The crumple zone uses up energy through plastic deformation.

117761.q: Which heat treatment makes work-hardened metal easy to shape again?
117761.e: During annealing, new grains with few dislocations form, and the material becomes softer and can be shaped again.

117763.q: Two springs of 100 N/m and 400 N/m hang in series and carry a load of 8 N. How far does the lower end drop?
117763.e: Each spring carries the full 8 N: the first stretches by 8 / 100 = 0.08 m, the second by 8 / 400 = 0.02 m, together 0.10 m.
117763.m: In a series arrangement, the extensions of the individual springs add up.

117764.q: Two springs of 200 N/m and 300 N/m are connected in parallel. What is the total spring constant?
117764.e: In parallel, D = 200 N/m + 300 N/m = 500 N/m.
117764.m: In parallel, the spring constants add up.

117765.q: Two springs of 200 N/m and 300 N/m are connected in series. What is the total spring constant?
117765.m: In series, the total spring constant is smaller than each individual one.

117766.q: Two identical springs are connected in series. How does the total spring constant compare with the spring constant of one spring?
a: It is four times as large
117766.m: Two identical springs in series are half as stiff.

117767.q: What force acts in each spring when two springs in series carry a load F?
117767.e: Each spring in the line has to pass on the whole load, like the links of a chain.
117767.m: In a series arrangement, each spring carries the whole load.

117768.q: Two identical springs hang side by side in parallel and together carry a load F. What force does each spring carry?
a: A quarter of the force F
117768.e: Both springs stretch by the same amount and share the load half and half.
117768.m: Identical springs in parallel share the load.

117769.q: Two parallel springs of 100 N/m each are connected in series with a third spring of 200 N/m. What is the total spring constant?
117769.e: The parallel pair gives 200 N/m; in series with 200 N/m, 1 / D = 1/200 + 1/200, so D = 100 N/m.
117769.m: You work out mixed spring arrangements step by step.

117770.q: How is shear stress τ defined?
a: Force parallel to the surface divided by the area
Force perpendicular to the surface divided by the area
117770.e: In shear, the force acts along the surface; τ = F / A.
117770.m: Shear stress is the tangential force per area.

117771.q: What is the material constant that links shear stress and shear angle called?
117771.e: In the elastic range, τ = G · γ, where G is the shear modulus and γ the shear angle.
117771.m: The shear modulus links shear stress and shear angle.

117772.q: What kind of load does a rivet experience when it holds two overlapping metal sheets against sliding sideways?
117772.e: The two sheets tend to slide against each other. The forces act across the rivet and try to shear it off at the joint.
117772.m: Rivets and bolts between sheets are loaded in shear.

117773.q: A bolt with a cross-section of 100 mm² is loaded in shear with 5000 N. What is the shear stress?
117773.e: τ = F / A = 5000 N / 100 mm² = 50 N/mm².
117773.m: Shear stress is shear force divided by cross-section.

117774.q: Why do liquids at rest have no shear modulus?
a: They give way to a shear force by flowing
117774.e: A liquid cannot withstand a static shear stress; it starts to flow under shear.

117775.q: Why do seismic S-waves not pass through the Earth's outer core?
a: It is liquid and does not transmit shear
It is too hot for any wave
117775.e: S-waves are shear waves; since the outer core is liquid, they cannot travel through it.
117775.m: Shear waves need a solid material.

117776.q: What is the job of a shear pin in a drive?
a: It breaks on purpose when overloaded and protects the machine
It increases the speed of rotation
117776.e: The shear pin is deliberately designed as the weakest link; if the torque is too high, it shears off before expensive parts break.
117776.m: A shear pin sacrifices itself when overloaded.

117777.q: What is the angle by which a body deforms under shear called?
117777.e: The shear angle γ describes the change of an originally right angle in the material.
117777.m: The shear angle measures deformation under shear.

117778.q: What does Empa mainly work on?
117778.e: Empa began as a testing institute for building materials. Today it researches new materials and technologies, for example for construction, energy and medicine.

117779.q: What did the abbreviation Empa originally stand for?
a: Federal Museum of Physics and Astronomy
117779.e: Empa began as an institute that tested building materials for strength. Today it is called the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology.
117779.m: Empa began as a materials testing institute.

117780.q: What can happen to a long, slender rod if you squeeze it hard along its length?
117780.e: Slender parts under compression can suddenly give way sideways. This buckling must be taken into account when building bridges, as the Münchenstein bridge disaster of 1891 showed.
117780.m: Slender rods under compression can buckle.

117781.q: Which three sites does Empa have?
117781.e: St Gallen was added in 1937 when a textile testing institute was incorporated, and Thun in 1994.
117781.m: Empa does research in Dübendorf, St Gallen and Thun.

117782.q: Which group of institutions does Empa belong to?
a: The association of cantonal grammar schools
117782.e: The ETH Domain includes the two Federal Institutes of Technology and the research institutes PSI, WSL, Empa and Eawag.
117782.m: Empa belongs to the ETH Domain.

117783.q: What did the testing institute in St Gallen, which became part of Empa in 1937, specialise in?
117783.e: In keeping with St Gallen's textile tradition, the institute tested fabrics and fibres.
117783.m: Empa's St Gallen site has its roots in textile testing.

117784.e: Tribology studies surfaces that touch and move relative to each other.
117784.m: Tribology is the science of friction, wear and lubrication.

117785.q: What did the British Jost Report of 1966 on friction and wear show?
a: They cost industry a great deal of money
117785.e: Peter Jost showed how much money is lost through friction and wear. After that, the field became known as tribology, from the Greek word for rubbing.
117785.m: Friction and wear cost the economy a lot of money.

117786.q: Why does an engine wear especially quickly right after a cold start?
a: The lubricating film has not fully built up yet
The petrol is still too warm
The engine has the most cooling water then
117786.e: At the start the oil is still cold and thick and does not reach all places at once. Until a load-bearing film of oil separates the parts, the surfaces partly touch directly.
117786.m: Wear is greatest without a complete lubricating film.

117787.q: In which state is the friction of a well-lubricated plain bearing smallest?
a: When the surfaces are completely separated by a lubricating film
117787.e: If a load-bearing lubricating film separates the surfaces completely, almost only the internal friction of the lubricant is left.
117787.m: A complete lubricating film greatly reduces friction.

117788.q: What is wear called when hard particles scratch and remove material from a surface?
117788.e: In abrasion, hard particles or rough peaks plough material out of the softer surface.
117788.m: Abrasion is wear by scratching and grooving.

117789.q: Which substance is often used as a solid lubricant?
117789.e: Graphite consists of layers that slide easily over each other, and it lubricates even where oil is not suitable.
117789.m: Graphite lubricates thanks to its sliding layers.

117790.q: What is the jerky switching between sticking and sliding called, which makes doors squeak, for example?
117790.e: As long as the surface sticks, tension builds up; when it breaks free, it slides on with a jerk until it sticks again. The same effect makes violin strings sound.
117790.m: The stick-slip effect comes from switching between sticking and sliding.

117791.q: Which plastic is known for its particularly low coefficient of friction?
117791.e: Polytetrafluoroethylene is one of the solids with the lowest coefficient of friction and is used for plain bearings and non-stick pan coatings.
117791.m: PTFE slides with particularly little friction.

117792.q: Which pair of materials has a particularly low coefficient of sliding friction of about 0.01?
117792.e: Skate blades glide very easily on ice, so the coefficient of sliding friction there is extremely small.
117792.m: Steel on ice slides with very little friction.

117793.q: Why does a train on steel rails need comparatively little energy to roll?
a: The rolling friction of steel on steel is very small
The rails are built on a downhill slope
The wheels do not touch the rail
Air resistance is zero for trains
117793.e: The hard steel wheels hardly deform, so the coefficient of rolling friction is about 0.001 to 0.002.
117793.m: Steel wheels on steel rails roll especially easily.

117794.q: What is wear called when surfaces briefly weld together at contact points and material is torn out?
117794.e: Under high pressure and without lubrication, rough peaks stick to each other; in extreme cases a bearing “seizes”.
117794.m: Adhesive wear comes from contact points welding together.

117795.q: What is the modular research building of Empa and Eawag in Dübendorf, where new building technologies are tested in everyday use, called?
117795.e: In NEST, opened in 2016, new materials and energy systems are tested under real conditions in exchangeable living and office units.
117795.m: In NEST, Empa tests new building technologies in everyday use.

117796.q: Which order did Gregor Mendel belong to as a monk?
117796.e: Mendel entered the Augustinian Abbey of St Thomas in 1843 and was given the religious name Gregor there.
117796.m: Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian monk.

117797.q: In which city did Gregor Mendel carry out his famous crossing experiments?
117797.e: Mendel experimented in the monastery garden in Brünn, today Brno in the Czech Republic.
117797.m: Mendel's experimental garden was in the monastery in Brno.

117798.q: With which plant did Gregor Mendel carry out his most important experiments on inheritance?
117798.e: For years Mendel crossed varieties of the garden pea (Pisum sativum). Peas have clearly distinguishable traits and are easy to pollinate in a controlled way.
117798.m: Mendel discovered the rules of inheritance using peas.

117799.q: In which year was Mendel's paper “Experiments on Plant Hybrids” published?
117799.e: Mendel presented his results to the Natural History Society in Brno in 1865. The paper was printed in its proceedings in 1866.

117800.q: How many pairs of pea traits did Mendel study in his experiments?
117800.e: Mendel chose seven traits, each with two clear forms, such as seed shape, seed colour and plant height.
117800.m: Mendel followed seven pairs of pea traits.

117801.q: Around which year were Mendel's laws independently rediscovered by several researchers?
117801.e: Around 1900, three botanists came across the same patterns independently of one another and then referred to Mendel.
117801.m: Mendel's work was only rediscovered around 1900.

117802.q: Which researcher was one of those who rediscovered Mendel's laws?
117802.e: Carl Correns published crossing results with peas and maize, among others, which confirmed Mendel's findings. Hugo de Vries and Erich von Tschermak did the same at almost the same time.
117802.m: Carl Correns was one of the rediscoverers of Mendel.

117803.q: Which position did Gregor Mendel take on in the monastery in 1868?
117803.e: In 1868 Mendel was elected abbot of the monastery of St Thomas. After that he had hardly any time left for research.
117803.m: Mendel became abbot of his monastery in 1868.

117804.q: Mendel crossed pure-breeding yellow-seeded peas with pure-breeding green-seeded peas. What did the seeds of the first generation of offspring look like?
117804.e: Yellow is dominant over green. So all offspring of the first generation are yellow. This is Mendel's law of uniformity.
117804.m: In the first generation of offspring, all offspring look the same.

117805.q: Which ratio of phenotypes is expected in the F2 of a monohybrid cross with dominant and recessive alleles?
117805.e: Aa crossed with Aa gives AA, Aa, Aa and aa. Three out of four show the dominant trait, one the recessive trait.
117805.m: A dominant-recessive cross splits three to one in the F2.

117806.q: Which ratio of genotypes arises in the F2 from the cross Aa times Aa?
117806.e: Each parent passes on A or a with equal probability. This produces the combinations AA, Aa, aA and aa.
117806.m: The genotypes of the F2 are distributed one to two to one.

117807.q: Which ratio do the phenotypes show in the F2 of a dihybrid cross with dominant and recessive alleles?
117807.e: Two independently inherited traits combine freely: (3 to 1) times (3 to 1) gives 9 to 3 to 3 to 1.
117807.m: With two traits, the F2 splits nine to three to three to one.

117808.q: In the F2 of a cross AaBb times AaBb, what proportion of plants has the genotype aabb?
117808.e: The proportion of aa is 1/4 and the proportion of bb is also 1/4. With independent inheritance, 1/4 times 1/4 equals 1/16.
117808.m: Double recessive plants make up one sixteenth of the dihybrid F2.

117809.q: Which cross is called a backcross or test cross?
a: A cross with a pure-breeding recessive partner
A cross of two F1 plants
A cross of two wild plants
117809.e: If you cross an individual showing the dominant trait with aa, the offspring reveal whether it is AA or Aa.
117809.m: A test cross with aa reveals the genotype.

117810.q: Which ratio results from a test cross Aa times aa?
117810.e: Aa produces half A and half a gametes, aa produces only a gametes. So half the offspring are Aa and half are aa.
117810.m: The test cross of a heterozygote gives one to one.

117811.q: Which flower colour does the F1 of the four o'clock flower show when a pure-breeding red plant is crossed with a pure-breeding white one?
117811.e: In the four o'clock flower (Mirabilis jalapa) flower colour is inherited in an intermediate way. The heterozygotes show an in-between form.
117811.m: Intermediate inheritance gives pink flowers in the four o'clock flower.

117812.q: Which exception limits the law of independent assortment?
a: Gene linkage on the same chromosome
117812.e: Genes that lie close together on the same chromosome are usually inherited together. They then do not combine freely.
117812.m: Linked genes are not inherited independently.

a: More than two sets of chromosomes per cell
The absence of a single chromosome
The doubling of a single gene
The exchange of pieces of chromosome
117813.e: Polyploid cells contain three, four or more complete sets of chromosomes. This is very common in plants.
117813.m: Polyploid organisms have more than two sets of chromosomes.

117814.q: Which substance from the autumn crocus is used to cause polyploidy artificially?
117814.e: Colchicine blocks the formation of the spindle apparatus. The chromosomes are doubled but not shared out between two daughter cells.
117814.m: Colchicine doubles chromosome sets because it blocks the spindle.

117815.q: How many sets of chromosomes does modern bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) have?
117815.e: Bread wheat arose from crosses of three grass species and is hexaploid with 42 chromosomes.

117816.q: Why do most cultivated bananas not produce seeds that can germinate?
117816.e: With three sets of chromosomes, the chromosomes cannot pair up properly in meiosis. Hardly any working gametes are formed.
117816.m: Triploid plants such as the cultivated banana are largely sterile.

a: Multiplication of the plant's own chromosome sets
Doubling of only the sex chromosomes
117817.e: Allopolyploids combine chromosome sets from different species, for example after a cross between species followed by doubling. Autopolyploids multiply their own set.
117817.m: Allopolyploids carry chromosome sets from different species.

117818.q: Why is a cross between two species often infertile, but fertile after the chromosomes have been doubled?
a: After doubling, every chromosome finds a partner in meiosis
Doubling turns the plant into a single species
117818.e: The chromosomes of two species do not match and cannot pair up in meiosis. After doubling, every chromosome has an identical counterpart. This is how allopolyploids such as oilseed rape or wheat arose.
117818.m: Doubled chromosome sets make crosses between species fertile.

117819.q: What level of ploidy does the common cultivated potato have?
117819.e: The cultivated potato (Solanum tuberosum) has four sets of chromosomes with 48 chromosomes in total.

a: As a triploid cross between a tetraploid and a diploid plant
By removing the seeds by hand
117820.e: If you cross a tetraploid line with a diploid one, you get triploid plants. Their fruits contain only soft, undeveloped ovules.

117821.q: Which characteristic do polyploid plants often show compared with the original diploid form?
a: A shorter lifespan for each cell
117821.e: More genetic material in the nucleus often leads to larger cells. This is called gigantism and is used in plant breeding.
117821.m: Polyploidy often leads to larger plant organs.

117822.q: What is the most important genetic feature of offspring produced by vegetative reproduction?
a: They are clones of the parent plant
They mix the genes of two parents
117822.e: In vegetative reproduction, offspring arise from body cells without fertilisation. Their genes are the same as the parent plant's.
117822.m: Plants reproduced vegetatively are genetically the same as their parent.

117823.q: Which organs does the garden strawberry use to reproduce vegetatively?
117823.e: The strawberry forms runners above the ground, and new daughter plants take root at their nodes.

117824.q: Which storage organ is used for reproduction when potatoes are planted?
117824.e: The potato is a thickened underground stem. New plants sprout from its eyes, which are buds.
117824.m: The potato is a stem tuber.

117825.q: Which plant forms little plantlets along the edges of its leaves?
117825.e: In mother of thousands, complete little plants with roots form in the notches of the leaf edge. When they drop off, they keep growing on their own.
117825.m: Mother of thousands forms young plants on the edge of its leaves.

117826.q: What do you call an underground stem growing horizontally, like the one ginger forms?
117826.e: A rhizome is a stem, usually underground, with buds. If you divide it, new plants grow.

117827.q: Which historical disaster shows the danger of low genetic diversity caused by growing clones?
a: The Great Smog of London in 1952
117827.e: In Ireland, only a few potato varieties propagated vegetatively were grown. Potato blight destroyed the harvests everywhere.
117827.m: Growing clones makes crops vulnerable to disease.

117828.q: What is the method called in which a shoot is bent down into the soil and takes root there before it is cut off?
117828.e: In layering, the shoot stays connected to the parent plant until it has formed its own roots.
117828.m: A layer takes root before it is separated from the parent.

117829.q: Which method makes it possible to grow a great many virus-free clones in the laboratory from a small amount of tissue?
117829.e: In meristem culture, tiny pieces of the shoot tip are multiplied on a nutrient medium. The tip is often free of viruses.
117829.m: Meristem culture produces many virus-free clones.

117830.q: Which roots form on a cutting?
117830.e: Roots that grow from a stem or a leaf are called adventitious roots. They do not develop from the seedling's first root.
117830.m: Cuttings take root with adventitious roots.

117831.q: To which group of plant hormones do most rooting agents belong?
117831.e: Auxins such as indole-3-butyric acid encourage adventitious roots to form. The cut end is dipped in powder or gel.
117831.m: Auxins encourage cuttings to form roots.

117832.q: Where is a tip cutting usually cut?
117832.e: At the node, the cells are especially ready to form roots. That is why the cut is made just below it.
117832.m: Cuttings are cut just below a node.

117833.q: Why are cuttings often kept under a cover in damp air?
a: Otherwise they lose too much water
They must not get any light
117833.e: Without roots a cutting can hardly take up any water. High humidity reduces evaporation through the leaves.
117833.m: High humidity protects cuttings without roots from drying out.

117834.q: Which houseplant is classically propagated by leaf cuttings?
117834.e: With the African violet, you put a leaf with its stalk into soil. Roots and new rosettes form at the base.
117834.m: African violets grow again from leaf cuttings.

117835.q: Which woody plants take root especially easily from leafless hardwood cuttings?
117835.e: Willow twigs quickly form roots in water or damp soil. That is why they are also planted to protect riverbanks.
117835.m: Willows take root very easily from hardwood cuttings.

117836.q: What do you call a cutting taken from a piece of root?
117836.e: In some plants, such as phlox or blackberry, pieces of root sprout new shoots. These are called root cuttings.
117836.m: New shoots sprout from root cuttings.

117837.q: What problem arises if a cutting keeps a lot of leaves?
117837.e: Large leaf areas lose a lot of water, which cannot be replaced without roots. That is why the lower leaves are removed or cut back.
117837.m: Fewer leaves make it easier for a cutting to take root.

117838.q: In grafting, what is the part that is placed on the rootstock called?
117838.e: The scion comes from the desired variety. The rootstock provides the roots and affects growth and hardiness.
117838.m: In grafting, a scion grows on a rootstock.

117839.q: Which tissue of the rootstock and the scion must meet in grafting?
117839.e: The cambium is tissue that can divide. The parts only grow together if the cambium layers touch.
117839.m: In grafting, cambium must meet cambium.

117840.q: What is the grafting method called in which just a single bud is inserted into a T-shaped cut in the bark?
117840.e: Oculation comes from the Latin “oculus” for eye. The inserted eye is a single bud of the desired variety.
117840.m: In budding, a single eye is inserted.

117841.q: Which pest forced Europe, from the late 19th century, to graft grapevines onto American rootstocks?
117841.e: The introduced phylloxera destroyed the roots of European vines. American vine roots are largely resistant.
117841.m: Because of phylloxera, European vines grow on American roots.

117842.q: Why are apple varieties often grafted onto a dwarfing rootstock?
a: The trees stay small and bear fruit early
The trees no longer need pruning
117842.e: A dwarfing rootstock slows the growth of the whole tree. This produces small trees that bear fruit after just a few years and are easy to harvest.
117842.m: The rootstock determines how vigorously an apple tree grows.

117843.q: Why are apple varieties such as “Gala” grafted instead of grown from pips?
a: Seedlings would not be true to the variety
Pips are poisonous to the soil
117843.e: Apple trees are usually heterozygous and cross-pollinated. A seedling therefore differs clearly from the parent variety.
117843.m: Only grafting keeps an apple variety unchanged.

117844.q: What is the grafting method called in which rootstock and scion of the same thickness are cut at a slant and placed together?
117844.e: In splice grafting both parts are given slanting cuts of the same length. These are fitted together exactly and wrapped tightly.
117844.m: In splice grafting, parts of equal thickness are joined at a slant.

117845.q: Why is the graft union of a fruit tree placed above the ground?
a: So that the scion does not form its own roots
So that the tree flowers sooner
117845.e: If the union is in the soil, the scion itself can take root. Then the influence of the rootstock, such as weak growth, is lost.
117845.m: The graft union belongs above the soil.

117846.q: What does apomixis mean in plants?
117846.e: In apomixis an embryo forms in the seed without gametes fusing. The offspring are usually clones of the mother.
117846.m: Apomictic plants form seeds without fertilisation.

117847.q: Which common meadow plant forms its seeds mainly by apomixis?
117847.e: The common dandelion usually forms its seeds without fertilisation. The plants in a meadow are therefore often clones.
117847.m: The dandelion usually forms its seeds without fertilisation.

117848.q: Which genus of berry bushes forms an especially large number of hard-to-tell-apart microspecies through apomixis?
117848.e: True blackberries (Rubus) often form their seeds by apomixis. That is why hundreds of microspecies have been described in Europe.
117848.m: Blackberries form a great many microspecies through apomixis.

117849.q: What is special about many seeds of citrus fruits such as oranges?
a: They often contain several seedlings that are clones of the mother
They only germinate after a forest fire
They form directly on the branch without a flower
117849.e: In many citrus species, extra embryos grow from the tissue of the ovule without fertilisation. So several seedlings can grow from one seed.
117849.m: Citrus seeds often contain several embryos.

117850.q: Why is apomixis so interesting for plant breeding?
a: Hybrid varieties could reproduce themselves true to type
Harvests would be twice as big
117850.e: At the moment hybrid seed splits up in the next generation. With apomixis the heterosis effect would be kept in the seeds.
117850.m: Apomixis could fix hybrid varieties permanently.

117851.q: What is the most important difference between apomixis and self-fertilisation?
117851.e: In self-fertilisation, pollen and egg cell from the same plant fuse. In apomixis the embryo arises without any fertilisation at all.
117851.m: Apomixis is seed formation without fertilisation.

117852.q: Why are the offspring of an apomictic plant such as lady's mantle almost genetically identical to the mother?
a: Its genes are passed on unchanged without fertilisation
They are always pollinated by the same insect
They grow in the same place
117852.e: Without fertilisation, no genes from a father are added. The seeds therefore contain practically clones of the mother plant.
117852.m: Apomictic offspring are clones of the mother.

117853.q: Which level of ploidy is especially common in apomictic plants?
117853.e: Many apomicts are polyploid, for example triploid dandelions. Their meiosis is often disrupted, and apomixis gets round this problem.

117854.q: What does self-incompatibility do in flowering plants?
a: The plant's own pollen cannot fertilise it
117854.e: The plant recognises its own pollen and prevents it from germinating or stops the pollen tube from growing.

117855.q: What advantage does self-incompatibility give a species?
117855.e: A plant that cannot fertilise itself depends on pollen from others. This mixes genes and avoids inbreeding.

117856.e: The S-locus holds genes for the recognition features of pollen and stigma. If the S-alleles match, the pollen is rejected.

117857.q: Why are several varieties planted next to each other in apple orchards?
a: Apples need pollen from another variety
Varieties protect each other from hail
117857.e: Most apple varieties are self-incompatible. Only pollen from a suitable pollinator variety leads to fruit setting.
117857.m: Apple trees need a pollinator variety.

117858.q: Where is the plant's own pollen stopped in self-incompatible plants?
a: On the stigma or in the style
117858.e: The plant recognises its own pollen on the stigma or in the style. There it does not germinate, or its pollen tube stops growing.
117858.m: The plant's own pollen is stopped on the stigma or in the style.

117859.q: Why is self-incompatibility a disadvantage for plants without insects or wind?
a: Without pollinators they hardly form any seeds
117859.e: Self-incompatible plants need pollen from another plant. If there are no pollinators or neighbours, no fruit is set.

117860.q: What is the phenomenon in primroses called, in which flowers have styles and stamens of different lengths?
117860.e: Primroses form short-styled and long-styled flowers. Successful pollination happens mainly between the two forms.

117861.q: Which naturalist studied the different flower forms of primroses in detail?
117861.e: In 1877 Darwin published a book on the different forms of flowers on plants of the same species. Primroses were at the centre of it.

117862.q: In which plant group does double fertilisation occur?
117862.e: Double fertilisation is a hallmark of the angiosperms, the flowering plants with an ovary.

117863.q: What forms when the second sperm cell fuses with the central cell?
117863.e: One sperm cell fertilises the egg cell, the other the central cell. The nutritive tissue develops from the latter.
117863.m: The fertilised central cell becomes the endosperm.

117864.q: How many sperm cells does a pollen tube bring to the ovule in angiosperms?
117864.e: The generative cell of the pollen grain divides into two sperm cells. Both are needed for double fertilisation.
117864.m: A pollen tube delivers two sperm cells.

117865.q: What is special about double fertilisation in flowering plants?
a: Two sperm cells fertilise two different cells
One egg cell is fertilised twice
Two pollen grains fuse with each other
The plant is fertilised twice a year
117865.e: One sperm cell fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote, the other with the central cell. This forms the endosperm, the nutritive tissue of the seed.
117865.m: Double fertilisation produces the embryo and the nutritive tissue.

117866.q: What is the female structure in the ovule where double fertilisation takes place called?
117866.e: The embryo sac is the greatly reduced female gametophyte. It contains the egg cell, the central cell and other cells.
117866.m: Double fertilisation happens in the embryo sac.

117867.q: What job does the endosperm have in the seed?
a: It protects the seed from being eaten
117867.e: The endosperm is a nutritive tissue made of starch, protein and fat. In a cereal grain it makes up the largest part and provides the flour.
117867.m: The endosperm is the nutritive tissue for the seedling.

117868.q: How do the sperm cells get from the pollen grain on the stigma to the egg cell?
a: Through the vascular bundles of the root
117868.e: The pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a tube that grows through the style to the ovule. Attractant substances show it the way.
117868.m: The pollen tube carries the sperm cells to the egg cell.

117869.q: What chromosome number does the zygote have after double fertilisation?
117869.e: A haploid egg cell and a haploid sperm cell fuse. This produces a diploid zygote, from which the embryo grows.

117870.q: What level of ploidy does the endosperm of most angiosperms have?
117870.e: The central cell has two haploid nuclei. Together with one sperm cell, this gives three sets of chromosomes.

117871.q: Which part of a coconut is liquid endosperm?
117871.e: The endosperm of the coconut is liquid at first. Later the firm white flesh is laid down from it on the inside of the shell.

117872.q: What does white flour mainly consist of?
a: The starchy part of the endosperm
117872.e: When white flour is milled, the germ and bran are removed. What remains is the starch-rich inner part of the grain.
117872.m: White flour comes from the endosperm of the grain.

117873.q: Which enzyme breaks down the starch in the endosperm into sugar when a cereal grain germinates?
117873.e: When the grain germinates, amylase is produced. It splits the stored starch into sugar, which the seedling uses for energy. This is also used when malting barley for beer.
117873.m: During germination, amylase turns starch into sugar.

117874.q: Which plant hormone from the seedling triggers the production of amylase in the aleurone layer?
117874.e: The seedling releases gibberellin. This starts the production of amylase, which breaks down starch, in the outermost layer of the endosperm.
117874.m: Gibberellin starts the breakdown of starch in the germinating grain.

117875.q: Where do the seeds of peas and beans mainly store their nutrients?
117875.e: In legumes the endosperm is almost completely used up while the seed ripens. The reserves are then in the thick seed leaves.
117875.m: Peas store nutrients in their seed leaves.

117876.q: What level of ploidy does the nutritive tissue in the seeds of conifers have?
117876.e: Gymnosperms have no double fertilisation. The nutritive tissue is the female gametophyte and is therefore haploid.
117876.m: Conifer seeds have a haploid nutritive tissue.

117877.q: What job does the endosperm have in the seed of a flowering plant?
a: It protects the seed from being eaten
117877.e: The endosperm is a nutritive tissue. It stores starch, fats or proteins, which the seedling uses up as it grows.
117877.m: The endosperm is the nutritive tissue of the seed.

117878.q: On which group of islands is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault?
117878.e: The seed vault is near Longyearbyen on Spitsbergen, which belongs to Norway.
117878.m: The global seed vault is on Spitsbergen.

117879.q: In which year was the Svalbard Global Seed Vault opened?
117879.e: The vault was officially opened on 26 February 2008.
117879.m: The seed vault on Spitsbergen has existed since 2008.

117880.q: At what temperature is the seed stored in the Svalbard Global Seed Vault?
117880.e: Cooling systems keep the storage rooms at around -18 degrees Celsius. At this cold temperature many seeds stay able to germinate for decades.
117880.m: The seeds are stored at around minus 18 degrees.

117881.q: What is the maximum number of seed samples the Svalbard Global Seed Vault can hold?
117881.e: The vault is designed for 4.5 million samples. With up to 500 seeds per sample, that would be over two billion seeds.
117881.m: The vault has room for 4.5 million seed samples.

117882.q: Why was seed taken back out of the Svalbard Global Seed Vault for the first time in 2015?
a: A gene bank in Syria could no longer be used because of the war
A fire had damaged the vault
The stored seeds could no longer germinate
Norway needed seed after a failed harvest
117882.e: Because of the civil war, the research centre ICARDA could no longer use its gene bank near Aleppo. With the backup copies it rebuilt its collections in Lebanon and Morocco.
117882.m: The first withdrawal took place in 2015 because of the war in Syria.

117883.q: Who owns the seed stored in the Svalbard Global Seed Vault?
a: The gene banks that deposit it
117883.e: The vault works on the principle of a black box. Only the gene bank that deposited them may open or take back its sealed boxes.
117883.m: The seed remains the property of the gene banks that deposit it.

117884.q: Why was Spitsbergen chosen as the location for the global seed vault?
a: The permafrost keeps it cold even during a power cut
117884.e: The permafrost inside the mountain naturally keeps the temperature below zero. The location is also remote and geologically stable.
117884.m: The permafrost is natural cooling for the vault.

117885.q: What happened at the entrance to the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in autumn 2016?
a: Meltwater got into the access tunnel
117885.e: After unusually warm and rainy weather, meltwater got into the access tunnel. The seed chambers were not damaged. The incident became known in 2017, after which the entrance was rebuilt.
117885.m: Thawing permafrost threatened the tunnel entrance in 2016.

117886.q: What is the special vigour and performance of F1 hybrids called?
117886.e: If you cross two different inbred lines, the F1 often outperforms both parents. This effect is called heterosis.
117886.m: Heterosis makes F1 hybrids especially productive.

117887.q: Why does a farmer have to buy F1 hybrid seed again every year?
117887.e: If you sow seeds from F1 plants, the traits split up according to Mendel. The uniform crop and the heterosis are lost.
117887.m: The F2 of hybrids is no longer uniform.

117888.q: Which parent plants are crossed with each other in hybrid breeding?
117888.e: Inbred lines are largely homozygous. Crossing them gives a uniform F1, as described by the law of uniformity.
117888.m: Hybrid seed comes from two inbred lines.

117889.q: Which crop did hybrid breeding help to achieve sharply rising yields in the USA in the 20th century?
117889.e: Hybrid maize became established in the USA from the 1930s. Yields per hectare then rose sharply.
117889.m: Hybrid maize was the first great success of hybrid breeding.

117890.q: What is usually observed if maize is pollinated only with itself over several generations?
a: The plants become weaker and smaller
The plants no longer form roots
117890.e: In maize, inbreeding leads to inbreeding depression and the plants become weaker. If you cross two different inbred lines, however, the offspring are especially strong.
117890.m: Inbreeding weakens maize, crossing two inbred lines strengthens it.

117891.q: What is removed when maize is “detasselled” in hybrid seed production?
117891.e: The tassel at the top carries the male flowers. If it is removed from the mother line, the mother line can only be pollinated by pollen from the father line.
117891.m: Detasselling prevents the mother line from pollinating itself.

117892.q: Why are mother plants that produce no working pollen popular in hybrid seed production?
a: They grow faster as a result
117892.e: Male-sterile mother plants can only be pollinated by pollen from the father line. This reliably produces hybrid seed without having to remove the pollen-bearing parts by hand.
117892.m: Male-sterile mother lines make hybrid seed production easier.

117893.q: Which researcher is considered the father of hybrid rice?
117893.e: In the 1970s the Chinese agricultural scientist Yuan Longping developed the first high-yielding hybrid rice varieties.

117894.q: How is hybrid seed usually labelled on seed packets in shops?
117894.e: The label F1 stands for the first generation of offspring from a cross. It shows that the seeds are hybrids.
117894.m: F1 on a seed packet means hybrid seed.

117993.q: What is the main job of surfactant in the air sacs of the lungs?
a: It carries oxygen into the blood
117993.e: Surfactant is a film at the boundary between air and fluid in the alveoli. It reduces surface tension and so stops the air sacs from collapsing when you breathe out.
117993.m: Surfactant keeps the air sacs open by lowering surface tension.

117994.q: What everyday thing is the effect of surfactant best compared with?
a: Washing-up liquid, which lowers the surface tension of water
117994.e: Like washing-up liquid, surfactant reduces surface tension. This makes the air sacs easier to open and stops them from collapsing.
117994.m: Surfactant lowers surface tension like washing-up liquid.

117995.q: Which class of substances makes up most of surfactant?
117995.e: Surfactant consists of around 90 per cent lipids, mainly phospholipids, and about 10 per cent proteins.

117996.q: Without surfactant, what would happen to small air sacs when you breathe out?
117996.e: Surface tension pulls the moist inner wall of the air sacs together. Without surfactant, small air sacs in particular would collapse.

117997.q: Which condition typically arises in premature babies because of a lack of surfactant?
117997.e: The lungs of babies born very early still make too little surfactant. The alveoli collapse and respiratory distress syndrome (IRDS) develops.
117997.m: A lack of surfactant causes respiratory distress syndrome in premature babies.

117998.q: Why is breathing so tiring for premature babies who lack surfactant?
a: The air sacs have to be opened again with every breath
They only breathe through their skin
117998.e: Without surfactant, the air sacs collapse when breathing out. Every breath in takes a lot of strength to open them again.
117998.m: A lack of surfactant makes every breath a big effort.

117999.q: According to Laplace's law, how does the pressure in an air sac depend on its radius if surface tension stays the same?
a: It is inversely proportional to the radius
It is proportional to the radius
It grows with the square of the radius
It does not depend on the radius
117999.e: According to Laplace, P equals 2 times surface tension divided by radius. Without surfactant, small alveoli would have a higher pressure and would empty into large ones.
117999.m: The smaller a bubble, the higher its internal pressure.

118000.q: How is artificial surfactant given to premature babies?
a: As an injection into the muscle
As a drip into a vein
118000.e: Surfactant has to reach the alveoli. That is why it is given directly into the windpipe through a tube or a thin catheter.
118000.m: Surfactant is given to premature babies directly into the windpipe.

118001.q: In which part of the brain is the respiratory centre mainly located?
118001.e: The neurons that create the breathing rhythm lie in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem. The pons also plays a part.
118001.m: The respiratory centre is in the medulla oblongata.

118002.q: Which stimulus is the strongest drive to breathe in a healthy person?
118002.e: Even small rises in CO2 partial pressure increase breathing clearly. Lack of oxygen only becomes an important drive when the O2 partial pressure is very low.
118002.m: In healthy people, carbon dioxide is the main drive to breathe.

118003.q: What do the central chemoreceptors in the brainstem mainly react to?
a: A drop in pH in the cerebrospinal fluid
A lack of oxygen in the cerebrospinal fluid
A lack of glucose in the blood
118003.e: CO2 passes easily through the blood-brain barrier and lowers the pH of the cerebrospinal fluid. The central chemoreceptors detect this acidification.
118003.m: Central chemoreceptors measure the acidification of the cerebrospinal fluid.

118004.q: Where are the peripheral chemoreceptors that mainly report a lack of oxygen?
a: In the carotid and aortic bodies
In the kidneys and adrenal glands
In the air sacs of the lungs
In the atria of the heart
118004.e: The carotid body at the fork of the carotid artery and the aortic bodies on the aortic arch measure the O2 partial pressure of the blood.
118004.m: Carotid and aortic bodies report a lack of oxygen to the brain.

118005.q: What prevents the lungs from being overstretched when you breathe in deeply?
a: Stretch receptors in the lungs stop the breath in
The heart squeezes the lungs together
The ribs break easily when overstretched
118005.e: Stretch receptors in the lungs report strong filling to the respiratory centre via the vagus nerve. Breathing in is then stopped.
118005.m: Stretch receptors protect the lungs from overstretching.

118006.q: Which muscle does most of the work when you breathe in calmly?
118006.e: The diaphragm contracts and flattens. This enlarges the chest cavity, and air flows into the lungs.
118006.m: The diaphragm is the most important breathing muscle.

118007.q: Why is heavy hyperventilating before diving dangerous?
a: The urge to breathe comes too late
118007.e: Hyperventilation mainly lowers the CO2 level, but hardly increases the oxygen supply. The urge to breathe then comes so late that you can pass out under water (shallow water blackout).
118007.m: Hyperventilating before diving can make you pass out under water.

118008.q: Why do we keep breathing in our sleep without thinking about it?
a: The respiratory centre in the brainstem controls breathing automatically
The lungs move by themselves without nerves
The heart pumps the air into the lungs
The cerebrum takes over control at night
118008.e: Nerve cells in the brainstem constantly create a breathing rhythm. You can influence breathing consciously, but it also carries on without your will.

a: The total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures
A gas dissolves in proportion to temperature
Gases always diffuse towards higher pressure
118009.e: In a gas mixture, each gas contributes its share to the total pressure. These partial pressures add up to the total pressure.
118009.m: The partial pressures of all gases together make up the total pressure.

118010.q: Roughly what is the O2 partial pressure of dry air at sea level?
118010.e: Oxygen makes up about 21 per cent of air. 0.21 times 101.3 kPa gives about 21 kPa, or roughly 160 mmHg.
118010.m: At sea level, the O2 partial pressure of air is about 21 kPa.

118011.q: Why is the oxygen partial pressure in the air sacs lower than in the outside air?
a: The air there is mixed with water vapour and CO2
Oxygen is burned in the windpipe
The air pressure in the lungs is much higher
118011.e: In the alveoli, water vapour and exhaled CO2 are added, and oxygen is constantly taken up into the blood. That is why the O2 partial pressure is about 100 instead of 160 mmHg.
118011.m: There is less oxygen in the air sacs than in the outside air.

118012.q: What happens to the CO2 partial pressure in the blood when you breathe very fast and deeply (hyperventilate)?
118012.e: When you hyperventilate, you breathe out more CO2 than the body makes. The CO2 partial pressure falls below the normal value of about 40 mmHg, which can cause tingling and dizziness.
118012.m: Fast breathing lowers the CO2 level in the blood.

118013.q: Roughly what is the O2 partial pressure of dry air at an air pressure of 500 hPa (oxygen share 21 %)?
118013.e: The oxygen share stays the same at altitude. 0.21 times 500 hPa gives 105 hPa.
118013.m: The O2 partial pressure falls in the same proportion as the air pressure.

118014.q: What happens to inhaled air in the airways before it reaches the air sacs?
a: It is warmed and saturated with water vapour
118014.e: The mucous membranes warm the air to body temperature and moisten it completely. The water vapour then takes up part of the total pressure.
118014.m: The airways warm and moisten the air.

118015.q: What determines the direction of gas exchange between alveolus and blood?
a: The blood pressure in the aorta
118015.e: Gases always diffuse from where the partial pressure is higher to where it is lower. That is how oxygen gets into the blood and CO2 into the alveolus.
118015.m: Gases move from higher to lower partial pressure.

118016.q: According to Fick's law of diffusion, which change reduces gas exchange in the lungs?
118016.e: The rate of diffusion is proportional to surface area, diffusion coefficient and partial pressure difference, but inversely proportional to the thickness of the membrane.
118016.m: A thick membrane slows down gas exchange.

a: The amount of dissolved gas is proportional to the partial pressure
The volume of a gas is proportional to temperature
Pressure is inversely proportional to volume
Light gases diffuse faster than heavy ones
118017.e: According to Henry, the higher the partial pressure of a gas above a liquid, the more of it dissolves. This also applies to O2 and CO2 in blood plasma.
118017.m: The higher the partial pressure, the more gas dissolves in a liquid.

118018.q: What shape is the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin?
118018.e: The curve is sigmoid: in the middle range saturation rises steeply, at high partial pressures it levels off.
118018.m: The haemoglobin binding curve is S-shaped.

118019.q: What causes the typical shape of the curve for oxygen binding to haemoglobin?
a: The cooperative binding of the four subunits
The binding of iron to plasma proteins
The breakdown of haemoglobin in the spleen
118019.e: When one oxygen molecule binds to a subunit, the affinity of the others rises. This cooperativity creates the steep middle part of the curve.
118019.m: The four subunits of haemoglobin work together when binding.

118020.q: What is the advantage of the upper, flat part of the oxygen dissociation curve?
a: The blood stays almost fully saturated even when there is a little less oxygen in the air
The blood releases a lot of oxygen there
The heart has to pump less there
118020.e: In the flat part, saturation hardly changes when the oxygen pressure drops a little. That is why the blood is still well loaded even at moderate altitude.
118020.m: The flat part of the curve secures oxygen uptake in the lungs.

118021.q: Which change shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right?
a: A fall in CO2 partial pressure
118021.e: Warmth lowers the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen. That is why more oxygen is released in warm, working tissue.
118021.m: Warmth makes it easier to release oxygen to the tissue.

118022.q: How does the body adapt to the lack of oxygen during a longer stay at high altitude?
a: It makes more red blood cells
118022.e: When oxygen is short, the kidney makes more EPO. The bone marrow produces more red blood cells, and the blood can carry more oxygen.
118022.m: At altitude the body makes more red blood cells.

118023.q: Where is the binding curve of fetal haemoglobin (HbF) compared with that of adult haemoglobin?
118023.e: HbF binds 2,3-BPG less well and therefore has a higher affinity for oxygen. This lets the fetus take over oxygen from the mother's blood.
118023.m: Fetal haemoglobin binds oxygen more strongly than adult haemoglobin.

118024.q: What shape is the oxygen binding curve of myoglobin?
118024.e: Myoglobin has only one haem group and does not bind cooperatively. Its curve is hyperbolic and lies far to the left, which makes it an oxygen store in muscle.
118024.m: Myoglobin has a hyperbolic binding curve.

118025.q: Roughly how much more strongly does haemoglobin bind carbon monoxide than oxygen?
118025.e: Carbon monoxide binds about 200 to 300 times more tightly to haemoglobin than oxygen does. Even low CO concentrations therefore block a lot of haemoglobin.
118025.m: Carbon monoxide pushes oxygen off haemoglobin very effectively.

118026.q: Roughly what is the oxygen saturation of arterial blood in a healthy person at sea level?
118026.e: At an O2 partial pressure of about 100 mmHg, the curve is in its flat upper part. Haemoglobin there is about 96 to 98 per cent saturated.
118026.m: In healthy people, arterial blood is almost fully saturated with oxygen.

118027.q: What does the Bohr effect describe?
a: Haemoglobin releases oxygen more easily as pH falls
Haemoglobin binds less oxygen in the cold
Carbon monoxide pushes oxygen off haemoglobin
118027.e: When CO2 partial pressure and proton concentration rise, haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen falls. Oxygen is then released more easily.
118027.m: An acidic environment loosens the binding of oxygen to haemoglobin.

118028.q: Which scientist is the Bohr effect named after?
118028.e: The Danish physiologist Christian Bohr described the effect. He was the father of the physicist Niels Bohr.
118028.m: The Bohr effect comes from the physiologist Christian Bohr.

118029.q: Which substance is produced in working muscles, lowers the pH of the blood and so helps haemoglobin release oxygen?
118029.e: Working muscles produce a lot of carbon dioxide. In the blood it forms carbonic acid, the pH falls, and haemoglobin releases more oxygen.
118029.m: A lot of carbon dioxide in the tissue helps release oxygen.

118030.q: Where in the body is the Bohr effect especially useful?
118030.e: Working muscles produce a lot of CO2 and acid. As a result, haemoglobin releases more oxygen there, exactly where it is needed.
118030.m: Active muscles get more oxygen thanks to the Bohr effect.

118031.q: In what form is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
118031.e: In the red blood cells, CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which breaks down into hydrogen carbonate and protons. Only a small part of the CO2 is dissolved or bound to haemoglobin.
118031.m: Carbon dioxide mostly travels in the blood as hydrogen carbonate.

118032.q: How does the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin shift when the blood becomes more acidic?
a: To the right, oxygen is released more easily
To the left, oxygen is bound more tightly
Not at all, pH has no effect
118032.e: In the Bohr effect, haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen falls. The curve shifts to the right, and at the same oxygen pressure more oxygen is released.
118032.m: Acidic blood shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right.

118033.q: What does the Bohr effect do in the lung capillaries, where CO2 is breathed out?
118033.e: When CO2 is breathed out, the pH of the blood in the lungs rises. Haemoglobin's affinity for O2 increases, and oxygen is bound more easily.
118033.m: In the lungs, the Bohr effect helps with oxygen uptake.

118034.q: What happens to the pH of the blood when you hyperventilate heavily and breathe out a lot of carbon dioxide?
118034.e: Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid in the blood. When a lot of CO2 is breathed out, this acid is missing and the pH rises. This is called respiratory alkalosis.
118034.m: Hyperventilation makes the blood more alkaline.

118035.q: From roughly what altitude does acute mountain sickness typically occur?
118035.e: Acute mountain sickness usually occurs above about 2500 m, especially when climbing quickly without acclimatising.
118035.m: Above about 2500 m there is a risk of altitude sickness.

118036.q: Which symptom is the most typical key symptom of acute mountain sickness?
118036.e: Headache is the most important sign. Nausea, loss of appetite, tiredness, dizziness and poor sleep are often added.
118036.m: A headache at altitude is a warning sign.

118037.q: What is the life-threatening form called in which fluid builds up in the lungs at altitude?
118037.e: In high-altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE), the high pressure in the lung vessels pushes fluid into the alveoli. Shortness of breath at rest and coughing are typical.
118037.m: Shortness of breath at rest at high altitude can mean pulmonary oedema.

118038.q: Which form of altitude sickness shows itself through unsteady walking and confusion?
118038.e: In high-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE), the brain swells. Unsteady walking (ataxia), confusion and reduced consciousness are alarm signs.
118038.m: Confusion at high altitude is an emergency.

118039.q: What is the most important measure in severe altitude sickness?
a: Taking a longer rest where you are
118039.e: Going down a few hundred metres quickly improves the oxygen supply. Medicines or hyperbaric bags only bridge the time until descent is possible.
118039.m: In severe altitude sickness you must descend immediately.

118040.q: What is the most effective way to prevent acute mountain sickness?
a: A slow ascent with rest days
A fast ascent, to spend little time at the top
Lots of coffee before the ascent
A day of fasting before the tour
118040.e: The body needs time to adapt to the lower oxygen pressure. Medicines such as acetazolamide can also help, but they do not replace a slow ascent.
118040.m: Climbing slowly is the best way to prevent altitude sickness.

118041.q: Why does faster, deeper breathing help the body adapt to high altitude?
a: It brings more oxygen into the lungs
It slows the production of red blood cells
118041.e: At altitude the oxygen pressure of the air is lower. If you breathe more, more oxygen reaches the air sacs. Medicines such as acetazolamide encourage this increased breathing.
118041.m: At altitude, breathing more brings more oxygen into the blood.

118042.q: Above 3000 m, by how much at most should your sleeping altitude rise per day?
118042.e: Common recommendations advise raising your sleeping altitude above 3000 m by no more than 300 to 500 m per day. That gives the body time to adapt.
118042.m: Above 3000 m, raise your sleeping altitude only slowly.

118043.q: Why does a portable hyperbaric bag help in severe altitude sickness?
118043.e: In the inflated bag, the air pressure rises. For the body it is as if it were a few hundred to over a thousand metres lower. This bridges the time until descent.
118043.m: A hyperbaric bag artificially brings the body to a lower altitude.

118044.q: What is it called when the body's tissue gets too little oxygen?
118044.e: Hypoxia means a lack of oxygen in the tissue. Hyperthermia is overheating, hypotension is low blood pressure and hyperglycaemia is blood sugar that is too high.
118044.m: Hypoxia means a lack of oxygen in the tissue.

118045.q: Why can tissue lack oxygen after heavy blood loss, even though you are breathing normally?
a: There are not enough red blood cells to carry it
The lungs no longer take up oxygen
The blood contains too much oxygen
The muscles no longer use oxygen
118045.e: In the blood, oxygen is mainly bound to the haemoglobin of the red blood cells. If many of them are missing, the blood carries too little oxygen despite good breathing.
118045.m: Without enough haemoglobin, the blood lacks the capacity to carry oxygen.

118046.q: Why is cyanide poisoning so dangerous, even though there is enough oxygen in the blood?
a: The cells can no longer use the oxygen
The blood can no longer bind oxygen
The heart beats far too slowly
118046.e: Cyanide blocks an enzyme of cellular respiration in the mitochondria. The oxygen does reach the cells, but cannot be used there to produce energy.
118046.m: In cyanide poisoning, the cells cannot use oxygen.

118047.q: How can you recognise cyanosis when there is a serious lack of oxygen?
a: By red spots on the neck
118047.e: Oxygen-poor haemoglobin is darker than oxygen-rich haemoglobin. If there is a lot of it in the blood, the lips, skin and fingertips look bluish.
118047.m: Cyanosis shows as a blue colour of the skin and lips.

118048.q: Which device measures oxygen saturation on the finger without taking blood?
118048.e: The pulse oximeter shines red and infrared light through the finger. From the different absorption it calculates the saturation.
118048.m: The pulse oximeter measures saturation with light.

118049.q: How does the body adapt to the lack of oxygen after a few weeks at high altitude?
a: It makes more red blood cells
It makes fewer red blood cells
118049.e: When oxygen is short, cells switch on protective programmes, including one for the hormone EPO. As a result, the number of red blood cells rises and the blood can carry more oxygen.
118049.m: At altitude the body makes more red blood cells.

118050.q: Which hormone does the kidney produce more of when oxygen is short?
118050.e: Erythropoietin (EPO) stimulates the production of red blood cells in the bone marrow. This increases the capacity to carry oxygen.
118050.m: When oxygen is short, the kidney makes more erythropoietin.

118051.q: The lungs divert blood from poorly ventilated areas to well ventilated ones. What is the purpose of this?
a: So that as much blood as possible can take up oxygen
So that the lungs need less energy
So that the heart beats more slowly
So that more carbon dioxide stays in the blood
118051.e: Blood flowing through poorly ventilated areas of the lungs hardly takes up any oxygen. That is why the vessels there narrow, and the blood flows to the well ventilated air sacs.
118051.m: Lung vessels narrow where there is a local lack of oxygen.

118052.q: Roughly how large is the anatomical dead space of an adult?
118052.e: In adults the anatomical dead space is about 150 ml. This air does not reach the alveoli.
118052.m: The anatomical dead space holds about 150 millilitres.

118053.q: What is part of the anatomical dead space?
118053.e: The nose, throat, windpipe, bronchi and bronchioles only conduct air. No gas exchange takes place in them.
118053.m: No gas exchange takes place in the conducting airways.

118054.q: What are ventilated alveoli called that receive no blood flow?
118054.e: If alveoli are ventilated but receive no blood, for example in a pulmonary embolism, they take no part in gas exchange. They form the alveolar dead space.
118054.m: Ventilated alveoli without blood flow are alveolar dead space.

118055.q: What does the physiological (functional) dead space consist of?
118055.e: The physiological dead space is the sum of all volumes without gas exchange. In healthy people it is almost the same as the anatomical dead space.
118055.m: The physiological dead space includes anatomical and alveolar dead space.

118056.q: Roughly what share of a normal 500 ml breath does not reach the alveoli?
118056.e: With a 500 ml breath, about 150 ml stays in the conducting airways. That is about a third; only the rest takes part in gas exchange.
118056.m: About a third of a normal breath stays in the dead space.

118057.q: Why is shallow, fast breathing not very effective?
a: A large part of each breath stays in the dead space
The alveoli are destroyed by it
118057.e: With small breaths, the dead space stays the same size but makes up a larger share. Little fresh air is left for the alveoli.
118057.m: Deep breaths are more effective than shallow ones.

118058.q: What does a very long snorkel do when diving?
118058.e: The tube is extra dead space. Exhaled, CO2-rich air is breathed in again, and fresh air reaches the alveoli less well.
118058.m: A snorkel extends the dead space.

118059.q: Why does a pulmonary embolism enlarge the dead space?
a: Ventilated alveoli no longer receive blood
The lungs are no longer ventilated
118059.e: In a pulmonary embolism, a clot blocks a pulmonary artery. The affected alveoli are still ventilated but no longer receive blood, and take no part in gas exchange.
118059.m: A pulmonary embolism creates ventilated alveoli without blood flow.

118060.q: What does vital capacity tell you?
a: The maximum volume you can breathe out after breathing in as far as possible
The volume of a normal breath at rest
The volume that stays in the lungs after breathing out
The amount of air per minute when breathing at rest
118060.e: Vital capacity is the sum of the inspiratory reserve volume, tidal volume and expiratory reserve volume.
118060.m: Vital capacity is the largest movable lung volume.

118061.q: Which lung volume cannot be measured with a simple spirometer?
118061.e: The residual volume stays in the lungs even after breathing out as far as possible. Because it is never breathed out, the spirometer cannot record it.
118061.m: The residual volume always stays in the lungs.

118062.q: What is the volume called that is breathed out in the first second of a forced breath out?
a: Forced expiratory volume in one second
118062.e: The forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) measures how much air you can breathe out forcefully in one second after a deep breath in. It falls when the airways are narrowed.
118062.m: FEV1 shows how fast you can breathe air out.

118063.q: Which spirometry value falls during an asthma attack because the airways are narrowed?
a: The amount of air you can breathe out in one second
118063.e: Air flows more slowly through narrowed bronchi. That is why you can forcefully breathe out less air in the first second.
118063.m: When the airways are narrowed, FEV1 falls.

118064.q: What is typically reduced in pulmonary fibrosis, where the lung tissue becomes stiff?
118064.e: Stiff lung tissue is hard to stretch. That is why you cannot breathe in as deeply and the vital capacity is smaller.
118064.m: A stiff lung has a smaller vital capacity.

118065.q: Roughly how large is an adult's tidal volume at rest?
118065.e: At rest, an adult moves about half a litre of air with each breath.
118065.m: A calm breath is about half a litre.

118066.q: Which simple device do people with asthma use at home to measure their maximum breathing-out flow?
118066.e: The peak flow meter measures the highest flow speed when you breathe out forcefully. Falling values show the airways are narrowing more.
118066.m: With a peak flow meter you check your airways at home.

118067.q: Why do you usually wear a nose clip during spirometry?
a: So that no air escapes through the nose
So that you do not sneeze
So that the nose does not dry out
So that you breathe in faster
118067.e: Only the air that flows through the mouthpiece is measured. If air escaped through the nose, the values would be wrong.
118067.m: During spirometry you breathe only through your mouth.

118068.q: Why do tall people usually have a higher vital capacity than short people?
a: They have a larger chest and larger lungs
They have more red blood cells
118068.e: Lung volumes depend strongly on body height. That is why measured values are always compared with reference values for age, sex and height.
118068.m: Vital capacity depends on body height.

118069.q: What is the most important cause of COPD in Switzerland and in industrialised countries worldwide?
118069.e: Smoking is the most important risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Stopping smoking is the most effective way to keep it from getting worse.
118069.m: Smoking is the main cause of COPD.

118070.q: Which test shows in COPD how much air you can breathe out and how fast?
118070.e: In spirometry you breathe out into a measuring device as hard as you can. In COPD, the amount of air in the first second is reduced compared with the total amount.
118070.m: COPD is detected with a lung function test.

118071.q: Which lung change with destroyed alveolar walls is often part of COPD?
118071.e: In emphysema, alveolar walls break down and large, floppy air sacs form. The exchange surface shrinks, and air gets trapped when breathing out.
118071.m: In emphysema the alveolar walls are destroyed.

118072.q: What does the word “obstructive” mean in the name COPD?
a: The lungs are inflamed and infectious
The lungs have grown too large
The respiratory centre in the brain is disturbed
118072.e: COPD stands for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Obstructive means that the airways are permanently narrowed and air escapes poorly when breathing out.
118072.m: In COPD the airways are permanently narrowed.

118073.q: Which three key symptoms are typical of COPD?
a: Breathlessness, skin rash, loss of appetite
118073.e: Typical of COPD are a chronic cough, sputum and breathlessness, at first during exertion. In German, the initials of these three words form the memory aid AHA.
118073.m: Cough, sputum and breathlessness are typical of COPD.

a: No, but its progress can be slowed
Yes, with a course of antibiotics
Yes, it heals by itself after a few weeks
118074.e: The damage to the bronchi and air sacs does not reverse. Stopping smoking, medicines and exercise training can, however, clearly slow down its progress.
118074.m: COPD cannot be cured, but its course can be slowed.

118075.q: Why do people with severe emphysema take up oxygen less well?
a: The exchange surface of the air sacs is smaller
Their blood no longer contains haemoglobin
118075.e: In emphysema, many small air sacs merge into large bubbles. This shrinks the surface through which oxygen enters the blood.
118075.m: Emphysema reduces the exchange surface of the lungs.

118076.q: Which breathing technique helps people with COPD stop the bronchi from collapsing when breathing out?
118076.e: In pursed-lip breathing, you breathe out against slightly closed lips. The back pressure keeps the floppy small airways open.
118076.m: Pursed-lip breathing keeps the airways open when breathing out.

118077.q: What happens in the lung tissue in pulmonary fibrosis?
a: Air bubbles form in the pleura
118077.e: In pulmonary fibrosis, the framework of the lungs scars. The tissue becomes stiff and gas exchange gets worse.
118077.m: In pulmonary fibrosis the lungs scar.

118078.q: What can today's medicines achieve against idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
118078.e: Antifibrotic drugs such as pirfenidone and nintedanib slow down the scarring, but cannot cure it. In severe cases, a lung transplant remains an option.
118078.m: Medicines slow pulmonary fibrosis but do not cure it.

118079.q: Which pulmonary fibrosis is caused by breathing in asbestos fibres?
118079.e: Inhaled asbestos fibres cause scarring of the lungs, called asbestosis. In Switzerland asbestos has been banned since 1990.
118079.m: Asbestos fibres can make the lungs scar.

118080.q: Which dust causes silicosis, a typical occupational disease of miners?
118080.e: Silicosis is caused by breathing in crystalline silicon dioxide (quartz), for example in tunnel building or in quarries.

118081.q: Why do people with pulmonary fibrosis find it especially hard to breathe in deeply?
a: The scarred lung tissue is stiff
The bronchi are blocked with mucus
The lungs are overinflated with air
118081.e: Scar tissue stretches poorly, so the lungs expand less well. When listening with a stethoscope, you often hear fine crackles at the end of breathing in.
118081.m: A scarred lung is stiff and hard to stretch.

118082.q: Which measured value is typically reduced in pulmonary fibrosis because the exchange membrane is thickened?
118082.e: The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) measures how well gas passes through the alveolar wall. It falls when the tissue is thickened.
118082.m: In pulmonary fibrosis the diffusing capacity falls.

118083.q: Which examination shows the scarring pattern of pulmonary fibrosis best?
a: A CT scan of the lungs
118083.e: In high-resolution CT, advanced fibrosis shows small cysts that look like a honeycomb.
118083.m: A CT scan shows the scars of pulmonary fibrosis.

118084.q: Besides inhaled dust, what else can cause pulmonary fibrosis?
a: Certain medicines, for example against cancer
118084.e: Some drugs, for example the cancer medicine bleomycin, can damage lung tissue. Radiation and autoimmune diseases can also cause fibrosis.
118084.m: Medicines can also cause pulmonary fibrosis.

118085.q: What is the minute ventilation with a tidal volume of 0.5 l and 12 breaths per minute?
118085.e: Minute ventilation is tidal volume times breathing rate. 0.5 l times 12 per minute gives 6 l/min.
118085.m: Minute ventilation is tidal volume times breathing rate.

118086.q: What is the alveolar ventilation with a tidal volume of 500 ml, a dead space of 150 ml and 14 breaths per minute?
118086.e: With each breath, 500 ml minus 150 ml, so 350 ml, reaches the alveoli. 350 ml times 14 gives 4900 ml, or 4.9 l/min.
118086.m: Alveolar ventilation only counts the air beyond the dead space.

118087.q: Which acid-base disorder is caused by hyperventilation?
118087.e: When you hyperventilate, too much CO2 is breathed out. The CO2 partial pressure falls, and the pH of the blood rises.
118087.m: Hyperventilation makes the blood more alkaline.

118088.q: What happens to the CO2 in the blood if someone breathes too shallowly and too slowly for a long time?
a: It builds up, and the blood becomes more acidic
It decreases, and the blood becomes more alkaline
It stays the same, only the oxygen falls
It decreases, and the blood becomes more acidic
118088.e: If too little is breathed out, CO2 stays in the blood. This forms carbonic acid, and the pH of the blood falls.
118088.m: If you breathe too little, CO2 builds up and the blood becomes more acidic.

118089.q: Roughly how much air does an adult breathe in and out per minute at rest?
118089.e: At rest, each breath is about 0.5 litres, with around 12 to 16 breaths per minute. That gives about 6 to 8 litres per minute.
118089.m: At rest you breathe about 6 to 8 litres of air per minute.

118090.q: Where in the lungs does gas exchange between the air and the blood take place?
118090.e: The air sacs have very thin walls and are surrounded by fine capillaries. There the gases pass back and forth between air and blood.
118090.m: Gas exchange happens in the air sacs.

118091.q: What happens during gas exchange in the air sacs?
a: Oxygen goes into the blood, CO2 into the air
CO2 goes into the blood, oxygen into the air
Nitrogen goes into the blood, oxygen stays in the air
Water goes into the blood, CO2 stays in the blood
118091.e: By diffusion, each gas moves to where its concentration is lower. That is how oxygen gets into the blood and CO2 into the air you breathe out.
118091.m: In the air sacs, oxygen and CO2 swap places by diffusion.

118092.q: Which device takes over breathing in intensive care when someone can no longer breathe enough on their own?
118092.e: A ventilator blows air with oxygen into the lungs. A defibrillator gives electric shocks to the heart, a dialysis machine replaces the kidney.
118092.m: A ventilator helps when your own breathing is not enough.

118093.q: Which formula do you use to calculate hydrostatic pressure in a liquid at rest?
118093.e: The pressure increases with the density ρ of the liquid, the gravitational acceleration g and the depth h below the surface.
118093.m: Hydrostatic pressure is the product of density, gravitational acceleration and depth.

118094.q: What is the hydrostatic pressure at a water depth of 3 m (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118094.e: p = 1000 kg/m³ · 9.81 m/s² · 3 m = 29,430 Pa, so about 29.4 kPa.
118094.m: Water pressure increases with every metre of depth.

118095.q: Roughly what is the hydrostatic pressure at the deepest point of Lake Zurich (136 m, g = 9.81 m/s²), not counting air pressure?
118095.e: p = 1000 kg/m³ · 9.81 m/s² · 136 m ≈ 1,334,000 Pa. That is about 13.3 bar.
118095.m: At the bottom of deep lakes the pressure is many bar.

118096.q: What is the hydrostatic pressure 20 m deep in the sea (ρ = 1025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118096.e: p = 1025 kg/m³ · 9.81 m/s² · 20 m = 201,105 Pa, so about 201 kPa.
118096.m: In denser seawater, pressure rises with depth a little faster than in fresh water.

118097.q: What is the hydrostatic pressure at the bottom of a mercury column 0.5 m high (ρ = 13,546 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118097.e: p = 13,546 kg/m³ · 9.81 m/s² · 0.5 m ≈ 66,443 Pa, so about 66 kPa.
118097.m: A dense liquid produces high pressure even at a small height.

118098.q: What is the density of a liquid if the hydrostatic pressure 2 m deep is 15.7 kPa (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118098.e: ρ = p / (g·h) = 15,700 Pa / (9.81 m/s² · 2 m) ≈ 800 kg/m³. That roughly matches ethanol.
118098.m: You can calculate the density of a liquid from pressure and depth.

118099.q: At what water depth is the hydrostatic pressure 50 kPa (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
118099.m: The depth is pressure divided by density times gravitational acceleration.

118100.q: What is the hydrostatic pressure right at the surface of a liquid at rest?
a: The same as at the bottom
Half as much as at the bottom
118100.e: There is no column of liquid above the surface, so h is 0. Only the outside air pressure acts there.
118100.m: Hydrostatic pressure starts at zero at the surface.

118101.q: What is the hydrostatic pressure in the Challenger Deep (about 10,935 m), calculated with ρ = 1025 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s²?
118101.e: p = 1025 kg/m³ · 9.81 m/s² · 10,935 m ≈ 1.1 · 10⁸ Pa, so about 1100 bar.
118101.m: In the deep sea the pressure is over a thousand bar.

118102.q: What causes the gravitational pressure in a liquid?
a: The weight of the liquid above
The movement of the molecules alone
118102.e: Each layer of liquid carries the weight of all the layers above it. The deeper you are, the greater this weight per area.
118102.m: Gravitational pressure comes from the weight of the liquid above.

118103.q: Which value is the standard air pressure at sea level?
118103.e: Standard atmospheric pressure is set at 101,325 Pa, which is 1013.25 hPa.

118104.q: How high is the mercury column of a barometer at standard pressure?
118104.e: Air pressure balances a mercury column about 760 mm high. That is where the unit mmHg comes from.
118104.m: Standard pressure holds up about 760 millimetres of mercury.

118105.q: Why can a suction pump lift water by at most about 10 m?
a: Air pressure can hold up a water column of at most about 10 m
The pump gets too hot at greater heights
The water turns to ice higher up
The pipes burst at greater heights
118105.e: A suction pump only creates low pressure. The water is pushed up by the outside air pressure, and this can balance a water column of at most about 10 m.
118105.m: A suction pump can only lift water about ten metres.

118106.q: What is one pascal equal to?
118106.e: Pressure is force per area. One pascal is a force of 1 N acting on 1 m².
118106.m: One pascal is one newton per square metre.

118107.q: Who showed the force of air pressure with the Magdeburg hemispheres?
118107.e: Otto von Guericke pumped the air out of two hemispheres placed together. Afterwards not even teams of horses could pull them apart.
118107.m: Otto von Guericke proved the force of air pressure with hemispheres.

118108.q: Which scientist invented the mercury barometer?
118108.e: Around 1643 the Italian Evangelista Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury and stood it upside down in a dish. The height of the column showed the air pressure.
